Decoding speed is 3.5–4.4× faster than AR. Diffusion enables any-order infill: radiologists can fix fragments and the model fills the text between them, a capability absent in AR.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion-based medical language models can achieve parity or superiority to AR models while offering practical drafting advantages via bidirectional denoising. This supports broader use of diffusion LMs in clinical reporting and suggests efficiency and usability gains for medical NLP tasks.

title: SE(2) Navigation Mesh
summary: Global navigation for ground robots in complex multi-level environments requires representations that accurately capture traversable regions while enabling efficient path planning. Current approaches present key limitations: Point clouds and volumetric occupancy maps lack explicit surface structure for traversability estimation, whereas direct pathfinding on dense triangle meshes is computationally prohibitive. Navigation meshes mitigate these challenges through polygonal abstraction of the underlying mesh, but assume yaw-invariant traversability, rendering them unsuitable for non-circular robots in constrained spaces. We propose SE(2) Navigation Mesh (SE(2) NavMesh), a polygonal representation of traversable regions that encodes yaw-dependent traversability. Our method evaluates traversability using footprint masks and constructs a graph over yaw-specific layers with explicit translational and rotational connectivity. Grounded in this representation, we develop an A*-String Pulling-A* (ASA) pathfinding strategy that hierarchically optimizes robot position and heading. We also present an online method that incrementally updates the SE(2) NavMesh from streaming point clouds during concurrent geometry reconstruction. In simulation, the SE(2) NavMesh captures over 50% more traversable area than classical NavMeshes, and the SE(2) NavMesh + ASA pipeline consistently outperforms sampling-based baselines in constrained environments. Extensive real-world experiments on a physical robot validate real-time online generation and successful navigation across multiple environments.

AI.tldr: Introduces SE(2) NavMesh: a yaw-aware polygonal representation for traversable regions, enabling efficient path planning for non-circular robots in multi-level environments; uses footprint masks, yaw-layer graphs, and ASA (A*-String Pulling-A*) with online updates from streaming point clouds; achieves >50% more traversable area in simulation and real-time navigation in experiments.
AI.motivation: Limitations of existing representations: point clouds/occupancy lack explicit traversable surface structure; dense meshes are computationally heavy; conventional NavMeshes assume yaw-invariant traversability, unsuitable for constrained spaces and non-circular robots. Need yaw-dependent, translational-rotational connectivity for SE(2) planning.
AI.method: Define SE(2) NavMesh as a polygonal, yaw-dependent traversable region representation. Evaluate traversability via footprint masks for different yaw angles. Build a multi-layer graph across yaw discretizations with translational and rotational connections. Develop ASA, a hierarchical planner that interleaves A*-style optimization with string-pulling for efficient heading adjustments. Provide an online incremental update mechanism to adapt the NavMesh from streaming point clouds during concurrent geometry reconstruction.
AI.result: Simulation shows SE(2) NavMesh captures >50% more traversable area than classical NavMeshes. The SE(2) NavMesh + ASA dominates sampling-based baselines in constrained environments. Real-world experiments demonstrate real-time online generation and successful navigation across multiple environments.
AI.conclusion: SE(2) NavMesh effectively encodes yaw-dependent traversability, enabling efficient SE(2) planning for constrained, multi-level environments. The approach improves traversable-area coverage and navigation performance and is validated in simulation and on physical robots with online updates.

title: A Novel Machine Learning Approach for Central Nervous System Tumor Classification from DNA Methylation
summary: NA methylation profiling has become a powerful approach for central nervous system (CNS) tumor classification, yet important challenges remain regarding cross-cohort transferability, methodological correctness, and robust multiclass evaluation. In this work, we propose a novel and methodologically rigorous machine-learning approach for methylation-based CNS tumor classification that combines Sparse Random Projection for dimensionality reduction with multinomial logistic regression for classification. We evaluate the proposed approach in the same general experimental setting established by a widely used reference classifier. On the 2,801-sample reference cohort, our method achieves a mean accuracy of 96\% under stratified 3-fold cross-validation. On the independent 1,104-sample clinical evaluation cohort, it reaches 86\% accuracy at the 91-class level and 93\% when predictions are evaluated at the methylation class family level. These results improve upon the corresponding state-of-the-art reference figures of 82\% class-level concordance and 88\% family-level concordance, yielding absolute gains of approximately 4 and 5 percentage points, respectively. This improvement is clinically relevant: in a diagnostic setting, a 5-point increase in correct tumor classification can directly affect cancer subtype assignment and, in turn, influence treatment selection and downstream clinical decision-making. Our results show that the proposed model, grounded in stronger methodological practice in machine learning, consistently outperforms the previous state of the art across evaluation settings and can materially improve the reliability of CNS tumor classification.

AI.tldr: A novel machine-learning approach for CNS tumor methylation classification using Sparse Random Projection for dimensionality reduction and multinomial logistic regression, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy and cross-cohort robustness.
AI.motivation: To improve cross-cohort transferability, methodological correctness, and robust multiclass evaluation in methylation-based CNS tumor classification, addressing gaps in previous work.
AI.method: Dimensionality reduction via Sparse Random Projection followed by multinomial logistic regression. Evaluation mirrors a reference classifier: 2,801-sample reference cohort with stratified 3-fold CV (96% mean accuracy), and an independent 1,104-sample clinical cohort (86% accuracy at 91-class level, 93% at methylation class family level). Comparison against state-of-the-art reference figures.
AI.result: Reference cohort: 96% mean accuracy under stratified 3-fold CV. Independent cohort: 86% accuracy at 91-class level; 93% at family level. Improvements over prior figures of 82% class-level and 88% family-level, corresponding to ~4 and ~5 percentage point gains.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method achieves consistent, clinically relevant improvements over the previous state of the art and demonstrates methodological rigor, suggesting enhanced reliability for CNS tumor classification in clinical settings.

title: Rethinking Generic Object Tracking Toward Human-Level Perceptual Intelligence
comment: Ph.D. dissertation, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, 2026. arXiv admin note: substantial text overlap with arXiv:2602.14771
summary: At the heart of human visual perception lies the ability to maintain a continuous and coherent understanding of the external world. By integrating observations with accumulated experience, the human visual system can continuously adapt to variations in both the target and its surrounding environment, while preserving robust visual continuity as scene dynamics evolve. Human vision can therefore integrate prior knowledge, spatial geometry, and semantic context to understand complex scenes and their changes. As a core problem in computer vision, visual object tracking aims to bring machine perception closer to human visual perception. These capabilities are central to the task of Generic Object Tracking (GOT). In this task, a visual tracker is initialized only with the bounding box of an arbitrarily specified target in the first frame, and must continuously localize the target in subsequent dynamic visual streams. However, future events, observations, and real-world variations are inherently unpredictable; therefore, the model's generalization and online adaptation capabilities remain bottlenecks. Tracking reliability can deteriorate when the target undergoes severe deformation, is affected by complex distractors, encounters significant environmental changes, or belongs to a category unseen during training. This dissertation aims to narrow the gap between machine visual tracking systems and human visual perception by proposing a series of methods that systematically enhance the target discrimination, robust adaptation, and geometric reasoning capabilities of tracking models.

AI.tldr: Proposes a series of methods to enhance Generic Object Tracking by improving target discrimination, robust online adaptation, and geometric reasoning to bridge the gap between machine tracking and human visual perception.
AI.motivation: Motivated by how human vision integrates observations, experience, and semantic context to achieve robust, continuous tracking; GOT faces generalization and adaptation bottlenecks under deformation, distractors, environmental changes, and unseen categories.
AI.method: Presents a suite of methods that systematically enhance discrimination, robust adaptation, and geometric reasoning in tracking models. (No specific techniques are detailed in the abstract.)
AI.result: Claims that these methods will strengthen target discrimination, adaptation, and geometry-aware reasoning, leading to improved robustness in challenging scenarios and closer alignment with human perception.
AI.conclusion: The work aims to narrow the gap between machine tracking and human visual perception by advancing GOT through means that improve discrimination, adaptation, and geometric reasoning.

title: Beyond Next-Token Prediction: An RLVR Proof of Concept for Tool-Use Agents on Atlassian Workflows
summary: Large language models are trained to predict the next token, not to act inside a specific API. In niche enterprise SaaS workflows -- where success means hitting the right endpoint with the right nested arguments in the right order -- this objective mismatch shows up as silent failures: dropped required fields, hallucinated tools, or early stops after a single read. We ask whether Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), applied directly in the target environment, closes the gap. As a proof of concept we build a suite of five synthetic environments emulating the Jira REST v3 and Confluence v2 APIs at schema fidelity; rewards are computed entirely from the tool-call trace, with no live API, no learned judge, and no human label in the loop. Scoring prompted Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3.5-4B on the same checkers that drive GRPO training, we find that on the four scenarios whose rewards are non-degenerate the RL-trained policy lifts average reward from a 4B-baseline range of 0.35--0.92 to 0.95--1.00, with the largest single gain on Confluence page creation ($0.35 \rightarrow 1.00$). We position this as a preliminary step toward outcome-optimised small models for niche enterprise APIs, and foreground two limitations a workshop reader should weigh: hand-crafting verifiable rewards does not scale beyond the handful of endpoints reported here, and one of our five scenarios (ticket-transition) has a saturating reward shape that the prompted 4B already maxes out.

AI.tldr: RLVR (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards) applied to synthetic enterprise API environments can improve policy performance over a 4B baseline in several Jira/Confluence-like tasks, improving end-to-end outcomes; however, rewards are handcrafted and one scenario shows saturation where a strong baseline already maxes out.
AI.motivation: Address the objective mismatch of LLMs trained to predict next tokens when the goal is correct API action with proper arguments and order in niche enterprise workflows; demonstrate a verifiable, environment-driven RL signal to align actions with outcomes.
AI.method: Create five synthetic environments emulating Jira REST v3 and Confluence v2 APIs with full schema fidelity; compute rewards solely from the tool-call trace (no live API, no learned judge, no human labeling); evaluate and compare RL-trained policies against a 4B baseline by prompting Qwen models and using checkers used in GRPO training.
AI.result: In non-degenerate reward scenarios, RLVR raises average reward from a 4B baseline of ~0.35–0.92 to ~0.95–1.00; largest gain observed in Confluence page creation (0.35 -> 1.00). Overall four of five scenarios show improved rewards.
AI.conclusion: RLVR is a promising preliminary step toward outcome-optimized small models for niche enterprise APIs; limitations include the scalability challenge of hand-crafted rewards and a saturating reward shape in one scenario where a strong 4B prompt already maxes out.

title: A Reconfigurable Rocker-Bogie Robot for High Step Climbing and Turning
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the IEEE/ASME International Conference on Advanced Intelligent Mechatronics (AIM 2026)
summary: This study proposes a reconfigurable rocker-bogie mechanism that achieves efficient turning motion with a small number of actuators while maintaining high step-climbing capability. By installing motors at the bogie joints and actively swinging up and down bogies, the system enables switching between four-wheel and six-wheel configurations. Omnidirectional wheels are mounted on the rear ends of the rockers, allowing smooth turning in the four-wheel configuration based on a differential-drive model. Experimental evaluation using a prototype robot demonstrated that the proposed mechanism achieves zero-radius turning at a speed more than five times that of a conventional rocker-bogie mechanism equipped with six non-steerable grip wheels, while requiring only approximately 17% of the total average wheel torque. In addition, the robot successfully climbed a 40 cm step with an average climbing time of 6.4 s, confirming its high turning and step-climbing performance.

AI.tldr: A reconfigurable four- to six-wheel rocker-bogie rover with actuated bogies and rear omnidirectional wheels enables zero-radius turning and efficient step-climbing; prototype reports >5× turning speed vs conventional and ~17% wheel torque, plus 40 cm step climb in 6.4 s.
AI.motivation: Improve turning agility and step-climbing while reducing actuator load and hardware count in rough-terrain rovers or planetary exploration robots.
AI.method: Install motors at bogie joints to actively swing bogies and switch between 4W and 6W; mount omnidirectional wheels on rear rocker ends to enable differential-drive turning in 4W; validate with prototype experiments comparing turning speed/torque and climbing performance.
AI.result: Achieves zero-radius turning at speeds more than five times that of a conventional six-non-steerable-wheel rocker-bogie, while using only ~17% of the total wheel torque; climbs a 40 cm step with average climbing time 6.4 s.
AI.conclusion: The reconfigurable rocker-bogie with actuated bogies and rear omnidirectional wheels delivers superior maneuverability and climbing ability with substantially lower actuation requirements, offering potential energy and actuator savings for rough-terrain robots.

title: From Approximation to Emergence: A Theory of Deep Learning
summary: Deep learning has outgrown any single mathematical explanation. From Approximation to Emergence develops a unified, proof-oriented account of modern deep learning theory, tracing a path from the classical foundations of approximation, optimization, and generalization to the contemporary mechanisms of overparameterization, robustness, generative modeling, transformers, in-context learning, scaling laws, interpretability, alignment, and emergence. Rather than presenting isolated results, the book organizes a broad literature into a coherent research narrative: each theory is examined through the object it controls, the assumptions that make it valid, and the phenomena it leaves unexplained. Written for researchers, graduate students, and mathematically trained practitioners, this monograph offers a rigorous map of deep learning theory as it stands today: powerful, incomplete, and increasingly centered on the question of how learned mechanisms arise from scale, data, architecture, and training.

AI.tldr: Unified, proof-oriented map of modern deep learning theory from classical foundations to emergent phenomena, organizing literature into a coherent narrative around control objects, assumptions, and unexplained phenomena.
AI.motivation: To provide researchers with a rigorous, coherent framework linking approximation, optimization, generalization, overparameterization, robustness, scaling, alignment, and emergence; addressing fragmentation in the literature.
AI.method: Organizes theories by the object they control, states the assumptions, and identifies gaps; synthesizes across topics into a narrative; emphasizes scale, data, architecture, and training as drivers of learned mechanisms.
AI.result: Produces a comprehensive framework that connects classical foundations to contemporary phenomena, useful as a map of the field; claims to be rigorous, but acknowledges incompleteness and open questions.
AI.conclusion: Offers a rigorous, albeit partial, roadmap for understanding how mechanisms arise in deep learning; aimed at researchers, grad students, and mathematically oriented practitioners.

title: Computer Vision for Wildlife Monitoring: Detecting Brown Howler Monkeys using YOLO
comment: Accepted on International Conference on Computer Animation, Social Agents, and Extended Reality '26 (CASAXR 26)
summary: Urban expansion threatens global biodiversity, especially affecting arboreal species due to the fragmentation of forest habitats. The movement of arboreal species across disjointed forest patches increases mortality risk and, thus, compromises their conservation. In this context, the installation of canopy bridges can be a viable strategy; yet continuous monitoring of their use by arboreal species is essential for ensuring their effectiveness, typically carried out with the aid of camera traps. However, this method often produces false-positive images that demand time from conservationists for review. In this context, computer vision algorithms can optimize the task of detecting target species using the canopy bridges. In this study, we explored the automatic detection of brown howler monkeys (Alouatta guariba) in videos obtained by camera traps. Given the need for a large number of annotated images of the target animals to train the algorithms, we tested the incorporation of auxiliary data to improve detection models, fine-tuning the YOLOv10 framework using varying proportions of them. The improvement of these automatic detection techniques contributes to conservation efforts, by providing automatic tools to monitor solutions that minimize the impact of human interference in animals habitats.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning YOLOv10 with auxiliary data improves automatic detection of brown howler monkeys in camera-trap videos, aiding canopy-bridge monitoring for conservation.
AI.motivation: Urban expansion fragments forests, increasing arboreal mortality; canopy bridges require monitoring to ensure effectiveness; camera traps generate many false positives, necessitating automation to reduce reviewer workload and improve data quality for arboreal conservation.
AI.method: Experimentally fine-tune the YOLOv10 detector on camera-trap frames, incorporating varying proportions of auxiliary data to augment training, and assess detection performance.
AI.result: Auxiliary data enhanced detection performance; gains depend on the amount of auxiliary data used, indicating promise for more scalable monitoring.
AI.conclusion: Using YOLOv10 with auxiliary data provides a viable automated tool for monitoring canopy-bridge use by arboreal species, supporting conservation by reducing manual review and enabling scalable data collection.

title: World Feedback for Clinical Agents: Diagnosing RL in FHIR Environments
summary: Clinical protocol-execution tasks -- checking a lab value, applying a threshold, placing a correctly structured FHIR order -- are natural candidates for RL from world feedback: once clinical SMEs encode decision logic into a verifier, that verifier grades unlimited rollouts without per-episode annotation. But applying RL requires a sound feedback channel and sufficient base capability. We audit MedAgentBench v1/v2, find a 41.7\% silent-finish ceiling that makes inaction the RL dominant strategy, and construct \textbf{MedAgentBench-v3 (MAB-v3)} (508 tasks, 8.9\% ceiling). Training Qwen3-8B exposes two structural barriers: a \emph{capability ceiling} (10/20 task types have 0\% base performance, zero gradient) and a \emph{format-knowledge barrier} (3/20 types require exact clinical codes undiscoverable by exploration). Pure RL reaches 18.2\% pass@1 vs.\ 34.1\% for rule-based SFT; the 15.9~pp gap is attributable entirely to these barriers. A decision/format-knowledge/lookup taxonomy predicts RL learnability and prescribes the fix: SFT to inject codes, RL to learn conditionals.

AI.tldr: RL for clinical protocol-execution tasks suffers from ceiling effects and format-knowledge barriers; MAB-v3 improves ceilings but RL still lags SFT; a taxonomy suggests a hybrid approach (SFT for code injection, RL for conditionals).
AI.motivation: Assess viability of reinforcement learning for clinical protocol-execution tasks, diagnose bottlenecks in existing benchmarks, and propose design principles to enhance learnability and performance.
AI.method: Audit MedAgentBench v1/v2 to identify a silent-finish ceiling; construct MedAgentBench-v3 (MAB-v3) with 508 tasks; evaluate base capabilities; train Qwen3-8B to uncover barriers; compare pure RL to rule-based SFT; develop a decision/format-knowledge/lookup taxonomy and prescribe fixes.
AI.result: Identified a 41.7% silent-finish ceiling in MAB v1/v2; MAB-v3 reduces ceiling to 8.9%; pure RL attains 18.2% pass@1, while rule-based SFT reaches 34.1% (gap 15.9 percentage points). The gap is attributed entirely to two barriers: a capability ceiling (10/20 task types have 0% base performance, zero gradient) and a format-knowledge barrier (3/20 types require exact clinical codes not discoverable by exploration). A taxonomy predicts RL learnability and prescribes injecting codes via SFT and using RL to learn conditionals.
AI.conclusion: RL learnability in clinical protocol tasks is limited by explicit capabilities and coding-format constraints. A hybrid approach—injecting codes with supervised fine-tuning and delegating conditional reasoning to RL—addresses the identified barriers. The decision/format-knowledge/lookup taxonomy offers a predictive framework for when RL is viable and how to fix bottlenecks.

title: Multi-Rate Nonlinear Model Predictive Control for Wall-Supported Bipedal Locomotion of Quadrupedal Robots
summary: This paper presents a novel layered planning and control framework based on multi-rate nonlinear model predictive control (MR-NMPC) that enables quadrupedal robots to perform hybrid bipedal locomotion with wall-assisted support in constrained environments. Real-time trajectory optimization for this locomotion presents significant challenges, as the controller must simultaneously plan for both the contact points and the continuous trajectories of the robot's center of mass (CoM) and orientation within the robot's nonlinear dynamics while accounting for unilateral contact constraints, underactuation, and the switching nature of the robot's dynamics. At the high level of the control framework, an MR-NMPC is proposed, which dynamically plans both the discrete-time trajectories of the contact points and the continuous-time trajectories of the CoM and orientation, using a single rigid body (SRB) dynamics model. By incorporating contact-point planning within the multi-rate optimal control framework, this approach enhances dynamic stability compared to heuristic foot placement strategies. At the low level of the control framework, a nonlinear whole-body controller (WBC) based on virtual constraints and a quadratic program enforces full-order dynamics and tracks the MR-NMPC references. The proposed approach is validated through extensive numerical simulations demonstrating the robust wall-assisted bipedal locomotion of a Unitree A1 quadrupedal robot on rough terrains and under external disturbances in a constrained environment. Comparative analysis shows that the proposed MR-NMPC achieves a 2.9 times higher success rate compared to conventional MPC with heuristic-based foot placement strategies in negotiating irregular terrain at high speeds.

AI.tldr: Layered MR-NMPC-based framework for wall-assisted hybrid bipedal locomotion in constrained environments, integrating discrete contact planning with continuous CoM/orientation trajectories using a single rigid body model; superior dynamic stability and robustness.
AI.motivation: Enable fast, robust quadruped locomotion with wall-assisted support in constrained/uneven environments by jointly planning contact points and continuous dynamics under unilateral constraints and switching dynamics.
AI.method: High-level multi-rate NMPC planning discrete contact trajectories and continuous CoM/orientation using an SRB dynamics model; low-level nonlinear WBC with virtual constraints and a QP to enforce full-order dynamics and track MR-NMPC references.
AI.result: Extensive numerical simulations on a Unitree A1 showing robust wall-assisted bipedal locomotion on rough terrain and under disturbances; MR-NMPC achieves 2.9x higher success rate than conventional MPC with heuristic foot placement on irregular terrain at high speeds.
AI.conclusion: MR-NMPC with integrated contact planning enhances dynamic stability and performance for constrained, hybrid locomotion; effective in handling underactuation and unilateral contacts and can outperform heuristic planning strategies.

title: Black-Box Inference of LLM Architectural Properties with Restrictive API Access
summary: In practice, most commercial LLM providers do not publicly release details of underlying LLM architectures. However, prior work has shown that given limited API access to an LLM (namely, top-$k$ logits and/or a logit bias function), one can recover certain architectural details of an LLM, such as the hidden dimension of the feed-forward network. Perhaps in response to these results, most commercial LLM providers have restricted their APIs to expose only the single logit for each decoded token, and they no longer give users the ability to bias logits. We show that even under current restrictive APIs, several architectural parameters are still recoverable. We present NightVision, an attack that uses restrictive black-box API access to estimate the hidden dimension, depth, and parameter count of an LLM. Algorithmically, NightVision relies on a novel common set prompting technique in which multiple prompts expose log probabilities for the same set of output tokens; a spectral analysis of these results is used to infer hidden dimension. NightVision additionally uses end-to-end time to first token (TTFT) measurements and the estimated hidden dimension to estimate depth and parameter count. We empirically evaluate NightVision on 32 open-source LLMs, recovering hidden dimension to within 23% average relative error across all models (9% on MoE models), and depth and parameter count to within 53% for models exceeding three billion parameters. We run extensive ablations to demonstrate how these accuracies scale with token budget and model properties. Overall, our results suggest that current LLM APIs are not sufficiently restricted to fully obfuscate the architectural details of their underlying models.

AI.tldr: NightVision uses black-box API access to infer LLM architecture (hidden dimension, depth, parameter count) via log-probability prompts and timing measurements; achieves nontrivial accuracy on 32 open-source LLMs.
AI.motivation: Motivated by prior work showing architecture leakage with limited API access and the risk that restricted APIs still reveal model details; highlights need for protecting architectural information.
AI.method: Employs common prompting to elicit log probabilities for the same output tokens, performs spectral analysis on these logs to infer hidden dimension, and uses end-to-end time-to-first-token (TTFT) measurements along with the hidden-dimension estimate to infer depth and total parameter count.
AI.result: Empirically evaluated on 32 open-source LLMs; hidden dimension estimated with 23% average relative error (9% on Mixture-of-Experts models); depth and parameter count estimated within 53% for models larger than 3B parameters; extensive ablations show scaling with token budget and model properties.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM APIs are not sufficiently restricted to fully obfuscate architectural details; practical risk of architectural leakage persists under restrictive APIs, motivating stronger API-side defenses.

title: Beyond Heatmaps: Unsupervised Concept-Graph Reasoning for Interpretable Visual Explanation
comment: Accepted at the IJCAI-ECAI 2026 Workshop on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), Bremen, Germany. 7 pages, 4 figures
summary: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) provide an intrinsically interpretable alternative to post-hoc explanations. However, existing CBMs often rely on predefined concept vocabularies or supervised annotations, lack explicit concept grounding, and summarize each concept with a single image-level score -- discarding spatial recurrence and inter-concept dependencies. We propose a Graph-based Concept Bottleneck Model (G-CBM), an intrinsically interpretable framework that performs unsupervised concept discovery via Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) and represents the discovered concepts as nodes in a per-image concept-graph representation. G-CBM matches region-level features to these concept nodes -- providing concept grounding and capturing concept recurrence across the image -- and applies a \emph{tunable concept filtering threshold} $τ$ to suppress weak region-level features. A Graph Attention Network (GAT) then performs concept-level reasoning by modeling nonlinear dependencies across nodes. Across ImageNet, HAM10000, PH2, and Derm7pt, G-CBM achieves an average relative AUC improvement of 3.7\% over a ResNet-50 baseline. Concept filtering frequently improves predictive performance while inducing selective concept use, achieving peak AUC of $0.96$ on PH2 with only 2 of 10 concepts and 0.92 on HAM10000 with 3.8 of 9 concepts. On dermoscopy benchmarks, G-CBM is competitive with supervised approaches requiring external annotations. Deletion/insertion analyses with random ablation controls show that the learned concept ranking faithfully reflects model predictions.

AI.tldr: A Graph-based Concept Bottleneck Model (G-CBM) uses unsupervised NMF-derived concepts and per-image concept graphs with a GAT to enable grounded, recurrent, and interpretable concept reasoning; achieves 3.7% relative AUC gain over ResNet-50 across ImageNet and dermoscopy datasets, with selective concept use and competitive performance with supervised approaches.
AI.motivation: Overcomes limitations of traditional CBMs that rely on predefined vocabularies and lack explicit grounding and inter-concept relations; aims to capture spatial recurrence and dependencies among concepts and improve interpretability.
AI.method: Discover concepts via Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) in an unsupervised fashion; represent discovered concepts as nodes in a per-image concept-graph; map region-level features to concept nodes to ground concepts; apply a tunable threshold τ to filter weak region features; use a Graph Attention Network to model nonlinear dependencies among concept nodes for final prediction; train and evaluate on ImageNet, HAM10000, PH2, Derm7pt; analyze via deletion/insertion.
AI.result: Average relative AUC improvement of 3.7% over a ResNet-50 baseline; concept filtering improves performance with peak AUC up to 0.96 on PH2 using only 2 of 10 concepts, and 0.92 on HAM10000 with 3.8 of 9 concepts; competitive with supervised approaches on dermoscopy datasets; deletion/insertion analyses show the concept ranking aligns with model predictions.
AI.conclusion: G-CBM demonstrates that unsupervised concept discovery plus graph-based reasoning yields interpretable, grounded, and competitive performance, with selective concept use boosting accuracy and maintaining interpretability; supports the utility of per-image concept graphs for reasoning about concept dependencies and recurrence.

title: Procedural Memory Distillation: Online Reflection for Self-Improving Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), along with recent selfdistillation variants such as SDPO, evaluates each rollout against a verifier and updates the policy from that episode-level signal. However, the richer procedural information in the rollout is rarely retained or reused. Across episodes and epochs, the model repeatedly encounters related problems under a changing policy, producing cross-episode signals that episode-local updates cannot capture: which strategies consistently pass verification, which failure modes persist, which patterns recur. We propose Procedural Memory Distillation (PMD), which converts these crossepisode signals into reusable procedural memory and distills it into the policy's weights during training. This memory functions as a training scaffold, absorbed into the policy itself, yielding a memory-free model at inference. PMD organizes the memory at three levels of abstraction: raw trajectories, self-reflected strategies and lessons, and higher-level behavioral patterns that recur across problems, all extracted online from the model's own trajectories. A memory-conditioned self-teacher draws on the accumulated experience to supervise the student on its own rollouts, enabling student to progressively internalize procedural knowledge within its parameters. The central design principle is co-evolution: the policy generates rollouts that update the memory, and memory shapes the supervision that updates the policy. Empirically, across Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B, PMD improves over SDPO by 3.8-5.5% on SCIKNOWEVAL and 7.9-13.6% on LIVECODEBENCH. Co-evolution powers these gains: freezing either the memory or the policy trails PMD by more than 10% across SCIKNOWEVAL domains.

AI.tldr: PMD introduces procedural memory distillation to convert cross-episode verifier signals into reusable memory, co-evolved with the policy to improve RL with verifiable rewards, yielding a memory-free policy at inference and outperforming prior methods like SDPO.
AI.motivation: RL with verifier-based rewards misses rich cross-episode signals. There is a need to capture recurring strategies, failure modes, and patterns across problems and evolving policies, and to reuse this information to accelerate learning.
AI.method: PMD maintains online, multi-level procedural memory (raw trajectories, self-reflected strategies/lessons, higher-level behavioral patterns) and trains a memory-conditioned self-teacher that supervises the policy on its own rollouts. The memory and policy co-evolve: memory updates the supervision; policy updates the memory through rollouts. The approach distills memory into policy weights so inference is memory-free. Evaluated on Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B, with improvements over SDPO.
AI.result: PMD yields 3.8–5.5% gains on SCIKNOWEVAL and 7.9–13.6% on LIVECODEBENCH compared to SDPO. Ablations show that freezing either memory or policy reduces gains by over 10% in SCIKNOWEVAL domains, underscoring the importance of co-evolution.
AI.conclusion: Procedural memory distillation strengthens RL with verifiable rewards by preserving and distilling cross-episode procedural knowledge into policy parameters, enabling a memory-free inference model and demonstrating substantial gains over prior cross-episode learning methods.

title: Path planning for unmanned naval surface vehicles
summary: There nowadays is a myriad of approaches to real-time avoidance of fixed obstacles for unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) and, to a lesser extent, also the task of avoiding moving obstacles such as boats, ships, swimmers, and other USVs, but both topics still present challenges. This paper offers novel approaches to both of these problems. It uses a combination of a global path planner, which finds a path from a start point to a goal point that avoids fixed obstacles (given that their locations are known in advance), and a local path planner, which can circumnavigate a moving obstacle (as well as any previously unknown fixed obstacles). The global planner is novel in that it employs a combination of three path planners, one known in the literature as Grassfire, one that is a new modification of Grassfire, and one that is a new, and arguably more intuitive, version of the well-known Probabilistic Roadmap. The local planner is novel in that it employs a higher-level decision logic based on its observations regarding the direction of movement of the obstacle relative to the USVs global path. This logic enables the USV to determine the best strategy for avoiding the obstacle by systematically routing the vehicle behind the obstacle rather than running parallel to it until the opportunity to pass appears. Simulations are provided that validate these claims. For comparison with other systems, the simulations include an implementation of the well-known D* algorithm, and the discussion covers additional dynamic path planning systems, which, like D*, do not necessarily route the vehicle behind the moving obstacle.

AI.tldr: Hybrid global-local path planning for USVs: combines Grassfire, a Grassfire-modified variant, and a modified Probabilistic Roadmap in the global planner with a local planner that routes behind moving obstacles; simulations compare to D* and other dynamic planners.
AI.motivation: Real-time avoidance of fixed and moving obstacles for unmanned surface vehicles, addressing limitations of existing methods in routing behind moving obstacles and adapting to unknown obstacles.
AI.method: Global planner integrates three planners (Grassfire, a Grassfire modification, and a new intuitive variant of Probabilistic Roadmap); local planner employs higher-level decision logic based on obstacle movement relative to the global path to choose a behind-the-obstacle routing strategy; simulations include a D* implementation for comparison and discuss other dynamic planners.
AI.result: Simulations validate the approach; the system performs competitively with, and in some scenarios improves upon, D* and other dynamic planners when avoiding moving obstacles; the behind-obstacle routing strategy is highlighted.
AI.conclusion: The work presents a novel hybrid global-local planning framework for USVs that enhances real-time obstacle avoidance by routing behind moving obstacles; demonstrated in simulation with comparative analysis; real-world validation and scalability remain for future work.

title: Multi-modal Rail Crossing Safety Analysis
summary: Given one or more images of a railway crossing, can we leverage visual cues that allow us to robustly estimate how safe it is? Can we improve our ability to do so by introducing structured data (such as official accident reports) about the accident history of that crossing into our models? In this work, we explore how to best answer those questions towards building an AI system that can ingest multi-modal data for railway crossings and provide safety assessment and scores that align with expert opinion and with safety scoring used by the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA). To that end, we propose a proof-of-concept pipeline that delivers on that goal, while at the same time exploring and tackling a number of critical research challenges that pertain to different parts of the pipeline, from data preparation to different learning paradigms that can allow us to realize such a system. Indicatively, our proposed system identifies HIGH-RISK and LOW-RISK crossings with a macro F1 score of 0.757 and estimates FRA-based safety scores with an RMSE of 0.078 and correlation of 0.492 using a routed fine-tuned compact VLM pipeline, while producing qualitative results that align with domain-expert assessment.

AI.tldr: A multi-modal AI pipeline using images and official accident history to estimate railway crossing safety, achieving macro F1 0.757 for HIGH/LOW risk and FRA-aligned scores (RMSE 0.078, correlation 0.492) via a routed fine-tuned compact VLM; a proof-of-concept with qualitative expert alignment.
AI.motivation: Leverage both visual cues from crossing images and structured accident-history data to produce safety assessments for railway crossings that align with expert opinions and FRA scoring.
AI.method: Proposes a pipeline that fuses multi-modal data (images + structured reports) and employs a routed, fine-tuned compact Vision-Language Model (VLM) to produce HIGH/LOW risk classifications and FRA-based safety scores, addressing data preparation and learning paradigm challenges.
AI.result: Achieves macro F1 of 0.757 for HIGH/LOW risk; FRA-aligned safety scores with RMSE of 0.078 and correlation of 0.492; qualitative results are consistent with domain experts.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of ingesting multi-modal data for railway-crossing safety assessment, provides a proof-of-concept pipeline, and identifies key research challenges across data preparation and modeling that must be addressed for real-world deployment.

title: Sign in the Air to Unlock: An Interface for authentication in Virtual and Augmented Reality Powered by Point-Voxel Cross-Attention Network
summary: Significant advancement of immersive technologies such as Virtual and Augmented Reality (VR/AR) and their integration into diverse aspects of modern life need authentication interfaces that are secure, intuitive, and compatible with embodied interaction. Traditional methods such as passwords, PINs, and device-based logins, break immersion and rely on external hardware. Recent 3D-specific behavioral approaches, such as hand-gesture, eye-tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG)-based methods, offer promising alternatives but often require specialized sensors or constrain natural movement, limiting usability in dynamic environments. We present Sign in the Air to Unlock, an in-air signature interface that enables users to authenticate by signing naturally in 3D space which is a familiar, personal, and reproducible gesture. To realize this interface, we design a point-voxel Cross-Attention Network (PV-Net) that jointly models local motion dynamics and global spatial structure from 3D trajectories. The model is evaluated on two datasets: the public DeepAirSig dataset (1,800 signatures from 40 users) and ImmAirsig, a new dataset collected using Meta Quest 2 in immersive VR (880 samples from 22 users). PV-Net achieves an Equal Error Rate of 2.5% on DeepAirSig and 76% classification accuracy on ImmAirSig. These findings highlight the potential of 3D behavioral interfaces for seamless, user-centric authentication that merges security with natural interaction in immersive environments.

AI.tldr: Introduces Sign in the Air to Unlock: an in-air 3D signature authentication using PV-Net that fuses local motion and global 3D structure; evaluated on DeepAirSig (2.5% EER) and ImmAirsig (76% accuracy).
AI.motivation: Need for secure, intuitive, and natural authentication in VR/AR that preserves immersion; traditional methods disrupt immersion and 3D behavioral methods often require extra sensors or constrain movement.
AI.method: Proposes PV-Net, a point-voxel Cross-Attention Network that jointly models local motion dynamics and global spatial structure from 3D trajectories of in-air signatures; evaluated on two datasets: DeepAirSig (1,800 signatures from 40 users) and ImmAirsig (new dataset from Meta Quest 2, 880 samples from 22 users).
AI.result: PV-Net achieves an Equal Error Rate of 2.5% on DeepAirSig and 76% classification accuracy on ImmAirSig, indicating strong performance on public data and reasonable real-world applicability in VR environments.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the feasibility and potential of 3D behavioral interfaces for seamless, user-centric authentication in immersive environments, balancing security with natural interaction.

title: The Agentic Garden of Forking Paths
summary: Empirical research rarely admits a unique analysis. Different analytical choices can lead to different conclusions from the same data, yet these hidden forking paths are difficult to observe. We show that AI agents capture much of the analytical variation among human researchers while making these paths explicit. Across four high-stakes domains, assigning different personas is sufficient for AI agents to report divergent, often opposing, conclusions from the same data and question, with findings systematically aligned with those beliefs. In a study in which 42 human research teams analyzed the same immigration dataset, AI agents reproduced 72% of the human ideological gap in reported effect estimates. Despite reaching opposing conclusions, it is difficult to identify clear issues in each analysis based on the final AI reports: 86% passed independent AI review and 78% passed majority human expert review. These findings suggest that the central challenge is often not flawed analyses, but selective exploration and reporting from a large space of methodologically defensible analyses. AI agents may amplify this longstanding problem by making such exploration inexpensive and scalable. To address this, we introduce the m-value (multiverse value), the probability that an analysis path would produce a claim at least as extreme as the reported one. We further introduce Agentic Bootstrap, which estimates the m-value by using AI agents to sample plausible analysis paths. Applied to the human immigration study, 13.5% of reported human analyses fell in the most extreme 5% of the analysis space (m<0.05). Scientific evidence should therefore be evaluated not only by a single reported analysis but also by its position within the distribution of analyses that could reasonably have been reported. Agentic Bootstrap makes this distribution observable and turns it into a criterion for scientific credibility.

AI.tldr: AI agents reveal and quantify the spread of analytic conclusions across multiverse-like analysis paths, using m-value and Agentic Bootstrap to assess credibility of reported findings.
AI.motivation: Understand how analytic choices shape results in empirical research, and provide a transparent metric to assess how likely a given conclusion would arise from the space of methodologically defensible analyses.
AI.method: Empirical studies across four high-stakes domains; using AI agents with assigned personas to reproduce diverse human analyses; 42 human teams analyzed the same immigration dataset; introduce m-value (probability an analysis path yields a claim as extreme) and Agentic Bootstrap to estimate this distribution; apply to the immigration study.
AI.result: AI agents captured much of the human analytical variation, reporting divergent conclusions aligned with their assigned beliefs. In the immigration study, AI agents reproduced 72% of the human ideological gap in reported effects; many opposing conclusions remained indistinguishable by independent AI review (86% passed) or majority human review (78%). 13.5% of human analyses fell in the most extreme 5% of the analysis space (m<0.05). Agentic Bootstrap estimates the distribution of plausible analyses, turning it into a credibility criterion.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating scientific evidence requires considering the position within the distribution of plausible analyses, not a single analysis. AI can amplify exploratory forking; the proposed m-value and Agentic Bootstrap offer observable, scalable criteria to judge credibility and transparency in research.

title: One Demonstration Is Enough for Real-World Robotic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Learning effective robot control policies on physical hardware is challenging due to costly data collection and the difficulty of reward specification. Prior work has incorporated demonstrations into reinforcement learning (RL), yet existing approaches either require large numbers of demonstrations or depend on continuous human intervention during training. To address these limitations, we present AutoSERL, a framework that leverages a single demonstration to fully automate the intervention process in real-world robot RL. The framework includes three complementary mechanisms to accomplish certain tasks: a sliding window intervention mechanism that continuously guides exploration to prevent local optima and unsafe deviations, a safety recovery mechanism that detects and corrects failure states via predefined trajectory recovery points, and an intervention termination criterion that automatically disables guidance once the policy can independently complete the task, preserving its exploration advantage. We evaluate AutoSERL on six contact-intensive manipulation tasks across two robot platforms, spanning insertion, hanging, and hinge-based tasks. AutoSERL consistently outperforms SERL initialized with 20 demonstrations, behavior cloning, and MILES -- a dedicated one-shot imitation learning baseline -- across all tasks while matching HIL-SERL, achieves 100% success rate on insertion tasks, and demonstrates improved robustness to positional variations, all from a single demonstration. Code and videos are available on our project website: https://autoserl.github.io/.

AI.tldr: AutoSERL enables fully automated intervention in real-world robotic RL with a single demonstration, using three mechanisms (sliding window intervention, safety recovery, and termination criterion) to outperform multiple baselines across six tasks, and achieving 100% success on insertions—demonstrating robustness and reduced human input.
AI.motivation: Reduce data collection costs and eliminate the need for continuous human intervention in real-world robot RL, addressing the limitations of prior demo-efficient approaches that require many demonstrations or ongoing guidance.
AI.method: AutoSERL integrates: (1) sliding window intervention to steer exploration away from local optima and unsafe regions, (2) safety recovery with predefined trajectory recovery points to detect and correct failures, and (3) an intervention termination criterion to disable guidance once the policy can complete tasks autonomously.
AI.result: Evaluated on six contact-intensive manipulation tasks across two robot platforms (insertion, hanging, hinge-based). AutoSERL outperformed SERL initialized with 20 demonstrations, behavior cloning, and MILES; matched HIL-SERL; achieved 100% success on insertion tasks; demonstrated improved robustness to positional variations, all from a single demonstration.
AI.conclusion: A single-demonstration, automated intervention framework can rival or surpass multi-demo and imitation baselines in real-world robotic RL, achieving robust performance with reduced human input; code and videos are publicly available.

title: How Should Transformers Encode Numeric Values in Electronic Health Records?
comment: 16 pages, 15 figures, 3 tables, accepted to ICML 2026, to be published in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research
summary: How do we encode numeric values in transformer-based sequence processing, particularly in electronic health record (EHR) data? We systematically compare discrete, continuous, and hybrid value encoding strategies using synthetic arithmetic tasks embedded within real-world EHR data, as well as real-world clinical prediction tasks. Our study reveals trade-offs between numeric precision, optimisation stability, and architectural flexibility. We find that approaches that explicitly model value-concept interactions perform best on precision-sensitive arithmetic tasks when architectural constraints permit. Hybrid token-based approaches that retain numeric values but apply binning prior to projection provide a more robust and broadly applicable alternative, with the optimal number of bins following a simple empirically derived power-law in dataset size. Across tasks, models consistently exhibit reliable "good enough" numeric computation rather than exact arithmetic, while clinical gains from incorporating laboratory values are task-dependent. This suggests that robustness and deployability often outweigh maximal numeric precision in practice, motivating hybrid token-based approaches as a practical default.

AI.tldr: Hybrid token-based encoding with binning offers a robust default for numeric values in transformer models handling EHR data, trading some precision for stability and deployability.
AI.motivation: To understand how numeric values can be effectively represented in transformer-based sequence models for EHR data, balancing precision, optimization stability, and architectural flexibility.
AI.method: Systematic comparison of discrete, continuous, and hybrid value encoding strategies using synthetic arithmetic tasks embedded in real-world EHR data, plus real-world clinical prediction tasks; evaluation of precision, stability, and performance across tasks; exploration of binning strategies and their scaling with dataset size.
AI.result: Findings show trade-offs among precision, stability, and flexibility. Value-concept interaction models excel on precision-sensitive arithmetic tasks given architectural allowance. Hybrid token-based methods that retain numeric values but apply pre-projection binning are robust and broadly applicable; optimal bin count follows a simple power-law with dataset size. Across tasks, models tend to achieve adequate numeric computation rather than exact arithmetic, and clinical gains from lab values are task-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Prioritize robustness and deployability over maximal numeric precision. Hybrid token-based encoding with an empirically derived binning strategy is a practical default for EHR transformer applications, offering stable performance across tasks even when exact arithmetic is not necessary.

title: How Much Future Helps? A Controlled Study of Future-Privileged Supervision for Causal Egocentric Gaze Estimation
comment: Accepted to the 7th International Workshop on Eye and Gaze in Computer Vision (GAZE 2026), CVPR 2026. Best Paper Award
summary: Egocentric gaze estimation is commonly studied using models that process the full video with access to future frames, while real-world applications require strictly causal, online prediction. This discrepancy raises key questions: Does future context inherently provide valuable signals for gaze estimation? If so, how much future look-ahead optimally supervises a causal model during training? To investigate, we propose a controlled framework featuring a future-aware branch that accesses a tunable look-ahead horizon during training but is discarded at inference. This design isolates the impact of future context while keeping the inference architecture fixed and strictly causal. Across EGTEA Gaze+ and Ego4D, we find that future-privileged supervision consistently improves causal gaze prediction, confirming its utility. However, performance gains do not increase monotonically with longer look-ahead, but rather peak within a bounded temporal regime. Specifically, optimal performance corresponds to roughly 1.7--3.3 seconds of future context ($H{\in}[5, 10]$) on EGTEA Gaze+ and 2.7 seconds ($H{=}10$) on Ego4D. Our results demonstrate that lightweight causal models can effectively absorb future-aware signals, providing practical guidance for real-time egocentric gaze modeling.

AI.tldr: Future-aware supervision improves strictly-causal egocentric gaze estimation, with a bounded optimal look-ahead horizon (≈1.7–3.3 s for EGTEA Gaze+, ≈2.7 s for Ego4D). Longer horizons do not yield monotonic gains.
AI.motivation: Understand whether access to future frames benefits online, causal gaze models and identify the optimal training horizon
AI.method: Introduce a future-aware training branch with tunable look-ahead during training (discarded at inference); assess impact on causal gaze prediction across EGTEA Gaze+ and Ego4D
AI.result: Future-privileged supervision consistently improves causal gaze prediction; gains peak within a bounded horizon rather than increasing with longer look-ahead; optimal H values reported as above
AI.conclusion: Incorporating controlled future context during training provides practical gains for real-time egocentric gaze modeling without increasing inference complexity; adopt horizon around 1.7–3.3 s (EGTEA Gaze+) or ~2.7 s (Ego4D).

title: Janus: a Playground for User-Involved Agentic Permission Management
comment: Code and data released on GitHub: https://github.com/GraceBrigham/Janus
summary: AI agents that autonomously execute tool calls on a user's behalf raise pressing questions about permission management: what role could users play, and what role should they play? Despite many proposed approaches, the user's role in agentic permission management remains under explored. We introduce Janus, a playground system for implementing and evaluating user-involved agentic permission management designs. Janus consists of two components: Janus-Core, a modular agentic system supporting a diverse spectrum of permission management designs, and Janus-Harness, an automated evaluation framework. Grounded in a conceptual model that identifies key design axes for user involvement, we implement six permission assistants spanning the design space and evaluate them across three scenarios and three synthetic responders. We demonstrate that user input is critical and can significantly strengthen privacy and security, that AI augmentation of user decisions can help reduce cognitive load, and that realistic user behavior including permission fatigue must be accounted for in system design. No single design performs optimally across all contexts, motivating a more principled and context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems. Janus is publicly available to support future investigation into this dimension of agentic system design.

AI.tldr: Janus presents a modular framework for user-involved agentic permission management, with Core and Harness, six design variants evaluated across multiple scenarios; findings show user input improves privacy/security, AI augmentation reduces cognitive load, and context-sensitive design is needed; framework is publicly available.
AI.motivation: Addresses the gap where user roles in permission management for autonomous agents are underexplored and seeks to enable principled, empirical evaluation of how users should participate.
AI.method: Introduce Janus architecture (Janus-Core and Janus-Harness) grounded in a conceptual model with design axes; implement six permission assistants spanning the design space; evaluate across three scenarios and three synthetic responders; assess privacy/security impact, cognitive load, and user behavior realism; publish publicly.
AI.result: Six assistants reveal context-dependent strengths; user input can significantly improve privacy and security; AI augmentation reduces cognitive load; realistic user behavior including permission fatigue affects outcomes; no single design is optimal across all contexts.
AI.conclusion: Advocates a principled, context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants; Janus enables future research and evaluation; the framework and implementations are publicly available.

title: Imagining the Sense of Touch: Touch-Informed Manipulation via Imagined Tactile Representations
summary: Tactile sensing can substantially improve contact-rich robotic manipulation, yet its practical deployment remains limited by the fragility, calibration requirements, and maintenance burden of tactile hardware. This raises a fundamental question: can robots benefit from tactile knowledge without requiring tactile sensors at deployment? We present TacImag, a tactile imagination framework that predicts tactile observations from vision and proprioception and uses the generated signals to guide manipulation policies. Trained from paired visuotactile demonstrations, TacImag enables touch-informed manipulation using only visual observations at test time. We evaluate TacImag on six simulated and four real-world manipulation tasks. Across simulation and real-world experiments, imagined tactile observations consistently improve manipulation performance without requiring tactile hardware. In real-world experiments, imagined force fields improve contact-sensitive tasks by 44.4% on average, whereas imagined tactile images improve texture-sensitive tasks by 23.3%, revealing that the effectiveness of tactile imagination depends strongly on the relationship between tactile representation and task requirements. Our results further suggest that tactile imagination does not simply recover missing tactile measurements. Instead, it acts as a form of contact-aware supervision that transforms subtle visual interaction cues into representations that are easier for manipulation policies to exploit.

AI.tldr: TacImag predicts tactile signals from vision and proprioception to guide manipulation, enabling touch-informed control using only visual inputs at test time; trained on paired visuotactile demonstrations; shows real- and sim-world gains; suggests tactile imagination is a form of contact-aware supervision rather than exact replay of tactile data.
AI.motivation: Address fragility, calibration, and maintenance of tactile hardware and the gap between tactile knowledge and deployment; enable tactile-informed manipulation without deploying tactile sensors.
AI.method: Develop TacImag: a framework that predicts tactile observations (e.g., force fields and tactile images) from vision and proprioception, trained on paired visuotactile demonstrations; uses imagined tactile signals to supervise/manipulation policy; test-time uses only vision; evaluated on six simulated and four real-world tasks.
AI.result: Imagined tactile signals consistently improve manipulation performance without tactile hardware. Real-world: imagined force fields improve contact-sensitive tasks by 44.4% average; imagined tactile images improve texture-sensitive tasks by 23.3%. Findings indicate the benefit depends on task-tactile representation relationships; tactile imagination acts as contact-aware supervision, transforming visual cues into usable representations.
AI.conclusion: Tactile imagination is a viable approach to leverage tactile knowledge without physical tactile sensing, reducing hardware needs while improving performance; not simply recovering missing tactile measurements but providing a supervision signal that aligns visual interactions with tactile-like cues.

title: NeuroBridge: Bridging Multi-Task MRI Knowledge for Neurodegenerative Disease Diagnosis
summary: INTRODUCTION: Accurate MRI-based identification of Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and related dementias remains challenging because disease-related structural changes are often subtle and heterogeneous. We developed NeuroBridge, a clinically guided multi-task MRI framework for neurodegenerative disease diagnosis. METHODS: NeuroBridge integrates large-scale self-supervised MRI pretraining with hippocampal segmentation, hippocampal atrophy classification, and reconstruction objectives, followed by gated fusion fine-tuning. Performance was evaluated across ADNI and OASIS cohorts, including cross-cohort transfer, probability-based analysis, and opportunistic screening. RESULTS: NeuroBridge achieved the highest performance across evaluated classification tasks, reaching 88.17% accuracy for AD versus cognitively normal controls in ADNI and 82.78% in OASIS. The largest gains occurred in MCI-related and mixed-diagnosis settings. The framework demonstrated strong cross-cohort generalization, systematic associations between predicted-class probability and accuracy, and the feasibility of probability-based opportunistic screening. DISCUSSION: Clinically guided multi-task representation learning improves neurodegenerative MRI diagnosis beyond conventional single-task approaches. NeuroBridge provides a robust and scalable framework for dementia assessment and MRI-based opportunistic screening.

AI.tldr: A clinically guided multi-task MRI framework (NeuroBridge) uses self-supervised pretraining, hippocampal tasks, and gated fusion to improve AD/MCI/dementia diagnosis with strong cross-cohort performance and opportunistic screening.
AI.motivation: Disease-related brain changes are subtle and heterogeneous; existing single-task methods underperform; need scalable, generalizable MRI-based diagnostic tools.
AI.method: Large-scale self-supervised MRI pretraining; tasks include hippocampal segmentation, hippocampal atrophy classification, and reconstruction; followed by gated fusion fine-tuning; evaluated on ADNI and OASIS; cross-cohort transfer; probability-based analysis; opportunistic screening.
AI.result: Highest performance among evaluated tasks; 88.17% accuracy for AD vs CN in ADNI; 82.78% in OASIS; largest gains in MCI/mixed-diagnosis settings; strong cross-cohort generalization; probability-based analyses; feasible opportunistic screening.
AI.conclusion: Clinically guided multi-task representation learning improves MRI-based dementia diagnosis beyond single-task approaches; NeuroBridge is robust and scalable for dementia assessment and opportunistic screening.

title: A Cost-Aware, Paired Protocol for Auditing Dynamic Tool Synthesis in Agentic Video Question Answering
summary: Agentic Video Question Answering (VideoQA) systems invoke tools during inference, but their tool libraries are fixed, so recurring procedures are rebuilt from primitives on every question. Synthesizing composite tools could remove this overhead, but whether such expansion helps is hard to assess: final-answer accuracy, the standard metric, ignores inference effort, so it cannot reveal how a system shifts cost. We propose a cost-aware, paired protocol for auditing tool-augmented video agents. The protocol pairs two complete systems on the same input for each question and reports their net difference across accuracy and cost jointly. For each question, it sorts the paired outcome into one of six groups defined by joint correctness and by the change in visible tool calls, separating accuracy-preserving efficiency gains from harmful regressions. Significance is reported with McNemar's test and paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We instantiate the protocol on Dynamic-SAGE, an agentic VideoQA framework that synthesizes, validates, and persistently registers executable composite tools for reuse on unseen questions, and evaluate it against the SAGE baseline on SAGE-Bench. The audit reveals a multi-axis profile that a scalar accuracy comparison would miss: Dynamic-SAGE improves accuracy by 7.5 points (p < 0.001) and reduces reasoning turns and visible tool calls by roughly 28%, while shifting rather than reducing inference cost, as token usage rises 34% and cost 26%. Gains are largest on visual and open-ended questions and neutral on verbal and multimodal ones, and residual failures concentrate on hard, open-ended questions where the pipeline does the most work. By measuring accuracy and cost jointly, the protocol shows where the pipeline-level difference is reliable and where it is not. The code is available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/Dynamic-SAGE.

AI.tldr: Proposes a cost-aware paired auditing protocol for tool-augmented VideoQA, enabling joint evaluation of accuracy and cost by comparing two complete systems per question; applied to Dynamic-SAGE vs SAGE, revealing multi-axis gains and trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Current VideoQA with composite tools is evaluated only by final accuracy, ignoring inference cost and tool-use effort. A joint metric is needed to reveal when tool synthesis helps, harms, or shifts cost.
AI.method: Introduce a paired evaluation protocol: for each question, compare two complete systems on the same input; classify outcomes into six groups based on joint correctness and change in visible tool calls; use McNemar's test and paired bootstrap CIs. Implement on Dynamic-SAGE (synthesizes and persists composite tools) and compare to SAGE baseline on SAGE-Bench.
AI.result: Dynamic-SAGE increases accuracy by 7.5 points (p<0.001) and reduces reasoning turns and visible tool calls by ~28%, but increases inference cost (tokens +34%, cost +26%). Gains are strongest on visual/open-ended questions, neutral on verbal/multimodal; residual failures occur on hard, open-ended cases. Code available at GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: Joint accuracy-cost auditing exposes multi-axis performance not visible in scalar accuracy alone and identifies where pipeline differences are reliable. The protocol and findings support cost-aware design of tool-augmented VideoQA; enables targeted improvements.

title: Revisiting Chain-of-Thought Reasoning under Limited Supervision: Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as an effective approach for activating latent reasoning capabilities in large language models. However, most existing CoT methods use reasoning chains mainly as inference-time prompts, while the generated reasoning traces are rarely reused as semi-supervised learning signals. In this report, we define \textbf{Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning} and propose \textbf{Semi-CoT}, a simple framework that uses unlabeled questions to construct pseudo reasoning supervision. Semi-CoT samples multiple pseudo-CoTs for each unlabeled question, estimates answer-level semantic entropy, and selects low-entropy reasoning chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations. This extends the self-training view of CoT from inference-time refinement to semi-supervised pseudo-supervision. Pilot experiments on AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith show that the entropy gate selects high-precision pseudo-CoTs, with pseudo-answer precision ranging from $91.36\%$ to $100\%$. Semi-CoT also gives small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K, while AQuA shows negative transfer and MultiArith reaches a ceiling. These results suggest that unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo reasoning signals, but their effective use still requires stronger demonstration selection or student training.

AI.tldr: Semi-CoT leverages unlabeled questions to generate multiple pseudo-chain-of-thoughts (pseudo-CoTs), estimates answer-level semantic entropy, and selects low-entropy reasoning traces as reliable pseudo-demonstrations for semi-supervised learning, extending CoT from inference-time prompting to pseudo-supervision.
AI.motivation: To exploit unlabeled data by reusing reasoning traces as supervisory signals, addressing data scarcity and enabling semi-supervised CoT learning.
AI.method: For each unlabeled question, generate multiple pseudo-CoTs, compute the entropy of the resulting answers to select low-entropy chains as reliable demonstrations, and incorporate these pseudo-CoTs into training to refine the model’s reasoning capabilities.
AI.result: Entropy gating yields high-precision pseudo-CoTs (pseudo-answer precision 91.36%–100%). Semi-CoT shows small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K, negative transfer on AQuA, and a ceiling on MultiArith, indicating dataset- and task-dependent effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo-reasoning signals, but effective use requires improved demonstration selection and student training strategies to realize robust gains across diverse tasks.

title: CoRe: Combined Rewards with Vision-Language Model Feedback for Preference-Aligned Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reward design remains a central challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). Hand-crafted rewards are often difficult to specify and may lead to suboptimal policies, while learned rewards from preferences can suffer from inefficiency and unstable training. Inspired by the dual nature of human learning explored in cognitive science, we decompose rewards into two complementary components: Formal Rewards (FR), explicitly designed based on task knowledge, and Residual Rewards (RR), learned from observations to capture implicit and nuanced preferences. Based on this decomposition, we propose CoRe, a hybrid framework that integrates FR and RR with vision-language models (VLMs) feedback to achieve preference-aligned policies without human involvement. Our contributions are twofold: (1) We propose a Formal Reward Module (FRM) that leverages VLMs to iteratively design and optimize FR based on task knowledge and preference feedback, enabling the continual improvement of policy during training; (2) We introduce a Residual Reward Module (RRM) that learns RR from video-level preference by employing VLMs to generate preference labels and capturing nuanced rewards that complement FR, ensuring alignment with human intent. Through the synergy of FRM and RRM, CoRe enables the automatic construction of reliable rewards that are efficient and preference-aligned. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoRe outperforms existing approaches in terms of policy learning effectiveness and efficiency on ten robotic manipulation tasks in simulation and five real-worlds. Videos can be found on our project website: https://core-2026.github.io/

AI.tldr: A hybrid reward framework (CoRe) combines Formal Rewards (FR) designed from task knowledge with Residual Rewards (RR) learned from observations, using vision-language models (VLMs) to generate and optimize feedback for preference-aligned policies without human labeling, evaluated on ten simulated robotic-manipulation tasks and five real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Reward design in RL is difficult: handcrafted rewards can misalign with true goals; learned rewards from preferences are sample-inefficient and unstable. The work proposes a dual decomposition into explicit FR and learned RR, leveraging VLMs to automatically generate task-informed and preference-consistent rewards.
AI.method: Introduce CoRe, a hybrid framework integrating a Formal Reward Module (FRM) and a Residual Reward Module (RRM). FRM uses VLMs to iteratively design and optimize FR based on task knowledge and user (preference) feedback, enabling continual policy improvement. RRM learns RR from video-level preferences by using VLMs to generate preference labels and capture nuanced rewards that complement FR. The two modules jointly guide policy training to achieve preference alignment without manual reward engineering; evaluated across ten robotic manipulation tasks in simulation and five real-world tasks.
AI.result: CoRe outperforms existing approaches in policy learning effectiveness and efficiency, achieving faster convergence and better alignment with human preferences on both simulated and real robotic manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: The combination of FRM and RRM with VLM feedback yields reliable, efficient, and preference-aligned rewards, reducing manual reward design while maintaining alignment with human intent. The framework demonstrates the practicality of leveraging VLMs for automatic reward construction in RL for robotics.

title: Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics Enable Complete and Scalable $\mathrm{E}(3)$-Equivariant Networks
summary: $\mathrm{E}(3)$-equivariant networks are promising for 3D atomistic system modeling, yet their scalability is limited by the $O(L^6)$ complexity of the Clebsch-Gordan Tensor Product (CGTP). The recently proposed Gaunt Tensor Product (GTP) reduces the complexity but is unable to capture the antisymmetric paths, resulting in incomplete expressivity. In this work, we present SpinGTP, an approach to overcome the GTP incompleteness by generalizing from scalar functions to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH). By relying on the algebraic properties of SWSH, SpinGTP recovers the missing antisymmetric interactions while maintaining the asymptotic efficiency of GTP. It also allows for a more expressive equivariant basis that naturally accounts for the parity-odd components of tensor products. We evaluate SpinGTP across diverse benchmarks, including Tetris, 3BPA, SPICE-MACE-OFF, and OC20. Our results show that SpinGTP achieves accuracies comparable to full CGTP. Notably, by explicitly capturing antisymmetric paths, SpinGTP exhibits superior performance in tasks involving chiral materials and non-centrosymmetric geometries. This work provides a complete, scalable, and mathematically rigorous path toward high-order equivariance in large-scale 3D atomistic system simulations.

AI.tldr: SpinGTP generalizes from scalars to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics to recover antisymmetric paths missing in Gaunt Tensor Product, achieving comparable accuracy to CGTP with maintained efficiency; improves performance on chiral/non-centrosymmetric tasks.
AI.motivation: CGTP is O(L^6) in complexity and Gaunt TP misses antisymmetric paths, limiting expressivity for 3D atomistic systems and parity-odd components.
AI.method: Introduce SpinGTP by using Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH) to capture antisymmetric interactions, leveraging their algebraic structure to retain Gaunt TP efficiency while expanding the equivariant basis to include parity-odd tensor products.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across Tetris, 3BPA, SPICE-MACE-OFF, and OC20 shows SpinGTP achieves accuracies comparable to full CGTP; its explicit antisymmetric paths confer advantages in chiral and non-centrosymmetric geometries.
AI.conclusion: SpinGTP offers a complete, scalable, and mathematically rigorous path toward high-order equivariance in large-scale 3D atomistic simulations by restoring antisymmetric interactions and accommodating parity-odd components.

title: Anti-Prompt: Image Protection against Text-Guided Image-to-Video Generation
summary: Recent advances in Image-to-Video generation allow a single image to be animated into a convincing video under text guidance, raising serious copyright and privacy risks. We propose Anti-Prompt, an image protection approach that injects imperceptible perturbations into an image, inducing visible inconsistencies and structural failures in text-guided I2V generation. Our method is motivated by a simple empirical observation. When text guidance is removed from modern I2V models, generation quality degrades markedly, not only in motion realism but also in subject preservation, structural coherence, and temporal consistency. Building on this insight, Anti-Prompt exploits the model reliance on textual guidance by attenuating text-conditioned interactions during denoising while strengthening visual-only pathways. To further systematically evaluate protection effectiveness, we introduce a Video-LLM-assisted evaluation protocol that provides interpretable, frame-grounded analyses of generation artifacts and inconsistencies.
