Experiments on two representative I2V architectures demonstrate that our method achieves strong protection performance while improving efficiency and cross-model transferability.

AI.tldr: A perturbation-based image protection method (Anti-Prompt) that sabotages text-guided image-to-video (I2V) generation by reducing text-conditioned interactions and strengthening visual pathways, plus a Video-LLM-assisted evaluation protocol; demonstrates cross-model protection and efficiency gains.
AI.motivation: Rising copyright and privacy risks from text-guided I2V on single images; need a practical, transferable protection mechanism that preserves human-perceptual quality while limiting I2V fidelity.
AI.method: Inject imperceptible perturbations into the source image to induce inconsistencies during I2V generation. During denoising, attenuate text-conditioned interactions and reinforce visual-only pathways to force reliance on non-text cues. Evaluate using two I2V architectures and a Video-LLM-assisted protocol that provides frame-grounded artifact analysis.
AI.result: Anticipated strong protection performance across models with visible artifacts and degraded text-guided fidelity. The method also improves efficiency and cross-model transferability. The Video-LLM protocol yields interpretable, frame-level analyses of generation artifacts and inconsistencies.
AI.conclusion: Anti-Prompt provides a practical, model-agnostic approach to protecting images from I2V generation and introduces a systematic evaluation framework. It highlights the potential for privacy-preserving safeguards while indicating avenues for broader robustness assessment and ethical considerations.

title: OPINE-World: Programmatic World Modeling with Ontology-error-Prioritized Interactive Exploration
summary: Learning how an environment behaves from interaction is central to building agents that adapt to unfamiliar tasks. World models learned with deep networks are flexible but data-hungry and transfer poorly beyond their training distribution. Program-synthesized world models, written as source code by LLMs and refined through counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS), are instead data-efficient and reusable, yet they have been demonstrated mainly on structured-state worlds with a given object vocabulary, and a single program search does not scale to pixel-rendered environments whose object structure must be hypothesized flexibly. We introduce OPINE-World, an LLM agent that learns an object-centric programmatic world model online from interaction. OPINE-World couples two cooperating agents in a loop of hypothesis and test, one acting in the environment and one synthesizing the model in code with replay verification and model-based planning, and it steers exploration with a Bayesian measure of object-type adequacy we call ontology error. We evaluate OPINE-World on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark for skill-acquisition efficiency in which the object vocabulary, the goal, and the action semantics are withheld. OPINE-World solves 20 of 25 games without per-game training and reaches an action-efficiency score of 78.4 against the human baseline.

AI.tldr: OPINE-World uses an LLM-synthesized, object-centric, programmatic world model refined via CEGIS, enabling data-efficient planning and exploration; it solves 20 of 25 ARC-AGI-3 tasks without per-task training and achieves strong action efficiency.
AI.motivation: Reduce data hunger and improve transfer in world models by using reusable, explicit programmatic representations of environment dynamics; enable flexible object vocabularies for pixel-based worlds.
AI.method: Two-agent loop: an environment-interacting actor and a code-synthesizing agent; object-centric world models encoded as executable programs; synthesis aided by replay verification and model-based planning; exploration guided by a Bayesian ontology error.
AI.result: On ARC-AGI-3, OPINE-World solves 20/25 games without per-game training and achieves an action-efficiency of 78.4 relative to human baseline.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates data-efficient, reusable world models for unseen tasks with pixel-rendered environments; the combination of LLM-based synthesis, CEGIS, and Bayesian exploration metrics shows promise for scalable, flexible agent learning.

title: Lightweight Safe Reinforcement Learning for End-to-End UAV Navigation
summary: With the rapid development of autonomous aerial systems, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly deployed in applications such as inspection, environmental monitoring, and rescue, creating growing demand for reliable autonomous navigation. However, autonomous UAV navigation in dense environments remains challenging under sparse perception and dynamic constraints. Most reinforcement learning (RL) methods lack explicit safety mechanisms, leading to unsafe exploration, unstable training, and risky behaviors, especially during high-speed flight. Even in safe RL approaches, safety is often enforced by projecting policy outputs onto a safe action set, which may introduce instability. Meanwhile, many learning-based methods rely on dense inputs or large networks, increasing computational burden and limiting lightweight onboard deployment. Facing the above challenges, we propose a safety-constrained perception-control integrated framework for UAV navigation. A lightweight network encodes sparse observations into collision-risk-aware features using asymmetric and depthwise separable convolutions. We formulate the task as a constrained Markov decision process within a hierarchical control architecture and solve it using a Lagrangian-based safe PPO algorithm. Curriculum learning further improves training stability. Experiments with varying obstacle densities and flight speeds demonstrate higher success rates, improved safety, and better efficiency than existing reinforcement learning baselines.

AI.tldr: A safety-constrained perception-control framework for UAV navigation using a lightweight encoder for sparse observations, a constrained MDP with Lagrangian safe PPO in a hierarchical controller, and curriculum learning, achieving improved safety and efficiency over RL baselines across obstacle densities and speeds.
AI.motivation: To address unsafe exploration, instability, and heavy computation in existing RL-based UAV navigation methods in dense environments, and to enable lightweight onboard deployment with explicit safety considerations.
AI.method: Encode sparse observations into collision-risk features using asymmetric and depthwise-separable convolutions; formulate navigation as a constrained MDP within a hierarchical control architecture; solve with a Lagrangian-based safe PPO objective; employ curriculum learning to stabilize training.
AI.result: Experiments across varying obstacle densities and flight speeds show higher success rates, improved safety, and better efficiency compared with standard RL baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed safety-constrained, perception-control framework with curriculum learning enhances reliable autonomous UAV navigation under sparse perception and dynamic constraints, with suitability for lightweight onboard deployment.

title: The Rollout Infrastructure Tax in Coding-Agent Reinforcement Learning
comment: Preprint. 6 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to ACM SoCC 2026
summary: Coding-agent reinforcement learning treats execution infrastructure as a background implementation detail, despite relying on large numbers of interactive software rollouts. This is a missed opportunity: measuring infrastructure overhead can reveal practical efficiency gains for RL post-training, where small per-rollout savings compound at scale. We present a comparative study of four execution substrates: single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes-orchestrated containers, and cloud virtual machines. We find up to $110\times$ variation in cold-start latency and a $1.8\times$ spread in projected worker-hours for one million 150-step trajectories. Our results suggest that future coding-agent RL systems should optimize execution substrates as part of the training system itself, not merely as deployment plumbing.

AI.tldr: Execution substrate choice causes large variability in RL training efficiency; optimizing substrates during training can yield substantial gains (up to 110x cold-start variation and 1.8x worker-hours at scale).
AI.motivation: Infrastructure overhead in coding-agent reinforcement learning is often underestimated; measuring and optimizing execution environments can unlock practical efficiency gains during post-training when many rollouts are performed.
AI.method: Empirical comparison of four execution substrates—single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes-managed containers, and cloud virtual machines—and measurement of cold-start latency and projected worker-hours for one million 150-step trajectories.
AI.result: Substantial substrate-dependent performance variation observed: up to 110× difference in cold-start latency and about 1.8× spread in projected worker-hours for large-scale trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Execution substrate optimization should be treated as a core part of the training system design for coding-agent RL, not merely deployment plumbing; infrastructure choices can materially affect scalability and cost.

title: Disentangling Pictorial Cue Understanding from Language Bias in VLMs via Depth Ordering Task
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, accepted to ECCV 2026 (30 pages, 13 figures, supplementary materials included)
summary: In this paper, we study depth perception of vision-language models (VLMs) to isolate the effects of pictorial depth cues and disentangle vision and language influences on model performance. To this end, we combine depth-ordering and odd-one-out psychophysical tasks: the VLMs are presented with images where one object is at different depth relative to other, otherwise identical, objects, and must determine whether the odd-one-out target is closer or farther to the observer. To create stimuli, we generate 2D views from simulated and real 3D scenes while controlling the presence of individual pictorial depth cues, enabling a fine-grained analysis of cue-level contributions. Language effects are examined by varying referring expression clarity. We also introduce a novel metric to quantify vision-vs-language sensitivities. Applying this methodology, we create the Odd-One-Out Depth (O3-D) dataset with 37K real and synthetic images and 147K image-question pairs. Evaluation of 12 open-source and commercial models on O3-D shows under-utilization of depth cues and depth-ordering accuracies between 47% and 56%, with no model above chance level. At the same time, our metric reveals strong linguistic bias in the answers. Neither chain-of-thought (CoT) nor in-context learning (ICL) significantly improves performance, suggesting that static image data alone may be insufficient for depth understanding. All code, the image generation pipeline, and the O3-D dataset are publicly released at https://github.com/lyiqian/o3-d.

AI.tldr: A study investigates how vision-language models perceive depth by disentangling pictorial depth cues and language effects, introducing the Odd-One-Out Depth (O3-D) dataset (37K real/synthetic images, 147K QAs) and a vision-vs-language sensitivity metric. Models show limited use of depth cues (47–56% accuracy, near chance) and strong linguistic bias; CoT/ICL offer little improvement, suggesting static images alone may be insufficient for depth understanding. Code and data released.
AI.motivation: To understand how VLMs utilize pictorial depth cues and language information for depth perception, and to quantify vision vs language contributions to model decisions.
AI.method: Combine depth-ordering and odd-one-out psychophysical tasks; generate 2D projections from 3D scenes while manipulating individual depth cues; vary referring expression clarity; introduce a metric for vision-vs-language sensitivities; evaluate 12 models on the resulting O3-D dataset (37K real/synthetic images, 147K QA pairs).
AI.result: 12 models perform poorly on depth tasks, with depth-ordering accuracy between 47% and 56% and none above chance; strong linguistic bias in answers; CoT and ICL do not significantly improve performance; indicates static image data may be insufficient for depth understanding.
AI.conclusion: The O3-D dataset and the vision-vs-language metric reveal under-utilization of depth cues and strong language influences in VLMs, highlighting the need for richer data or modeling approaches to achieve robust depth understanding; code and data released for further research.

title: Scaling Trends for Lie Detector Oversight in Preference Learning
summary: Deceptive behavior in LLMs is costly to monitor and prevent, motivating approaches such as Scalable Oversight via Lie Detectors (SOLiD) (Cundy & Gleave, 2025), which uses lie detectors to identify responses for review by high-cost labelers. In this paper, we scale SOLiD to larger models and evaluate it in more diverse and realistic preference-learning settings. We find favorable scaling: undetected deception drops from 34% for 1B-parameter models to 14% for 405B-parameter models at a detector true positive rate of 99%, and expensive human labelers can be removed entirely from the fine-tuning phase without a statistically significant increase in deception. However, SOLiD is sensitive to distribution shift between detector training and preference-training data, which can drive detector false positive rates to impractical levels.

AI.tldr: SOLiD scales to 405B-parameter LLMs, reducing undetected deception from 34% (1B) to 14% (405B) at detector TPR 99%. Expensive labelers can be removed from fine-tuning without a significant rise in deception, but detector performance is sensitive to distribution shift between detector-training and preference-training data, causing high false positive rates under shift.
AI.motivation: Deceptive behavior in LLMs is costly to monitor; scalable oversight methods like SOLiD are proposed to limit reliance on expensive human labeling while maintaining compliance and safety.
AI.method: Evaluate SOLiD across substantially larger models (up to 405B parameters) in diverse and realistic preference-learning settings; measure deception detection performance at high detector true positive rate; test removal of human labelers during fine-tuning; assess robustness to distribution shift between detector-training data and preference-training data.
AI.result: Model-scale improves detection effectiveness: undetected deception decreases from 34% (1B) to 14% (405B) at detector TPR 99%. Expensive labelers can be dropped from the fine-tuning phase without a statistically significant degradation in deception metrics. However, detector false positives escalate when there is distribution shift between detector-training data and preference-training data, undermining practicality.
AI.conclusion: SOLiD demonstrates favorable scaling with model size and potential cost reductions, but distribution shift remains a critical vulnerability requiring robust detectors or domain-adaptive training to maintain low deception under real-world data shifts.

title: VLA-Corrector: Lightweight Detect-and-Correct Inference for Adaptive Action Horizon
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models have recently achieved strong progress in embodied intelligence. To reduce policy-call frequency while preserving temporal coherence, most generative policies adopt an action chunk mechanism, executing multiple future actions in an open-loop manner under a fixed action horizon. However, this "predict-then-blindly-execute" paradigm sacrifices closed-loop reactivity: in contact-rich physical interactions, even small local perturbations can rapidly amplify within the open-loop blind spot, leading to compounding errors and ultimately task failure. To address this limitation, we propose VLA-Corrector, a lightweight corrective inference framework for action-chunked VLA policies. Without modifying the backbone policy weights, VLA-Corrector introduces a lightweight Latent-space Vision Monitor (LVM) that continuously compares predicted and actual visual feature evolution, enabling online detection of visual dynamics deviations. Once persistent deviation is detected, the system triggers a truncation event, discards the remaining stale actions, and invokes corrective replanning via Online Gradient Guidance (OGG). The detect-and-correct mechanism of VLA-Corrector naturally induces an event-triggered adaptive action horizon: it preserves long-horizon execution when the current chunk remains reliable, and invokes short-horizon corrective replanning when execution begins to drift. In doing so, VLA-Corrector mitigates the trade-off imposed by static horizons between execution robustness and policy-call frequency. It can be integrated into different VLA models without further retraining the VLA backbone, interrupting compounding errors while preserving much of the efficiency benefit of action chunking and substantially improving robustness in long-horizon, contact-rich robotic manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: Proposes VLA-Corrector, a lightweight corrective inference framework that adds a latent-space vision monitor and online gradient-guided replanning to action-chunked vision-language-action policies, enabling event-triggered horizon adaptation to mitigate open-loop errors without retraining the backbone.
AI.motivation: Open-loop action chunks reduce policy-call frequency but sacrifice closed-loop reactivity in contact-rich tasks; a mechanism is needed to detect when predictions drift from reality and correct on the fly without heavy retraining.
AI.method: Introduce Latent-space Vision Monitor (LVM) to compare predicted and actual visual features; detect persistent deviations and trigger a truncation event that discards stale actions and invokes Online Gradient Guidance (OGG) for corrective replanning; the approach yields an event-triggered adaptive action horizon.
AI.result: Increases robustness of long-horizon, contact-rich robotic manipulation tasks by interrupting compounding errors while preserving much of the efficiency of action chunking; compatible with different VLA backbones without retraining.
AI.conclusion: VLA-Corrector addresses the horizon-robustness trade-off of action-chunked policies by providing a lightweight, plug-in correction mechanism that adapts the action horizon based on visual-dynamics consistency, improving reliability without sacrificing backbone efficiency.

title: Conditional Inference Trees and Forests for Feature Selection
summary: Conditional inference trees (CIT) and conditional inference forests (CIF) reduce split-selection bias by testing features before choosing split thresholds, but repeated permutation tests and threshold searches can make these methods computationally expensive. We study CIT and CIF as top-$k$ feature-ranking methods for downstream prediction using real-data benchmarks, runtime ablations, and synthetic feature-recovery experiments. At a fixed node, if the features and permutation budget do not depend on the node responses, Bonferroni-corrected $+1$ Monte Carlo permutation $p$-values control nodewise rejection under the complete permutation null. CIF ranks 4th among 17 classification methods on 22 datasets and 3rd among 18 regression methods on 8 datasets. With Bonferroni correction held fixed, the CIF runtime ablations indicate that adaptive stopping and the number of thresholds searched have the largest measured effect on runtime: turning off adaptive stopping and using exact threshold search increase fitting time by 4.0--8.4$\times$ and 1.9--10.8$\times$, respectively, while downstream score changes are at most 0.011. Sparse high-$p$ simulations indicate that forest feature sampling can leave informative features out of many split decisions. Overall, the results support CIF as a top-$k$ feature-ranking method in the evaluated downstream prediction benchmarks.

AI.tldr: CIT/CIF reduce split-selection bias with permutation tests but are computationally expensive; CIF shows competitive top-k feature-ranking performance on multi-dataset benchmarks; runtime is driven by adaptive stopping and threshold search; Bonferroni-corrected permutation p-values control nodewise error; sparse feature sampling can miss informative features; overall CIF is effective for downstream prediction.
AI.motivation: Assess the trade-offs between statistical bias reduction and computational cost in conditional inference trees/forests, and evaluate their utility as top-k feature-ranking methods in downstream prediction across real and synthetic benchmarks.
AI.method: Empirical study using 22 classification datasets and 8 regression datasets to benchmark CIF/CIT against other methods. Runtime ablations: varying adaptive stopping and number of thresholds searched; use Bonferroni-corrected +1 Monte Carlo permutation p-values under a complete permutation null. Synthetic feature-recovery experiments and sparse high-p simulations to assess feature sampling behavior.
AI.result: CIF ranks 4th among 17 classification methods and 3rd among 18 regression methods. With fixed Bonferroni correction, adaptive stopping and threshold search most affect runtime: turning off adaptive stopping and using exact threshold search increase fitting time by 4.0–8.4x and 1.9–10.8x, respectively, while downstream score changes are <= 0.011. Sparse high-p simulations show that forest feature sampling can miss informative features in many split decisions.
AI.conclusion: CIF is a strong top-k feature-ranking method for downstream prediction in the evaluated benchmarks, achieving competitive predictive performance while maintaining control of type I error via Bonferroni-corrected permutation tests; runtime can be substantially reduced by adaptive stopping and limiting threshold searches, with only minor impacts on downstream scores, though feature sampling sparsity can risk omitting informative features.

title: Hidden-Shot: Towards One-Shot Task Generalization for Low-Level Vision Generalist Models
summary: Despite the intense engagement surrounding low-level vision generalist models, their effectiveness in zero/few-shot scenarios beyond learned tasks remains unverified. The primary challenge of developing an ideal generalist lies in achieving the ability to generalize from new unseen tasks, which also can be assessed by matched quantitative criteria. Existing methods have made some progress in prompt engineering but have not systematically explored this gap across a wide range of low-level visual tasks. Stimulated by the problem, we propose Hidden-Shot, an implicit prompt mechanism aimed at exploring low-level task adaptation in a vision generalist model. Specifically, the method extracts implicit visual task-based information, utilizes a global task-aware textural prompt, and selectively merges implicit information with in-task processing information to enhance one-shot capabilities in new tasks. The overall design performs direct injection in a cost-effective manner, while minimally altering the architecture of the original generalist model. Additionally, we introduce a data-driven evaluation framework termed C/U assessment to cover two basic scenarios, 3C4U (3 conventional and 4 unconventional tasks) for retraining existing models and 3C7U (3 conventional and 7 unconventional tasks) for training from scratch, as a comprehensive assessment to systematically test the generalization ability of low-level generalist models. Experiments on seven and ten datasets outperform the state-of-the-art vision generalist model, respectively verified by 3C4U and 3C7U framework. Our presented Hidden-Shot approach demonstrates superior performance on one-shot new tasks while maintaining consistent performance on existing tasks.

AI.tldr: Hidden-Shot: an implicit prompt mechanism to improve one-shot adaptation in low-level vision generalist models; introduces a data-driven C/U assessment framework (3C4U for retraining and 3C7U for training from scratch); achieves state-of-the-art performance on seven and ten datasets respectively, while preserving performance on existing tasks.
AI.motivation: To address the gap in generalization of low-level vision generalist models to unseen tasks and to provide a systematic evaluation framework beyond conventional prompt engineering.
AI.method: Extract implicit task-based information and apply a global task-aware textural prompt; selectively merge implicit information with in-task processing, enabling direct, low-overhead injection into the generalist model with minimal architectural changes.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art vision generalist models under the proposed 3C4U and 3C7U evaluations across respective dataset counts (seven and ten datasets). Demonstrates superior one-shot adaptation to new tasks while maintaining performance on existing tasks.
AI.conclusion: Hidden-Shot offers an effective, cost-efficient pathway to enhance one-shot generalization in vision generalists and provides a comprehensive, data-driven evaluation framework for assessing cross-task generalization in low-level vision.

title: EO-Agents: A Three-Agent LLM Pipeline for Earth Observation Hypothesis Generation
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop
summary: Large language models have recently been explored for scientific hypothesis generation, but most prior work relies on unstructured literature and free-form textual claims. We present a pipeline for Earth observation that grounds hypothesis generation directly in the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph. A heterogeneous graph neural network trained on historical co-usage relations ranks candidate dataset pairings, and a three-agent LLM pipeline filters, generates, and evaluates structured research hypotheses. Applied to 1,475 NASA datasets, the system produces 160 hypotheses spanning multiple Earth-science domains, including ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol--cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, and stratospheric chemistry. Model-predicted novel dataset pairings are rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages from the literature, indicating that the pipeline surfaces scientifically coherent yet unexplored combinations. A 2*2*2 factorial experiment across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 shows that hypothesis rankings remain stable, while absolute scores depend strongly on judge identity, highlighting limitations of single-judge LLM evaluation.

AI.tldr: Grounded hypothesis generation in Earth observation using the NASA Knowledge Graph, combining a heterogeneous graph neural network with a three-agent LLM pipeline to rank and evaluate dataset pairings. On 1,475 NASA datasets, 160 hypotheses were generated; model-predicted pairings were rated nearly as plausible as real co-usages, with rankings robust across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 but evaluation scores varying by judge.
AI.motivation: To move hypothesis generation from unstructured literature to grounding in a structured knowledge graph, enabling more coherent and testable scientific hypotheses in Earth observation.
AI.method: Construct the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph; use a heterogeneous graph neural network trained on historical co-usage relations to rank candidate dataset pairings; deploy a three-agent LLM pipeline to filter, generate, and evaluate structured hypotheses; apply to 1,475 NASA datasets to produce 160 hypotheses across Earth-science domains; evaluate using cross-model comparisons (2x2x2 factorial across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6) to assess robustness and evaluator effects.
AI.result: Generated 160 hypotheses spanning ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol–cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, and stratospheric chemistry. Predicted novel dataset pairings rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages. Rankings remained stable across model variants, while absolute scores depended strongly on judge identity.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates that grounding hypothesis generation in a knowledge graph can yield coherent, unexplored dataset pairings. Limitations include evaluator variance and reliance on historical co-usage signals; future work could broaden domains, incorporate additional validation, and pursue multi-judge consensus.

title: DL-SLAM: Enabling High-Fidelity Gaussian Splatting SLAM in Dynamic Environments based on Dual-Level Probability
summary: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have enabled significant progress in dense dynamic Simultaneous Localization And Mapping (SLAM). Prevailing methods typically discard predefined dynamic objects, ignoring that transiently static objects offer valuable geometric constraints for pose estimation. A recent work attempts to leverage this potential by employing per-pixel uncertainty maps to quantify the magnitude of motion. While this approach enables transiently static objects to enhance pose estimation, it erroneously integrates these objects into the static map, resulting in persistent artifacts. Moreover, its reliance on purely geometric information leads to ambiguous object boundaries in the uncertainty maps. To overcome these limitations, we present DL-SLAM, a monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM system built upon a novel dual-level probabilistic framework. Our method computes dynamic probability maps by combining semantic and geometric information. These pixel-level probabilities are lifted to 3D and aggregated to derive an object-level dynamic probability for each instance. Object-level probability enables the categorical pruning of dynamic Gaussians, resulting in an artifact-free static map. The static map, in turn, provides a geometrically consistent guidance to refine the pixel-wise probabilities, enhancing their reliability. Experimental results demonstrate that DL-SLAM outperforms existing approaches, improving tracking accuracy by up to 13\% while generating high-fidelity semantic maps.

AI.tldr: DL-SLAM introduces a dual-level probabilistic framework for monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM to separate dynamic from static elements, preventing artifacts and improving pose estimation and semantic maps.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of prior 3DGS-based dynamic SLAM: transient static objects provide constraints but previous methods either ignore or mis-handle them, and purely geometric uncertainty yields blurred boundaries.
AI.method: Compute pixel-level dynamic probabilities by fusing semantic and geometric cues; lift to 3D to obtain object-level dynamic probability per instance; prune dynamic Gaussians based on object-level probabilities; use a static map as geometric prior to refine pixel-level probabilities iteratively.
AI.result: Outperforms existing approaches, with up to 13% tracking accuracy improvement and higher fidelity semantic maps; artifact-free static maps.
AI.conclusion: Dual-level probabilistic DL-SLAM improves robustness to dynamic scenes and enhances both pose estimation and semantic mapping; potential for broader adoption in monocular SLAM.

title: On the Utility and Factual Reliability of Pruned Mixture-of-Experts Models in the Biomedical Domain
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer inference speedups via selective activation but impose substantial memory requirements because the whole network must remain loaded. Structured expert pruning is a practical approach for reducing deployment costs in resource-constrained settings. However, prior studies primarily evaluate benchmark utility, leaving the effect of pruning on factual reliability underexplored, particularly in high-stakes domains such as biomedicine. In this paper, we investigate how domain-specific expert pruning affects both utility and reliability. We assess four MoE models, six pruning methods, and multiple pruning ratios across generation and classification tasks under in-domain (biomedical) and cross-domain settings. Results reveal that moderate pruning preserves in-domain utility without immediate reliability decline, although hallucination risks increase at extreme pruning ratios. When shifting to the general domain, both utility and reliability degrade rapidly. These findings indicate that safe compression depends heavily on the task and domain. Evaluating pruned MoE models solely on utility is inadequate for high-stakes deployment without reliability assessment.

AI.tldr: Moderate pruning of Mixture-of-Experts preserves in-domain biomedical utility with limited immediate reliability loss, but extreme pruning increases hallucinations; cross-domain transfer rapidly degrades both utility and reliability. Overall, safe compression is task- and domain-dependent; evaluating only utility is insufficient for high-stakes deployment.
AI.motivation: MoE models incur high memory and inference costs due to the full network being loaded. Structured expert pruning is a practical approach to reduce deployment costs, but its impact on factual reliability—especially in high-stakes domains like biomedicine—has been underexplored.
AI.method: Empirically evaluate four MoE models, six pruning methods, and multiple pruning ratios across generation and classification tasks, comparing in-domain biomedical and cross-domain settings.
AI.result: In-domain: moderate pruning preserves utility with no immediate reliability decline; hallucination risk increases at extreme pruning. Cross-domain: both utility and reliability degrade rapidly.
AI.conclusion: Safe compression depends heavily on the task and domain. Evaluating pruned MoE models solely on utility is insufficient for high-stakes deployment without reliability assessment.

title: Boosting Infrared Small Target Detection via Logit-Domain Contrast and Adaptive Shape Refinement
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Infrared small target detection (IRSTD) remains challenging due to tiny target size, low signal-to-noise ratio, severe foreground-background imbalance, and blurred boundaries in complex scenes. Existing methods usually rely on post-activation probability-domain supervision for discrimination, where weak targets and strong clutter may produce saturated and close probabilities, limiting weak-target discrimination. Meanwhile, blurred boundaries and halo-like predictions mainly stem from thermal diffusion, tiny target scale, boundary uncertainty, and insufficient explicit contour constraints. To address these issues, we propose Adaptive-Contrastive SLSIoU (AC-SLSIoU), a plug-and-play discriminative and shape-aware loss for IRSTD. Specifically, a Logit-Domain Margin Constraint (LDMC) is introduced to enlarge the response gap between targets and informative hard negatives in the logit space, thereby enhancing weak-target discrimination. Adaptive Boundary Suppression (ABS) applies scale-aware annular penalties to refine target contours and suppress halo-like overflow responses. In addition, False-Alarm Focal Loss assigns larger weights to high-probability negative samples, further penalizing persistent high-confidence false alarms. Without introducing extra inference overhead, the proposed method can be seamlessly integrated into existing detectors and consistently improves both detection accuracy and shape quality. Extensive experiments and cross-backbone evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness, robustness, and generalization ability of the proposed method for infrared small target detection.

AI.tldr: Proposes AC-SLSIoU, a plug-and-play discriminative and shape-aware loss for infrared small target detection (IRSTD), addressing weak-target discrimination, boundary refinement, and false-alarm suppression. It introduces LDMC, ABS, and False-Alarm Focal Loss to improve detection accuracy and shape quality without extra inference cost, validated across backbones.
AI.motivation: Infrared small target detection struggles with tiny targets, low SNR, foreground-background imbalance, and blurred contours. Post-activation probability supervision can saturate for weak targets; diffusion causes boundary ambiguity and halo artifacts. A discriminative, shape-aware loss with explicit contour constraints is needed to improve both detection and contour quality.
AI.method: 1) Logit-Domain Margin Constraint (LDMC) enlarges the margin between targets and hard negatives in logit space to boost weak-target discrimination. 2) Adaptive Boundary Suppression (ABS) applies scale-aware annular penalties to refine contours and suppress halo-like responses. 3) False-Alarm Focal Loss increases weights for high-probability negatives to penalize persistent false alarms. These components are plug-and-play and do not add inference overhead.
AI.result: Extensive experiments and cross-backbone evaluations show the method improves detection accuracy and shape quality, demonstrating robustness and generalization across detectors and backbone networks.
AI.conclusion: AC-SLSIoU provides discriminative, shape-aware supervision for IRSTD with no extra inference cost, enhancing weak-target discrimination, contour accuracy, and false-alarm suppression across diverse backbones.

title: Hawk: Harnessing Hardware-Aware Knowledge for High-Performance NPU Kernel Generation
summary: Developing high-performance kernels for Neural Processing Units (NPUs) is a critical industry bottleneck, requiring developers to manually navigate implicit hardware constraints and strict memory hierarchies. While large language models offer immense automation potential, they fail catastrophically on NPUs due to a fundamental lack of hardware-specific priors. Naively transplanting code snippets from similar NPU kernels may pass the compiler, but it consistently triggers runtime crashes and performance degradation by blindly violating underlying hardware constraints. To overcome this, we introduce Hawk, a training-free framework that harnesses hardware-aware knowledge through three core modules: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis Module, which employs a Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation to inherently couple the error context with executable semantics; (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval Module, which implements a 2D-Retrieval paradigm to project queries into orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; and (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation Module, which leverages LLM-driven semantic arbitration to continuously distill the knowledge by pruning errors and consolidating redundancies based on the empirical execution feedback. Extensive evaluations on real-world NPU workloads demonstrate that Hawk elevates generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0%, while achieving up to a 2.2x execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: Hawk is a training-free framework that uses hardware-aware knowledge to generate and optimize NPU kernels via three modules: Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis (Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation), Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval (2D-Retrieval into orthogonal syntactic/semantic spaces), and Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation (LLM-driven arbitration with empirical feedback), achieving higher accuracy and speed on real NPU workloads.
AI.motivation: Developers face hardware-specific constraints and memory hierarchies when writing NPU kernels. Large language models lack hardware priors and naive code reuse often crashes or underperforms. A training-free, hardware-aware framework is needed to bridge LLM capabilities with device-specific constraints.
AI.method: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis Module using Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation to couple error context with executable semantics. (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval Module with 2D-Retrieval projecting queries into orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces. (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation Module employing LLM-driven semantic arbitration to distill knowledge using empirical execution feedback and prune errors.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on real-world NPU workloads show Hawk increases generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0% and achieves up to 2.2× execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: Hawk demonstrates that a training-free, hardware-aware knowledge framework can substantially improve correctness and performance of NPU kernel generation by tightly coupling execution context, hardware constraints, and empirical feedback through a novel tri-part knowledge representation and retrieval/distillation pipeline.

title: SPLC: Social Preference Learning for Crowd Robot Navigation
summary: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) holds significant potential for crowd robot navigation in human-robot coexistence applications. However, the inherent complexity of pedestrian motion renders the design of effective reward functions for promoting socially compliant robot behaviors a persistent challenge. This paper proposes a Social Preference Learning for Crowd Robot Navigation (SPLC) algorithm to eliminate the need for detailed reward design. Its core innovation lies in the introduction of a social preference feedback mechanism to automatically generate preference data through principled preference evaluation criteria. By explicitly accounting for the intricacies of pedestrian dynamics, the pipeline mitigates the reward bias and facilitates the systematic quantification of broad social norms, thereby fostering socially compliant behaviors. Extensive experiments integrating SPLC with offline RL methods demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across standard performance metrics. Furthermore, real-world experiments on the TurtleBot4 further validate the effectiveness of SPLC in practical human-robot coexistence settings. Our code and video demos are available at https://github.com/sklus949/SPLC.

AI.tldr: SPLC introduces a social preference feedback mechanism to automate data generation for offline RL in crowd robot navigation, reducing reward design bias and improving social compliance, with positive offline and real-world TurtleBot4 results and public code.
AI.motivation: Reward design and bias are major barriers to socially compliant robot navigation in crowds; explicit modeling of pedestrian dynamics is needed to quantify social norms and guide learning without hand-crafted rewards.
AI.method: Propose Social Preference Learning for Crowd Robot Navigation (SPLC) that uses a social preference feedback mechanism to automatically generate preference data via principled evaluation criteria; integrates with offline RL to learn policies that respect pedestrian dynamics and social norms.
AI.result: Experimental results show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines on standard metrics; real-world TurtleBot4 experiments validate practicality; code and demos available.
AI.conclusion: SPLC effectively eliminates the need for detailed reward design in offline RL for crowd navigation and yields socially compliant policies, with demonstrated offline and real-world efficacy.

title: Geometry-Aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
summary:
We propose a novel hybrid neural architecture, the Geometry-aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (GRS-KAN), which integrates V.L.Rvachev's R-functions into the Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) framework. The proposed approach combines two complementary modeling mechanisms: smooth nonlinear structure is learned by KAN branches, while known geometric or logical constraints are encoded analytically using differentiable R-functions. This enables explicit representation of discontinuities, feasible regions, and implicit geometric boundaries within a trainable neural architecture.
  The framework implements differentiable logical operations through R-conjunctions and R-disjunctions, allowing complex geometric supports to be represented analytically and incorporated directly into regression models. Several GRS-KAN variants are introduced, including additive, multiplicative, and agnostic branch-weighted architectures.
  The method is demonstrated on regression problems involving discontinuities with circular and rectangular supports. Numerical experiments show that explicit geometric encoding substantially improves predictive accuracy and boundary localization compared with standard KANs. In the considered benchmarks, geometry-aware GRS-KAN models reduce test RMSE by up to 67% while simultaneously improving interpretability through explicit analytical representation of the learned geometric structure. The agnostic variant further demonstrates the ability to automatically determine whether geometric priors are beneficial for a given learning task.

AI.tldr: Hybrid Geometry-aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (GRS-KAN) integrates differentiable R-functions with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks to encode geometric/logical priors, enabling explicit discontinuities and feasible regions. Variants include additive, multiplicative, and agnostic branch-weighted architectures; demonstrated on regression with circular/rectangular supports, yielding up to 67% RMSE reduction and improved interpretability; agnostic variant selects whether priors help.
AI.motivation: To incorporate known geometric or logical constraints into neural regression models, enabling explicit representation of discontinuities and feasible regions, and improving accuracy and interpretability beyond purely data-driven KANs.
AI.method: Extend KAN by embedding differentiable R-functions (R-conjunctions and R-disjunctions) to encode geometry and logic. Develop additive, multiplicative, and agnostic branch-weighted variants. Train on regression problems with geometric discontinuities (e.g., circular/rectangular supports) and compare to standard KANs, evaluating predictive accuracy and boundary localization.
AI.result: Geometry-aware GRS-KAN outperforms standard KAN, with substantial predictive gains (RMSE reductions up to 67%) and enhanced boundary localization and interpretability due to explicit analytic geometric representations. The agnostic variant can automatically determine when geometric priors are beneficial.
AI.conclusion: GRS-KAN provides a principled mechanism to fuse geometric priors with trainable neural models, achieving improved performance and interpretability. The agnostic variant offers automatic selection of prior usefulness, suggesting practical applicability across tasks with known geometric structure.

title: Mind the Gap: Standard 3DGS Evaluation Primarily Measures Near-Trajectory Interpolation
summary: Standard MipNeRF360-style 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) evaluation holds out every N-th frame -- but these frames have trained neighbors on both sides, so the metric measures near-trajectory interpolation rather than spatial generalization. We introduce a fair matched-count protocol that isolates this effect: both arms train on the same number of images and differ only in whether the holdout is spread evenly (interpolation) or forms a contiguous spatial sector (extrapolation). Our primary finding is a large, consistent interpolation-extrapolation gap of 3~12dB -- several times the differences typically reported between competing methods. The gap is robust to training noise, is in two cases large enough to flip a method ranking under multi-seed confirmation, and -- crucially -- persists across three representation families, including a non-Gaussian volumetric neural radiance field (NeRF), so it reflects spatial coverage rather than any one representation. Diagnostically, it is dominated by a diffuse/geometry-proxy component and tracks each view's angular distance to its nearest training view, a zero-cost signal that also guides capture planning; loss-side regularization yields only marginal gains. Standard holdouts remain useful for near-trajectory rendering but should not, alone, be read as evidence of spatial generalization. Prior work notes protocol sensitivity; ours is, to our knowledge, the first to combine matched-count paired holdout, cross-representation quantification, and a diagnostic analysis Table 1. We describe a spatial-holdout benchmark toolkit with standardized splits and baselines for 16 scenes, which we are preparing for public release.

AI.tldr: Matched-count, spatial-holdout evaluation reveals a robust interpolation-extrapolation gap (3–12 dB) in 3D scene representations, persisting across methods and representations; introduces a standardized spatial-holdout benchmark toolkit for 16 scenes.
AI.motivation: To isolate true spatial generalization from near-trajectory interpolation in 3D scene representations (e.g., MipNeRF360, 3DGS) by removing bias from holdout frames adjacent to trained views.
AI.method: Introduce a matched-count holdout protocol where the holdout set is either evenly spread (interpolation) or forms a contiguous spatial sector (extrapolation) while training on the same number of images. Evaluate across multiple representation families (including Gaussian splatting and non-Gaussian NeRFs), perform cross-representation quantification, and use a diagnostic analysis based on angular distance to the nearest training view. Validate with multiple seeds and 16 scenes; provide a spatial-holdout benchmark toolkit.
AI.result: A large, consistent 3–12 dB interpolation-extrapolation gap is found, robust to training noise and large enough to flip rankings under multi-seed tests. The gap persists across three representation families, indicating it reflects spatial coverage rather than a specific representation. Diagnostics show the gap is dominated by a diffuse/geometry-proxy component and correlates with each view’s angular distance to the nearest training view. Loss-side regularization yields only marginal gains. Standard holdouts remain informative for near-trajectory rendering but do not alone evidence spatial generalization.
AI.conclusion: Spatial-holdout evaluation is essential for assessing true spatial generalization in 3D scene representations. The work provides a protocol that combines matched-count paired holds, cross-representation analysis, and diagnostic metrics, and offers a public spatial-holdout benchmark toolkit for 16 scenes.

title: Safe and Adaptive Cloud Healing: Verifying LLM-Generated Recovery Plans with a Neural-Symbolic World Model
summary: As the scale and complexity of cloud-based AI systems continue to escalate, ensuring service reliability through rapid fault detection and adaptive recovery has become a critical challenge. While existing approaches integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) for semantic understanding and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for policy optimization, they often rely on sequential, loosely coupled architectures that underutilize the generative and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. In this paper, we propose a paradigm shift with PASE, a Planning-Aware Semantic self-healing engine, a novel fault self-healing framework that reconceptualizes recovery as a neuro-symbolic program synthesis task. PASE employs an LLM as a core Plan Synthesis Engine to generate structured recovery plans from a library of semantic primitives. A Neural-Symbolic World Model verifies plan feasibility through simulation, while a Meta-Prompt Optimizer, trained via DRL, learns to generate optimal prompts that guide the LLM's planning process. This tight reason-plan-verify-adapt loop enables dynamic, context-aware recovery strategy generation beyond predefined action spaces. Experiments on a real-world cloud fault injection dataset demonstrate that PASE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, reducing average system recovery time by over 40% and improving fault detection accuracy in unknown fault scenarios. Our framework advances autonomous system management by unifying LLM-based reasoning with model-assisted verification and meta-learned guidance.

AI.tldr: PASE reframes cloud fault recovery as neuro-symbolic program synthesis, uniting LLM-based planning, neural-symbolic verification, and DRL-tuned prompts to achieve faster, more accurate self-healing beyond fixed action spaces.
AI.motivation: As cloud AI systems scale, reliability requires rapid fault detection and adaptive recovery; existing LLM+DRL approaches rely on sequential, loosely coupled architectures that underutilize LLMs.
AI.method: PASE uses an LLM as Plan Synthesis Engine to generate structured recovery plans from semantic primitives; a Neural-Symbolic World Model verifies plan feasibility via simulation; a Meta-Prompt Optimizer (DRL-trained) learns prompts to guide the LLM's planning; operates in a tight reason-plan-verify-adapt loop.
AI.result: On real-world cloud fault injection data, PASE reduces average recovery time by >40% and improves fault detection accuracy in unknown fault scenarios, outperforming state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: PASE advances autonomous system management by unifying LLM-based reasoning with model-assisted verification and meta-learned guidance, enabling dynamic recovery strategy generation beyond predefined action spaces.

title: PhysMani: Physics-principled 3D World Model for Dynamic Object Manipulation
comment: ECCV 2026. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/vLAR-group/PhysMani
summary: Manipulating fast and dynamically moving targets in unstructured 3D environments remains challenging for embodied AI. Existing visual-language-action models and world models struggle with accurate 3D geometry and physically meaningful forecasting. We propose PhysMani, a framework that couples a physics-principled 3D Gaussian world model with a future-aware action policy model. The world model learns a divergence-free Gaussian velocity field via online optimization for fast and physically grounded future dynamics prediction. The policy model integrates the predicted 3D scene future dynamics through a learnable token based cross-attention module. We introduce PhysMani-Bench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark with 16 tasks, and demonstrate a superior success rate over strong baselines in both simulation and real-world robot experiments.

AI.tldr: PhysMani introduces a physics-principled 3D Gaussian world model with a future-aware action policy for dynamic 3D manipulation, plus PhysMani-Bench benchmark; achieves superior success rates in simulation and real-world experiments.
AI.motivation: Current visual-language-action models and world models struggle with accurate 3D geometry and forecasting in dynamic 3D manipulation tasks within unstructured environments.
AI.method: Couples a divergence-free Gaussian velocity field world model learned via online optimization to predict future dynamics; policy model uses a learnable token-based cross-attention module to integrate predicted dynamics; 3D Gaussian world model is physics-principled; introduces PhysMani-Bench with 16 tasks; demonstrates results in both simulation and real-robot experiments.
AI.result: Superior success rate over strong baselines across 16 dynamic manipulation tasks in both simulation and real-world robot experiments.
AI.conclusion: PhysMani provides a viable framework for fast, physically grounded dynamic manipulation in unstructured 3D environments, and the benchmark validates its effectiveness across simulated and real settings.

title: Token Geometry
summary: Language models learn continuous programs over discrete symbols, with the embedding table and LM-head acting as the read/write interface between them. We show that this interface has gradient geometry distinct from dense hidden weights which can be exploited to improve the Pareto frontier across supervised finetuning, RL, and pretraining, while only utilizing kilobytes of optimizer state. We introduce Ember, a lightweight optimizer for embedding and LM-head matrices that utilizes O(V + D) VRAM, instead of Adam's O(2VD), and forgoes the need to shard both token table optimizer states. We provide empirical evidence that Ember scales effectively across batch size and parameter count. We show that the optimization trajectory of tokens can be well described by a simple 1D ray, counter to the popular belief that neural net parameters navigate a heavily nonconvex landscape. We provide a principled view on the surprisingly narrow space of optimizers that suffice for Transformer training. Finally, we open-source our distributed Ember implementation that merges cleanly with existing ZeRO/FSDP setups to support further research at https://github.com/katop1234/ember

AI.tldr: Ember is a lightweight optimizer for embedding and LM-head matrices that leverages distinct gradient geometry from dense weights to improve the training Pareto frontier (performance vs. memory) across supervised finetuning, RL, and pretraining, with O(V+D) VRAM usage and kilobytes of optimizer state; it integrates with ZeRO/FSDP and is open-sourced.
AI.motivation: Embedding tables and the LM-head serve as the read/write interface between discrete symbols and continuous representations. This interface exhibits gradient geometry that differs from dense hidden weights. Exploiting this geometry can reduce memory and improve optimization efficiency across transformer training.
AI.method: Introduce Ember, a memory-efficient optimizer specifically for embedding and LM-head matrices. It uses O(V + D) VRAM rather than Adam's O(2VD) and avoids sharding both token table optimizer states. Provide a distributed implementation that merges with ZeRO/FSDP. Empirically evaluate scale across batch size and parameter count, analyze the optimization trajectory as a 1D ray, and present a principled view on the narrow set of optimizers sufficient for Transformer training.
AI.result: Ember scales effectively with batch size and parameter count, delivering improved Pareto frontiers for supervised finetuning, RL, and pretraining. It achieves large memory savings (kilobytes of optimizer state) and integrates with existing distributed training frameworks. The authors provide an open-source implementation at the linked repository.
AI.conclusion: The gradient geometry of embedding/LM-head interfaces is distinct and exploitable. A small, principled class of optimizers may suffice for Transformer training, enabling efficient scaling with minimal optimizer-state memory. Ember demonstrates practical gains and invites broader adoption and further research.

title: MVFusion-GS: Motion-Variance Guided Temporal Attention for High-Quality Dynamic Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis for static scenes. Extending it to dynamic scenes via deformation fields has recently attracted significant attention, particularly for dynamic scene reconstructionband distractor-free. However, existing deformation networks lack explicit motion awareness: they neither capture long-term motion intensity nor exploit short-term temporal coherence, leading to inaccurate foreground deformation and pseudo-static residuals in the background. We present MVFusion-GS, a method that enhances deformation networks with two complementary motion-aware mechanisms. The Motion-Variance Guided Refinement aggregates per-Gaussian deformation statistics across time to estimate motion variance and uses it to guide dynamic-static separation during deformation prediction. The MotionFormer Temporal Attention module applies Transformer self-attention over neighboring timesteps to model local motion dependencies and improve temporal consistency. Extensive experiments on both dynamic scene reconstruction and distractor-free reconstruction benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, showing that explicit motion awareness improves both foreground motion modeling and static background reconstruction.

AI.tldr: MVFusion-GS enhances 3DGaussian Splatting with explicit motion awareness via Motion-Variance Guided Refinement and MotionFormer Temporal Attention, achieving state-of-the-art dynamic scene reconstruction and distractor-free static background.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of explicit motion awareness in deformation networks for dynamic scene synthesis, which leads to inaccurate foreground deformation and background residuals.
AI.method: Two components: (1) Motion-Variance Guided Refinement computes per-Gaussian deformation statistics over time to estimate motion variance and uses it to separate dynamic vs static regions during deformation prediction; (2) MotionFormer Temporal Attention applies Transformer self-attention over neighboring timesteps to model local motion dependencies and improve temporal consistency.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on dynamic scene reconstruction and distractor-free benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, with improved foreground motion modeling and static background reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: Explicit motion awareness, via variance-guided refinement and temporal attention, improves deformation prediction for dynamic scenes, enabling better dynamic foreground modeling and static background reconstruction; MVFusion-GS sets a new standard for motion-aware dynamic NeRF-like methods.

title: SemHash-LLM: A Multi-Granularity Semantic Hashing Framework for Document Deduplication
summary: Large scale document deduplication must preserve semantic equivalence while remaining efficient over massive corpora. We present SemHash LLM, a multi granularity framework that unifies semantic projection hashing, attention weighted MinHash, contrastive boundary learning, and selective LLM based adjudication. The method combines character, token, and document level signals through gated fusion, then applies a cascaded filtering pipeline for efficient candidate reduction. Semantic projection hashing learns compact binary codes in distilled LLM embedding space, while attention weighted Min- Hash suppresses boilerplate and emphasizes informative content. Adaptive decision boundaries and uncertainty estimation further improve robustness across template pollution, short text perturbation, containment, and viral fragments. Experiments show that SemHash LLM achieves strong duplicate detection quality with less than one percent neural verification cost.

AI.tldr: A multi-granularity framework (SemHash LLM) for large-scale document deduplication that combines semantic projection hashing, attention-weighted MinHash, contrastive boundary learning, and selective LLM adjudication to achieve accurate duplicates with minimal neural verification.
AI.motivation: To preserve semantic equivalence in deduplication across massive corpora while keeping computational cost low, addressing boilerplate, noise, and perturbations.
AI.method: Fusion of character-, token-, and document-level signals via gated fusion; cascaded filtering for candidate reduction; semantic projection hashing to binary codes in distilled LLM space; attention-weighted MinHash to downweight boilerplate; adaptive decision boundaries and uncertainty estimation for robustness (template pollution, short text perturbation, containment, viral fragments); selective LLM adjudication.
AI.result: Empirical results show strong duplicate detection with less than 1% neural verification cost.
AI.conclusion: SemHash LLM provides an effective, scalable solution for semantic deduplication with high accuracy and low neural verification burden, suitable for very large corpora.

title: A Stereo Visual SLAM System Using Object-Level Motion Estimation and Geometric Filtering Based on Cross Disparity
summary: This paper presents OCD SLAM, a dynamic stereo visual SLAM framework that extends ORB-SLAM2 by jointly addressing dynamic objects and dynamic features in the scene. Usual visual SLAM systems operating in dynamic environments often fail in the presence of moving objects, due to the static-world assumption used in pose estimation and mapping. To address this predicament, we introduce a novel geometric approach based on the discrepancy between disparity and a newly proposed notion called ``cross disparity'', which exploits both temporal and stereo inconsistency to identify dynamic feature points. Complementary to this feature-level motion analysis, OCD SLAM integrates a 3D object detection module (SMOKE) with Kalman filter-based object tracking to perform object-level motion classification, enabling robust separation of static and dynamic scene elements for accurate pose estimation. The proposed approach has been evaluated on various sequences from the KITTI Odometry and KITTI Raw datasets. Results demonstrate that OCD SLAM achieves significant improvement in trajectory accuracy compared to ORB-SLAM2 and several state-of-the-art dynamic SLAM methods. Ablation studies further demonstrate the effectiveness of the cross disparity module in the KITTI Raw dataset and show that this method is able to detect dynamic features that are missed by the 3D object detection scheme alone.

AI.tldr: A dynamic stereo visual SLAM (OCD SLAM) extends ORB-SLAM2 to handle dynamic scenes by cross disparity-based dynamic feature detection and object-level motion classification via SMOKE and Kalman tracking; evaluated on KITTI datasets with improved trajectory accuracy and ablation showing cross disparity effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Static-world assumptions in traditional SLAM fail in dynamic environments; robustly identifying and excluding dynamic elements is necessary for accurate pose estimation and mapping.
AI.method: Introduce cross disparity as a measure that exploits stereo and temporal inconsistencies to identify dynamic feature points; couple a 3D object detector (SMOKE) with Kalman-filter-based object tracking for object-level motion classification; integrate these components to separate static/dynamic elements within the ORB-SLAM2 framework; validate on KITTI Odometry and KITTI Raw sequences; include ablation studies.
AI.result: Significant improvement in trajectory accuracy compared to ORB-SLAM2 and several state-of-the-art dynamic SLAM methods; ablation shows the cross disparity module effectively detects dynamics and can identify dynamic features missed by the object-detection pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Cross disparity combined with explicit object-level motion modeling yields robust dynamic SLAM in stereo setups, enhancing pose estimation and map quality even when dynamic elements are present; cross-disparity provides complementary motion cues beyond 3D object detections.

title: Class-Grouped Normalized Momentum and Faster Hyperparameter Exploration to Tackle Class Imbalance in Federated Learning
summary: Class imbalance poses a critical challenge in federated learning (FL), where underrepresented classes suffer from poor predictive performance yet cannot be addressed by standard centralized techniques due to privacy and heterogeneity constraints. We propose FedCGNM (Federated Class-Grouped Normalized Momentum), a client-side optimizer in FL that partitions classes into a small number of groups based on minimum within-group variance, maintains a momentum per group, normalizes each group momentum to unit length, and uses the summation of the normalized group momentums as an update direction. This design both equalizes gradient magnitude across majority and minority groups and mitigates the noise inherent in rare-class gradients. We further provide a theoretical convergence analysis explicitly accounting for time-varying resampling-rates. Additionally, to efficiently optimize these rates in small-client regimes, we introduce FedHOO, an X-armed-bandit (XAB) based algorithm that exploits federated parallelism that evaluates many combinations of two candidate rates per client at linear cost. Empirical evaluation on four public long-tailed benchmarks and a proprietary chip-defect dataset demonstrates that FedCGNM consistently outperforms baselines, with FedHOO yielding further gains in small-scale federations.

AI.tldr: FedCGNM introduces class-grouped normalized momentum for class-imbalanced federated learning, with a convergence analysis and FedHOO for efficient rate optimization; demonstrates gains on long-tailed benchmarks and proprietary data.
AI.motivation: Address class imbalance in federated learning under privacy and data heterogeneity constraints, where standard centralized imbalance remedies are inapplicable.
AI.method: Partition classes into a small number of groups by minimizing within-group variance; maintain a momentum per group; normalize each group's momentum to unit length; use the sum of normalized group momentums as the update direction. Provide convergence analysis with time-varying resampling rates. Introduce FedHOO, an X-armed-bandit based rate-optimization algorithm that exploits federated parallelism to evaluate many combinations of two candidate rates per client at linear cost.
AI.result: FedCGNM consistently outperforms baselines on four public long-tailed benchmarks and a proprietary chip-defect dataset; FedHOO yields additional gains in small-scale federations.
AI.conclusion: Class-grouped normalized momentum improves minority-class performance and stabilizes gradients in FL; FedHOO provides efficient rate optimization in small-client settings, enhancing overall performance.

title: VLAFlow: A Unified Training Framework for Vision-Language-Action Models via Co-training and Future Latent Alignment
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have recently advanced robotic manipulation, yet the effects of different robot-data pre-training paradigms remain difficult to compare because existing models often differ in architecture, data, action space, and evaluation protocol. We present VLAFlow (Vision-Language-Action Flow), a unified flow-matching framework for controlled comparison of VLA training objectives. Using a heterogeneous robot corpus, OXEMix, containing approximately 5,000 hours of data from DROID, OpenX-Embodiment, OpenX-Augmented, and RoboCOIN, we evaluate four paradigms under the same pi0-style architecture, shared VLM backbone, action expert, and 14-dimensional action space: action-only modeling (MindPI), language-supervised co-training (MindLPI), future latent alignment (MindWPI), and their combination (MindLWPI). Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv show that action-only pre-training is sensitive to heterogeneous data. In contrast, language supervision helps preserve vision-language generalization, while future latent alignment improves state-transition and action-outcome modeling. By combining both signals, MindLWPI achieves the most stable overall transfer performance across benchmarks. These results suggest a meta-action space view: language and future latent representations provide complementary intermediate constraints that make heterogeneous action supervision smoother and more transferable.

AI.tldr: A unified framework (VLAFlow) enables fair comparison of vision-language-action pre-training paradigms on heterogeneous robot data. Language supervision preserves vision-language generalization; future latent alignment enhances state-transition modeling; combining both yields the most stable cross-benchmark transfer, supporting a meta-action-space view where language and latent representations act as complementary constraints.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA pre-training studies use varied architectures, data, and protocols, hindering fair comparison. A controlled, unified framework and diverse robot data are needed to disentangle the effects of action-only vs language-supervised vs latent-forecast objectives on transfer performance across benchmarks.
AI.method: Introduce VLAFlow, a unified flow-matching framework with a pi0-style architecture and shared VLM backbone. Use OXEMix (~5k hours from DROID, OpenX-Embodiment, OpenX-Augmented, RoboCOIN) to evaluate four paradigms (MindPI, MindLPI, MindWPI, MindLWPI) with a 14D action space across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv.
AI.result: Action-only pre-training is sensitive to data heterogeneity. Language supervision preserves vision-language generalization; future latent alignment improves state-transition and action-outcome modeling. The combination MindLWPI gives the most stable overall transfer across benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: A meta-action-space view emerges: language and future latent representations provide complementary constraints that make heterogeneous action supervision smoother and more transferable, enabling more robust VLA transfer across diverse robotic tasks and datasets.

title: Profit-Based Counterfactual Explanations for Product Improvement: A Case Study of Manga Sales in Japan
summary: Counterfactual explanation (CE) is widely used to enhance the interpretability of machine learning models and support data-driven decision-making based on model predictions. However, existing CE methods typically require two exogenously specified inputs: a desired output value (target) and a distance function that quantifies changes in explanatory variables. In regression settings, neither the validity of target specification nor the practical interpretation of the distance metric has been sufficiently addressed. Furthermore, most existing CE methods focus on altering predictions rather than optimizing a decision objective, even though real-world decision-making often requires explicit objective maximization. To address these limitations, we formulate CE as a profit maximization problem in management and marketing contexts and propose a framework termed profit-based counterfactual explanation (PBCE). PBCE eliminates the need for exogenous target specification by directly maximizing profit as the primary optimization objective. Concurrently, the distance term is reinterpreted as the cost of modifying product attributes, providing a clear and economically grounded interpretation.

AI.tldr: Profit-based counterfactual explanations (PBCE) reformulate CE as profit maximization, removing the need for an exogenous target and interpreting the distance metric as modification cost, to better align explanations with decision objectives in management/marketing.
AI.motivation: Counterfactual explanations typically require an externally specified target and a distance function; in regression, the validity and interpretability of the target and distance can be questionable. Real-world decision-making often aims to maximize an objective (e.g., profit) rather than merely alter predictions.
AI.method: Formulate CE as a profit-maximization problem. Eliminate the need for an exogenous target by directly maximizing profit; reinterpret the distance term as the cost of modifying product attributes, providing economic interpretation.
AI.result: Proposes the PBCE framework: a theoretical formulation that yields profit-driven counterfactuals with an economic interpretation of attribute changes.
AI.conclusion: PBCE aligns counterfactual explanations with real-world decision objectives and economics, potentially improving decision support; future work should include empirical validation, extension to multi-objective settings, and robustness analyses.

title: Cross-Platform Control for Autonomous Surface Vehicles via Adaptive Reinforcement Learning
summary: Autonomous surface vehicles vary widely in hydrodynamic and actuation characteristics, yet most controllers are designed for single-platform deployment. We present an adaptive reinforcement learning approach for trajectory tracking that enables zero-shot cross-platform deployment using a single policy. Since the deployment platform's dynamics are unknown to the policy, we address cross-platform generalization with the standard partial-observability approach of conditioning on interaction history, employing a teacher-student architecture in which a learned module infers a latent representation of the platform dynamics. The policy is trained in simulation under randomized vessel dynamics and is deployed zero-shot to two real-world platforms without any fine-tuning, despite relying on a simple analytical dynamics model rather than a high-fidelity hydrodynamic simulator. In real-world experiments on two different platforms, the adaptive policy outperforms non-adaptive learning-based baselines by up to 58% in position mean absolute error while approaching the tracking accuracy of a platform-specific tuned controller.

AI.tldr: Adaptive RL policy for trajectory tracking on diverse autonomous surface vehicles that generalizes cross-platform via a teacher-student latent dynamics module, enabling zero-shot deployment with no tuning.
AI.motivation: Cross-platform deployment of AUV controllers is challenging due to wide variation in hydrodynamics and actuation; a single policy that generalizes across platforms is highly desirable.
AI.method: Train an adaptive RL policy under partial observability by conditioning on interaction history. Use a teacher-student architecture where a learned module infers a latent representation of platform dynamics. Train in simulation with randomized vessel dynamics; deploy zero-shot to two real platforms using a simple analytical dynamics model rather than a high-fidelity hydrodynamic simulator.
AI.result: On two real platforms, the adaptive policy outperforms non-adaptive learning baselines by up to 58% in position mean absolute error and approaches the tracking accuracy of platform-specific tuned controllers.
AI.conclusion: Zero-shot cross-platform deployment of a single policy is feasible for heterogeneous surface vehicles using latent-dynamics inference within an adaptive RL framework; simple dynamics models can suffice, though real-world robustness and scalability to more platforms remain to be explored.

title: How to Allocate Your Tokens? Scaling Laws with Training Steps and Batch Size
summary: We propose a scaling law that takes into account model size and training data while explicitly splitting the latter into training steps and batch size (called three-term law). Fitting the proposed law on a large set of training runs, we find that it correctly recovers the scaling of the optimal batch size. Moreover, because it makes use of training runs with suboptimal batch size, our proposed law can be robustly fit with a significantly smaller amount of training runs. We further show that the three-term law can be used to derive scaling laws for suboptimal batch sizes, and that it matches previous empirical findings related to the critical batch size.

AI.tldr: Three-term scaling law that explicitly models batch size alongside model size and data; enables accurate recovery of optimal batch size scaling and robust estimation from suboptimal-batch runs, plus derivation of suboptimal-batch scaling and alignment with critical batch size findings.
AI.motivation: To unify model-scale and data-scale scaling with explicit incorporation of batch size, enabling robust, data-efficient predictions of training efficiency.
AI.method: Propose a three-term scaling law incorporating model size, training data, and batch size. Fit this law across a large corpus of training runs that include suboptimal batch sizes. Compare its performance to prior two-term laws and analyze its ability to recover optimal-batch-size scaling and to yield suboptimal-batch scaling laws and critical-batch-size behavior.
AI.result: The three-term law accurately recovers how optimal batch size scales with model/data, can be robustly fitted using suboptimal-batch runs, and allows derivation of scaling laws for suboptimal batch sizes. It aligns with existing empirical findings on the critical batch size.
AI.conclusion: The proposed three-term law provides a practical framework for scaling that explicitly accounts for batch size, enabling data-efficient fitting and actionable guidance for batch-size selection across model and data regimes.

title: Multi-THuMBS: Multi-person Tracking of 3D Human Meshes Beyond Video Shots
