summary: Tracking multi-person 3D human meshes from in-the-wild videos is a highly challenging problem due to complex interactions, frequent occlusions, and severe truncation inherent in unconstrained environments. While recent approaches have improved robustness against these issues, they largely overlook the critical challenge prevalent in real-world footage: frequent shot changes. These abrupt transitions in camera viewpoints often cause existing methods to lose track of human identities and fail in reconstructing temporally coherent trajectories. Although several recent works have explored 3D human mesh tracking under shot changes, they are still limited to single-person scenarios, making them inadequate for real-world videos where multiple people interact and appear simultaneously. To address this limitation, we propose Multi-THuMBS (Multi-person Tracking of 3D Human Meshes Beyond Video Shots) that leverages a state-of-the-art 3D scene prior to reconstruct the two boundary frames in a single shared 3D space. Human meshes are then registered within the shared 3D space, maintaining per-person identity and motion consistency across shot changes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach yields significant improvements in 3D human mesh recovery, camera pose estimation, and identity tracking, thereby ensuring high-fidelity motion reconstruction with consistent identity preservation across shots compared to previous state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: Multi-THuMBS tracks multiple 3D human meshes across video shot changes by aligning two boundary frames in a shared 3D space using a scene prior, preserving per-person identities and improving 3D reconstruction and camera pose estimation over single-person shot-change methods.
AI.motivation: In unconstrained videos, abrupt shot changes disrupt identity tracking and temporal coherence; existing shot-change methods focus on single-person scenarios and fail in multi-person settings.
AI.method: Leverages a state-of-the-art 3D scene prior to reconstruct the two boundary frames in a shared 3D space; registers per-person meshes into this space to maintain identity and motion consistency across shots.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show significant improvements in 3D mesh recovery, camera pose estimation, and identity tracking across shot changes compared with previous SOTA methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables high-fidelity multi-person 3D mesh tracking across video shots with consistent identities in unconstrained settings.

title: Scaling with Confidence: Calibrating Confidence of LLMs for Adaptive Test Time Scaling
summary: Training large language models (LLMs) with reinforcement learning (RL) has significantly advanced their performance on reasoning and question-answering tasks. However, prevailing RL reward designs typically prioritize response correctness, neglecting to incentivize models to express their confidence accurately. This leads to a critical problem: performance gains are often accompanied by poor calibration between confidence and accuracy, misleading models to overconfidently hallucinate when uncertain. To address this limitation, we propose $\textbf{C}$orrectness and $\textbf{C}$onfidence $\textbf{C}$alibration $\textbf{R}$einforcement $\textbf{L}$earning ($\textbf{C3RL}$), a novel RL algorithm integrating correctness, calibration and dataset-informed reference accuracy rewards together. Comprehensive evaluation across 8 text and multimodal datasets demonstrates that C3RL enhances calibration without sacrificing accuracy, outperforming the current state-of-the-art method in both performance and calibration metrics. Utilizing the well-calibrated verbalized confidence from C3RL, we further introduce $\textbf{C}$onfidence-based $\textbf{A}$daptive Test Time $\textbf{S}$caling ($\textbf{CAS}$), an adjustable inference-time strategy that allocates computational resources based on response confidence. Experiments show that CAS surpasses majority voting on both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets while reducing the inference budget by up to 12.33 times. We believe the synergy of C3RL and CAS paves the way for deploying more reliable and resource-efficient LLMs. The code, data and models will be released.

AI.tldr: C3RL introduces a reinforcement learning objective for LLMs that jointly optimizes correctness and confidence calibration using dataset-informed reference accuracy; coupled with Confidence-based Adaptive Test Time Scaling (CAS) for resource-aware inference; achieves better calibration without loss of accuracy and reduces inference cost (up to 12.33x) compared to baselines.
AI.motivation: RL rewards for LLMs typically optimize correctness but neglect confidence calibration, leading to overconfident errors (hallucinations). There is a need to align model confidence with actual accuracy and enable efficient inference.
AI.method: Develop C3RL: an RL objective that combines correctness, calibration, and dataset-informed reference accuracy rewards. Evaluate on 8 text and multimodal datasets. Introduce CAS: an inference-time strategy that allocates computing resources based on elicited response confidence, improving efficiency while maintaining or improving accuracy. Compare against state-of-the-art baselines and majority voting.
AI.result: C3RL improves calibration without sacrificing accuracy across multiple datasets and surpasses SOTA in both performance and calibration metrics. CAS further enhances resource efficiency, outperforming majority voting on in-domain and out-of-domain data and reducing inference budget by up to 12.33x.
AI.conclusion: The combination of C3RL and CAS enables more reliable and resource-efficient LLMs. The authors plan to release code, data, and models to support reproducibility and practical deployment.

title: Guided Action Flow: Q-Guided Inference for Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Flow-matching vision-language-action policies generate robot action chunks through an iterative transport process, creating an opportunity for test-time guidance without retraining the base policy. We study this opportunity in Guided Action Flow, an inference-time framework that keeps a pretrained SmolVLA policy frozen and uses a learned action-chunk critic to guide its reverse-time flow sampler. The critic is trained from real success and failure rollouts, can condition on task-description features from the frozen SmolVLA language pathway, and is used only through action gradients during sampling. We evaluate the approach on LIBERO manipulation tasks. A single-task critic improves success from 68.0% to 82.0% on one seed window and from 82.0% to 86.0% on another. A multi-family task-description critic improves validation success from 46.0% to 56.0%, while the locked held-out test gain is positive but modest, from 65.0% to 67.5%. These results support the feasibility of Q-guided inference for frozen flow-matching VLA policies, while showing that critic generalization and uncertainty-aware guidance remain the central bottlenecks.

AI.tldr: Inference-time guidance via a learned action-chunk critic improves the performance of a frozen flow-matching VLA policy on LIBERO tasks, showing feasibility but highlighting critic generalization and uncertainty-aware guidance as key bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: Enable test-time improvement of a frozen base policy without retraining by steering the reverse-time sampling with a critic conditioned on task descriptions.
AI.method: Train an action-chunk critic from real success and failure rollouts; condition the critic on task-description features from the SmolVLA language pathway; apply the critic exclusively through action gradients during sampling; keep the base policy frozen; evaluate on LIBERO manipulation tasks with single-task and multi-family task descriptions.
AI.result: Single-task critic improved success from 68.0% to 82.0% on one seed window and from 82.0% to 86.0% on another. A multi-family task-description critic improved validation success from 46.0% to 56.0%, with held-out test gain from 65.0% to 67.5%. These gains support the feasibility of Q-guided inference for frozen flow-matching VLA policies, but generalization and uncertainty-aware guidance remain central bottlenecks.
AI.conclusion: Q-guided inference for frozen flow-matching VLA policies is feasible; however improvements in critic generalization and uncertainty-aware guidance are needed to fully exploit test-time guidance.

title: Don't Let Gains FADE: Breaking Down Policy Gradient Weights in RL
summary: Reinforcement learning post-training dramatically improves LLM reasoning, but suffers from training instability and diversity collapse. Advantage functions offer an appealing fix: they reshape the training objective, reweight which rollouts drive learning, and are trivial to implement. Yet a proliferation of methods makes it unclear which advantage to use and when. We cut through the confusion with a unifying framework that decomposes any advantage into its positive and negative gradient mass along two orthogonal axes. On the sign axis, imbalanced updates collapse either entropy or weight geometry. On the difficulty axis, hard-problem focus sharpens signal but costs sample size. Both trade-offs shift during training: exploration favors balance and hard focus; exploitation favors suppression and medium focus. This motivates FADE (Focal Advantage with Dynamic Entropy), a self-adapting advantage that reads training dynamics to schedule the gradient weight automatically. FADE reaches peak pass@1 20k steps earlier than the best static baseline at the 7B scale and 2k steps earlier at the 32B , while achieving the best accuracy-diversity trade-off across all pass@k on LiveCodeBench and AIME.

AI.tldr: A unified gradient-analysis framework for RL-based post-training of LLMs, introducing FADE (Focal Advantage with Dynamic Entropy) to adaptively balance gradient mass and entropy to improve efficiency and diversity.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning post-training can boost LLM reasoning but suffers from training instability and diversity collapse; there is confusion over which advantage function to use; a principled understanding and adaptive mechanism are needed.
AI.method: Decompose any advantage into positive and negative gradient mass along two orthogonal axes (sign axis and difficulty axis). Analyze how imbalanced updates affect entropy and weight geometry; propose FADE that self-adapts the gradient weight based on training dynamics to balance exploration/exploitation and hard/medium focus.
AI.result: FADE achieves earlier peak pass@1 by 20k steps at the 7B scale and 2k steps at the 32B scale; it attains the best accuracy-diversity trade-off across all pass@k on LiveCodeBench and AIME.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, self-adaptive advantage scheduling improves RL-based LLM post-training by stabilizing training, maintaining diversity, and delivering superior performance on established benchmarks.

title: Online Segment 3D Gaussians via Launching Virtual Drones
summary:
Interactive segmentation of 3D Gaussians offers a compelling opportunity for real-time manipulation of 3D scenes, thanks to the real-time rendering capability of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). However, existing methods require a time-consuming per-scene setup - typically tens of seconds or even minutes - before interactive segmentation can begin on a raw 3DGS scene. This setup involves multi-view mask preparation, mask lifting, and feature distillation, creating a major bottleneck for online applications.
  To address this limitation, we aim to completely eliminate the setup stage for interactive 3DGS segmentation while keeping the segmentation time practical (under 1 second). In this work, we present SAGO (Segment Any Gaussians Online), a novel setup-free framework for interactive 3DGS segmentation. By introducing virtual drones, our method reframes the 3D segmentation problem as an online Next-Best-View (NBV) planning task formulated within a Markov process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAGO can extract clean 3D assets directly from 3D Gaussians with sub-second latency, thereby enabling a broad range of downstream applications such as object manipulation and scene editing. Moreover, our method achieves over a 50x speedup compared to the previous setup-free 3DGS segmentation frameworks.

AI.tldr: SAGO provides a setup-free, real-time interactive segmentation for 3D Gaussian Splatting by reframing the problem as online Next-Best-View planning using virtual drones, achieving sub-second latency and over 50× speedup versus prior setup-free methods.
AI.motivation: To remove the costly per-scene pre-processing (multi-view masks, mask lifting, feature distillation) required for interactive 3DGS segmentation, enabling real-time online applications.
AI.method: Introduce virtual drones and formulate the segmentation task as an online Next-Best-View planning problem within a Markov decision process. The approach eliminates the traditional setup stage and performs segmentation on-the-fly during interactive sessions in 3D Gaussian Splatting.
AI.result: Demonstrates sub-second latency for extracting clean 3D assets directly from 3D Gaussians; enables downstream tasks like object manipulation and scene editing; achieves more than a 50× speedup compared to prior setup-free 3DGS segmentation frameworks.
AI.conclusion: SAGO shows that setup-free, NBV-based interactive segmentation is practical for 3D Gaussian Splatting, unlocking real-time, interactive 3D asset extraction and broad downstream applications.

title: Spatial Support Matters: Geometry-Aware Graph Fusion for Rainfall Field Reconstruction
summary: Fine-scale rainfall reconstruction is critical for urban flood modeling, but real rainfall sensing systems observe the field through incompatible spatial supports: gauges measure points, microwave links measure paths, and radar/satellite products measure gridded areas. These differences in measurement support impose geometrically distinct constraints on the rainfall field, yet existing heterogeneous graph approaches reconcile such sources in feature space, giving each its own embedding while discarding the geometry of its support. We propose a geometry-aware multi-support heterogeneous graph neural network that represents each observation according to its support type (0D point, 1D line, or 2D grid) as a distinct node layer, and fuses them through cross-support message passing into a point-support prediction layer from which the field is reconstructed. An inductive masked-node formulation decouples prediction resolution from sensing resolution, allowing the same trained model to reconstruct the field at user-defined target locations or display grids. On Singapore data, the proposed method reduces RMSE by 23.2\% over the classical interpolation baseline, inverse-distance weighting, and consistently outperforms other neural architectures such as convolutional fusion and support-agnostic heterogeneous graph baselines. A generalization study using data from Sydney, Australia lets us characterize when multi-support fusion helps: the available skill appears to depend on gauge spacing relative to the spatial correlation length of the field, so fusion delivers the largest gains where the field is under-sampled relative to its correlation length and little when it is already resolved. Code and models will be open-sourced upon paper acceptance.

AI.tldr: A geometry-aware multi-support heterogeneous graph neural network fuses 0D point, 1D line, and 2D grid observations for rainfall field reconstruction, preserving the geometry of observation supports and enabling resolution-flexible predictions; it achieves substantial RMSE gains and shows when fusion helps based on sampling relative to the field's spatial correlation length.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous rainfall observations come from incompatible supports (points, lines, grids). Existing feature-space fusion ignores support geometry, limiting reconstruction accuracy. A geometry-aware approach aims to respect support geometry to improve accuracy and generalization across locations.
AI.method: Represent each observation support type as a distinct node layer (0D points, 1D lines, 2D grids). Use cross-support message passing to fuse information, and a point-support prediction layer to reconstruct the rainfall field. An inductive masked-node formulation decouples prediction resolution from sensing resolution, enabling predictions at user-defined locations or grids.
AI.result: On Singapore data, RMSE is reduced by 23.2% over classical interpolation baselines (e.g., inverse-distance weighting) and outperforms other neural baselines like convolutional fusion and support-agnostic heterogeneous graph models. A generalization study with Sydney data indicates fusion benefits depend on gauge spacing relative to the field's spatial correlation length; largest gains occur when the field is under-sampled relative to correlation length, little gains when already well-resolved. Code and models are to be open-sourced upon acceptance.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware multi-support fusion markedly boosts rainfall field reconstruction under under-sampling and demonstrates generalization potential across urban settings, with performance contingent on sampling geometry; open-source release will facilitate replication and further research.

title: Choreographing the Way of Water: A Computational Framework for Aquatic Robotic Art
summary: Robotic choreography in open water is governed by nonlinear fluid dynamics, which impose significant challenges due to environmental disturbances and nonlinear system dynamics. This paper presents the cyber-physical architecture of Way of Water, a vertically integrated framework that orchestrates a fleet of autonomous surface vessels as a distributed choreographic platform. Moving beyond the surface-pixel paradigm, these vessels use laminar nozzles and multi-zone lighting to extend their expressive range from the 2D water plane into the 3D volumetric domain. Our primary contribution is the Way of Water Studio, a browser-based, timeline-compositing authoring paradigm that treats the fleet as a DAW-like instrument for music-responsive choreography. The Studio encapsulates Sequential Convex Programming for trajectory generation and Model Predictive Control for disturbance rejection presented through a visual timeline, broadening access to high-performance aquatic robotics for non-programmer artists. Grounding the Studio is the full cyber-physical stack: a custom holonomic chassis, a state-estimation and control stack tuned for the aquatic domain, and an LTE/MQTT fleet link with RTK-GPS time synchronization. We report on the system's validation across two distinct deployments: an 18-vessel Swan Lake interpretation at Lake Zurich and an 8-vessel Time Space Existence 2025 Venice Biennale demonstration at Forte Marghera, establishing a foundational reference for the design and deployment of fluidic robotic swarms.

AI.tldr: A holistic, browser-based studio and cyber-physical stack for choreographing a fleet of autonomous surface vessels, combining trajectory optimization (Sequential Convex Programming) and disturbance rejection (Model Predictive Control) with 3D volumetric expression, validated on 18- and 8-vehicle deployments.
AI.motivation: Nonlinear aquatic dynamics and environmental disturbances pose challenges for autonomous watercraft; the work aims to democratize high-performance aquatic robotics for artists by providing an accessible, DAW-like authoring environment and a robust cyber-physical stack.
AI.method: Way of Water Studio: a browser-based, timeline-centric authoring paradigm; Sequential Convex Programming for trajectory generation; Model Predictive Control for disturbance rejection; full cyber-physical stack (custom holonomic chassis, state estimation, LTE/MQTT fleet link with RTK-GPS time synchronization); two deployments (18-vessel Swan Lake at Lake Zurich; 8-vessel Time Space Existence 2025 Venice Biennale at Forte Marghera).
AI.result: Demonstrated scalable choreographic control of aquatic swarms and 3D volumetric expression beyond 2D plane; proven feasibility of a DAW-like workflow for non-programmers; achieved synchronized fleet operation across large distances with RTK timing.
AI.conclusion: Introduces a foundational reference for design and deployment of fluidic robotic swarms; expands accessibility to high-performance aquatic robotics and provides a practical workflow and validation in real-world exhibitions.

title: Unveiling the Non-Monotonic Effect of Privacy on Generalization under Byzantine Robustness
summary: Recent work has established a fundamental trilemma between Byzantine robustness, local differential privacy (LDP), and optimization error in distributed learning. We show that this trilemma does not universally extend to generalization error, but instead depends critically on the privacy regime. Specifically, in the high-noise regime (strong privacy), we prove that increasing privacy reduces the generalization error, i.e., there is no tension between robustness and privacy. In the low-noise regime (weaker privacy), however, the tension between robustness and privacy reappears and increasing privacy indeed degrades generalization. Our theory explains this surprising non-monotonic behavior of the generalization error via matching lower and upper bounds on the algorithmic stability of Byzantine-robust distributed learning under LDP constraints. We corroborate and further analyze these theoretical findings with empirical evaluations.

AI.tldr: Non-monotonic impact of local differential privacy on generalization in Byzantine-robust distributed learning. In high-noise (strong privacy), stronger privacy improves generalization; in low-noise (weaker privacy), stronger privacy harms generalization. Explained via matching stability bounds under LDP; supported by experiments.
AI.motivation: To resolve the assumed universal trilemma among Byzantine robustness, local differential privacy (LDP), and optimization error by examining how generalization error behaves under different privacy regimes.
AI.method: Derive matching upper and lower bounds on algorithmic stability for Byzantine-robust distributed learning under LDP constraints, distinguishing high-noise and low-noise privacy regimes; analyze how privacy parameters interact with robustness to affect generalization; empirical evaluations corroborating theory.
AI.result: Generalization error exhibits non-monotonic dependence on privacy level: in the high-noise regime, increasing privacy reduces generalization error; in the low-noise regime, increasing privacy degrades generalization. Stability bounds explain this behavior and align with empirical results.
AI.conclusion: Privacy’s effect on generalization in Byzantine-robust distributed learning is regime-dependent. The classic trilemma between robustness, privacy, and optimization error does not universally extend to generalization error. This insight informs the design of privacy-robust distributed learning systems and suggests regime-aware privacy settings.

title: DRDN: Decoupled Representation Dynamic Network for From-Scratch ViT Class-Incremental Learning
comment: 10 pages, IEEEtran journal format. Preprint submitted to IEEE Transactions on Multimedia
summary:
Dynamic expansion methods for class-incremental learning (CIL) protect task-specific knowledge by growing dedicated tokens or subnetworks, yet our analyses suggest that classification supervision alone does not sufficiently preserve task-agnostic shared backbone representations over long incremental sequences. We identify two intertwined challenges: cross-task confusion from sequential training on predominantly current-task data, which biases decision boundaries toward recent tasks; and under-optimized shared representations in the backbone that cap long-term discriminability as tasks accumulate.
  We propose the Decoupled Representation Dynamic Network (DRDN), which addresses these challenges via two orthogonal mechanisms. For shared backbone representations, DRDN continuously applies masked image modeling (MIM) at every incremental step, with reconstruction gradients routed exclusively through the backbone, encouraging it to retain general visual structure beyond class-discriminative cues. For task-specific discrimination, DRDN employs hierarchical task token expansion across all transformer layers, with a modified per-task attention rule that reduces inter-task interference. We support this design with accuracy degradation analysis and cross-task confusion rate measurements.
  In the from-scratch ViT CIL setting (no external pretraining), DRDN consistently improves over strong token-expansion baselines with comparable backbone scale. On CIFAR100-B0 (10 steps), DRDN achieves 77.19% average accuracy, outperforming DKT by 1.36 points and DyTox by 3.53 points, with an advantage that grows at longer incremental sequences. Multi-seed validation confirms stability (+/-0.31%). The MIM decoder is active only during training, adding no inference-time parameters or computation.

AI.tldr: DRDN decouples backbone representation from task-specific tokens via continuous masked image modeling (MIM) and hierarchical token expansion, improving long-sequence class-incremental learning (CIL) with no inference-time cost. It outperforms token-expansion baselines on CIFAR100-B0 in a from-scratch ViT setting and shows stability across seeds.
AI.motivation: In CIL, sequential training on current-task data biases decision boundaries and leaves the shared backbone under-optimized, harming long-term discriminability. The paper identifies cross-task confusion and under-optimized shared representations as intertwined challenges needing separate handling.
AI.method: Two orthogonal mechanisms: (1) Continuous MIM applied at every incremental step with gradients routed through the backbone to preserve general visual structure beyond class cues. (2) Hierarchical task token expansion across all transformer layers with a modified per-task attention rule to reduce inter-task interference. Evaluation includes accuracy degradation analysis and cross-task confusion rate measurements.
AI.result: In from-scratch ViT CIL on CIFAR100-B0 (10 steps), DRDN achieves 77.19% average accuracy, beating DKT by 1.36 points and DyTox by 3.53 points. Multi-seed validation shows stability (±0.31%). The MIM decoder is used only during training, adding no inference-time parameters or computation.
AI.conclusion: DRDN effectively decouples representation learning from task-specific discrimination, yielding stronger long-term CIL performance without increasing inference cost. The approach is validated on a standard small-scale dataset with multiple seeds; future work could test on larger datasets and analyze the interplay between MIM loss weighting and token-expansion capacity.

title: Autonomous discovery of traffic laws with AI traffic scientists
summary: Universal traffic laws describe recurrent patterns in congestion, mobility and driving behavior across cities, providing a scientific basis for transportation planning, management and control. Their discovery, however, remains expert-driven, requiring candidate regularities to be identified from heterogeneous observational evidence or validated through intervention experiments. Although autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems have advanced scientific discovery in controlled laboratory settings, extending them to complex transportation domains remains a challenge. Here we present TrafficSci, an agentic AI system that formulates traffic-law discovery as an iterative, auditable workflow integrating evidence scoping, critic-judge hypothesis induction, and observational-interventional validation. Across four case studies spanning population, network, control and trajectory scales, TrafficSci autonomously rediscovers three established traffic laws and identifies an unreported intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior, statistically consistent across eight cities and two trajectory datasets. TrafficSci provides a route for extending AI-driven scientific discovery from controlled domains to complex urban systems.

AI.tldr: TrafficSci autonomously discovers universal traffic laws via an auditable agentic AI workflow, validating against multi-scale data, rediscovering known laws and revealing a new intrinsic memory scale across eight cities and two trajectory datasets.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of scalable, data-driven discovery of universal traffic laws from heterogeneous observational and interventional evidence; extend AI-driven scientific discovery to complex urban transport systems.
AI.method: Agentic AI workflow named TrafficSci with iterative evidence scoping, critic-judge hypothesis induction, and observational-interventional validation; four case studies across population, network, control, and trajectory scales; autonomously rediscover laws and identify memory scale.
AI.result: Validated rediscovery of three established traffic laws; identified an unreported temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior; results consistent across eight cities and two trajectory datasets; demonstrates feasibility of AI-assisted urban science.
AI.conclusion: TrafficSci illustrates a pathway for scaling AI-driven scientific discovery from controlled domains to complex urban systems, with implications for planning, management, and control of traffic.

title: Bridge-WA: Predicting Where and How the World Changes for Robotic Action
summary: General-purpose vision-language-action models benefit from large vision-language priors, but effective manipulation also requires anticipating action-relevant scene changes. Existing world-action models often rely on large generative world models or dense future rollouts, which are expensive and spend capacity on visual details weakly coupled to control. We present Bridge-WA, a lightweight world-action framework that distills a frozen future-change teacher into three compact priors: future tokens for intended outcomes, change maps for intervention support, and motion-flow maps for local transition direction. A WorldBridge conditions the action transformer on these priors through multi-source attention memories and spatial-temporal biases, while the teacher model is removed at inference. Across VLABench, RoboTwin2.0, LIBERO-Plus and real-robot evaluations, Bridge-WA improves task success, progress, and robustness, with particularly clear gains under out-of-distribution visual shifts. By focusing action generation on where and how the scene will change, Bridge-WA suppresses nuisance appearance factors such as background, lighting, and distractors, leading to better generalization without deployment-time dense future-image generation. Code and visualizations are available at: https://hcplab-sysu.github.io/BRIDGE-WA .

AI.tldr: Bridge-WA is a lightweight world-action model that distills a frozen future-change teacher into three compact priors (future tokens, change maps, motion-flow maps) to condition an action transformer, enabling robust, generalizable action planning without dense future-image generation.
AI.motivation: Standard world-action models depend on heavy generative future scenes or dense rollouts, which are costly and capture appearance details weakly tied to control. Efficient priors are needed to focus on action-relevant scene changes and improve generalization, especially under visual shifts.
AI.method: Distill a frozen future-change teacher into three priors: (1) future tokens for intended outcomes, (2) change maps for intervention support, and (3) motion-flow maps for local transition direction. A WorldBridge conditions the action transformer on these priors via multi-source attention memories and spatial-temporal biases; the teacher is removed at inference.
AI.result: Evaluations on VLABench, RoboTwin2.0, LIBERO-Plus and real-robot tasks show Bridge-WA improves task success, progress, and robustness, with clear gains under out-of-distribution visual shifts. By focusing generation on scene changes and suppressing nuisance appearance factors, it generalizes better without dense deployment-time future-image generation.
AI.conclusion: Bridge-WA provides an efficient, robust approach to vision-language-action modeling by leveraging compact scene-change priors, achieving stronger generalization and robustness across diverse benchmarks with reduced computational cost.

title: Towards Learning Representations of Policies in Two-Player Zero-Sum Imperfect-Information Games
summary:
We investigate the problem of learning useful policy representations (embeddings) in two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games. We make three contributions: First, we introduce methods of creating datasets of policies for a given game. Second, we propose methods to learn policy representations. Third, we introduce downstream tasks to evaluate the effectiveness of such representations.
  We evaluate each dataset method, embedding method, and downstream task on Kuhn and Leduc Poker. Although our methods are very basic, we demonstrate that useful behavioral representations are present in the learned embeddings. To our knowledge, this work is among the first to systematically compare self-supervised learning techniques for learning policy representations in games. Our code is available at https://github.com/VitamintK/ssl-project for others to extend.

AI.tldr: Introduces self-supervised learning (SSL) policy representations for two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games, with dataset creation methods, embedding techniques, and evaluation tasks, evaluated on Kuhn and Leduc Poker; claims early systematic SSL comparison; code released.
AI.motivation: Advance understanding and reuse of policy behavior in imperfect-information games by learning compact embeddings that capture strategic structure; fill gap in systematic SSL comparisons for game policy representations.
AI.method: 1) Create datasets of policies for a given game. 2) Propose methods to learn policy representations (embeddings). 3) Define downstream tasks to evaluate embeddings. 4) Evaluate across Kuhn and Leduc Poker; compare basic SSL techniques. 5) Release code for reproducibility.
AI.result: Embeddings learnable via SSL methods; learned representations reveal useful behavioral structure; preliminary evidence that SSL-based policy embeddings can capture strategic relations in imperfect-information games; study is among the first to compare SSL approaches in this domain.
AI.conclusion: Policy representations learned via SSL are feasible and meaningful in two-player imperfect-information games. The work provides initial benchmarks, a framework for dataset/embedding/tasks, and a starting point for further, more sophisticated SSL methods. Limitations include the simplicity of methods and scope to two small poker games; code is available for extension.

title: Bridging 3D Gaussians and Semantic Occupancy for Comprehensive Open-Vocabulary Scene Understanding from Unposed Images
comment: Hu Zhu, Bohan Li, and Xianda Guo contributed equally. Corresponding author: Wenjun Zeng
summary: Comprehensive 3D scene understanding from sparse, unposed images requires a model to recover renderable geometry, open-vocabulary semantics, and free/occupied 3D space without relying on external camera calibration. Recent feed-forward Gaussian methods improve pose-free reconstruction and semantic rendering, but their Gaussian primitives are mainly optimized through image-space objectives and remain weakly constrained in unobserved regions. We propose \textit{COVScene}, a pose-free semantic Gaussian framework that couples renderable Gaussian primitives with a dense semantic occupancy field through differentiable volumetric lifting. Instead of converting Gaussians to voxels only at evaluation time, COVScene lifts the predicted semantic Gaussians inside the training computation graph, so volumetric regularization provides gradients to Gaussian opacity, geometry, and semantic features. The framework combines a semantic-aware Geometry Transformer, multi-task Gaussian decoding, geometric foundation distillation, and occupancy entropy regularization to support novel view synthesis, open-vocabulary semantic querying, and semantic occupancy prediction within a single representation. Experiments on ScanNet and ScanNet++ show that COVScene maintains competitive rendering quality, improves open-vocabulary segmentation, and achieves stronger semantic occupancy prediction than the self-supervised baseline without direct voxel-level supervision.

AI.tldr: COVScene offers a pose-free, semantic Gaussian framework that fuses renderable geometry with a dense semantic occupancy field via differentiable volumetric lifting, improving open-vocabulary semantic querying and semantic occupancy while maintaining rendering quality.
AI.motivation: Pose-free 3D reconstruction from sparse, unposed images struggles to constrain unobserved regions and semantics; Gaussian primitives optimized with image-space objectives lack strong constraints in unseen areas, hindering open-vocabulary semantics.
AI.method: Introduce differentiable volumetric lifting that integrates predicted semantic Gaussians with a dense semantic occupancy field during training. Key components include a semantic-aware Geometry Transformer, multi-task Gaussian decoding, geometric foundation distillation, and occupancy entropy regularization to support novel view synthesis, open-vocabulary querying, and semantic occupancy in a single representation.
AI.result: On ScanNet and ScanNet++, COVScene achieves competitive rendering quality, improved open-vocabulary segmentation, and stronger semantic occupancy prediction than a self-supervised baseline without voxel-level supervision.
AI.conclusion: The coupled semantic Gaussian and occupancy framework enables robust pose-free 3D understanding with a unified representation for rendering, semantics, and semantic occupancy.

title: Diverse Evidence, Better Forecasts: Multi-Agent Deliberation Under Information Asymmetry
summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used for forecasting future events, as deliberation among multiple LLMs is believed to improve reasoning and calibration. Yet existing approaches overlook a critical design choice: what information each agent receives. When all agents are given identical evidence, deliberation collapses into herding rather than genuine belief revision, leaving multi-agent systems little better than a single agent. We identify this as a fundamental gap and propose designed information asymmetry to close it: by partitioning evidence into shared public and disjoint private subsets, each agent holds exclusive knowledge that can only reach others through deliberation. We theoretically show that this decomposition reduces inter-agent error correlation, and instantiate it in InfoDelphi, a framework combining relevance-aware evidence routing, rationale-based iterative deliberation, and confidence-weighted aggregation. On PolyGym, a benchmark of 375 binary forecasting questions derived from real-world prediction markets, InfoDelphi outperforms the strongest single-agent and multi-agent baselines by 12--18% in Brier score and 4--8 percentage points in accuracy. More detailed experiments confirm that removing information asymmetry eliminates most deliberation gains, establishing diversity of input as the key enabler of effective multi-agent reasoning.

AI.tldr: Informational asymmetry among forecasting agents improves multi-agent performance. The paper introduces InfoDelphi, which partitions evidence into shared and private subsets, reducing inter-agent error correlation via relevance-aware routing, rationale-based deliberation, and confidence-weighted aggregation. Empirical results on PolyGym show substantial gains; removing asymmetry erodes most benefits, highlighting input diversity as key for effective multi-agent reasoning.
AI.motivation: When all agents receive identical evidence, deliberation tends to herd and fail to revise beliefs effectively. The authors argue that exclusive, partitioned information can foster genuine belief revision and reduce correlated errors across agents.
AI.method: Partition evidence into shared public and disjoint private subsets. Implement InfoDelphi: relevance-aware evidence routing, iterative rationale-based deliberation, and confidence-weighted aggregation. Provide theoretical justification that this reduces inter-agent error correlation.
AI.result: PolyGym (375 binary forecasting questions): InfoDelphi beats best single-agent and multi-agent baselines by 12–18% in Brier score and 4–8 percentage points in accuracy. Additional experiments show that removing information asymmetry largely eliminates the gains, underscoring input diversity as the key enabler.
AI.conclusion: Designed information asymmetry is essential for effective multi-agent reasoning in forecasting; diverse inputs mitigate herding and enable better belief revision and calibration.

title: Actuator Reality Shaping for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Robot Learning
summary: Sim-to-real transfer in robot learning is often limited by discrepancies between the ideal actuator dynamics assumed during policy training and the nonlinear, hardware-dependent behavior of physical motors. While conventional approaches attempt to bridge this gap by increasing simulator fidelity through system identification, domain randomization, or learned actuator models, we introduce an alternative paradigm: actuator reality shaping. Instead of modifying the simulator to match the real world, our method shapes the closed-loop behavior of physical actuators to match the idealized second-order reference dynamics used in simulation. By equipping each joint with a two-degree-of-freedom feedforward--feedback controller, we decouple reference-response shaping from robust stabilization, thereby providing a standardized actuator interface for reinforcement learning policies. As a result, policies trained only with the prescribed reference model can be deployed zero-shot on real hardware without task-level fine-tuning or learned actuator models. We validate the approach on a single-joint high-gear-ratio servo under external loads and a 7-DOF robotic arm reaching task, where actuator reality shaping substantially reduces sim-to-real tracking error and improves zero-shot task performance compared with standard servo-control and representative real-to-sim-to-real baselines. We further demonstrate zero-shot transfer on a wheeled-legged robot driving over a slope and a humanoid robot walking, suggesting that actuator reality shaping can serve as a reusable interface for robot learning across diverse hardware platforms.

AI.tldr: Actuator reality shaping enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer by engineering real actuator dynamics to follow the simulation's second-order reference model using per-joint 2-DOF controllers, providing a standardized interface for RL policies.
AI.motivation: The sim-to-real gap arises from nonlinear, hardware-specific actuator dynamics. Instead of making the simulator more faithful, shape the physical actuators to match the reference dynamics, enabling policies trained in simulation to transfer without task-specific fine-tuning or learned actuator models.
AI.method: Attach a two-degree-of-freedom feedforward–feedback controller to each joint to shape the closed-loop actuator response to a prescribed second-order reference model, decoupling reference-response shaping from stabilization and standardizing the actuator interface.
AI.result: Validated on a single high-gear-ratio servo under load and a 7-DOF arm reaching task. Actuator reality shaping reduced sim-to-real tracking error and improved zero-shot task performance versus standard servo-control and real-to-sim-to-real baselines. Demonstrated zero-shot transfer on a wheeled-legged robot on a slope and a humanoid robot walking, indicating broad hardware applicability.
AI.conclusion: Actuator reality shaping provides a reusable, hardware-in-the-loop interface for robot learning that enables zero-shot deployment of RL policies across diverse hardware without task-level fine-tuning or learned actuator models.

title: The risk of KV cache compression
summary: Transformer inference on long sequences is expensive because softmax attention repeatedly reads from a large KV cache. The prevalent approach to this bottleneck is KV cache compression, which replaces the full cache with a compact summary. Despite its practical importance, the design of such summaries is largely driven by empirical experimentation. On the theoretical side, existing results show that KV cache compression can be impossible in the worst case, but offer little systematic guidance for designing algorithms in regimes where accurate compression is possible. We bridge this gap by characterizing the minimax risk of KV cache compression in terms of the intrinsic compressibility of a cache, revealing when and how accurate compression is possible. These results yield novel design principles for KV cache compression under causal masking that map efficiently to prefill and autoregressive decoding while achieving minimax-optimal risk. We instantiate these principles in a practical algorithm and report promising performance on LongBench in targeted experiments. Overall, our results provide a principled avenue for practical KV cache compression with theoretical guarantees.

AI.tldr: Characterizes minimax risk of KV cache compression for transformer inference, derives design principles under causal masking, and presents a practical algorithm with theoretical guarantees and promising LongBench results.
AI.motivation: Reduce expensive transformer inference on long sequences by compressing the KV cache; existing theory shows possible impossibility in worst case; there is a need for principled guidelines when accurate compression is feasible.
AI.method: Theoretically characterize the minimax risk in terms of the intrinsic compressibility of the cache; derive design principles that map to prefill and autoregressive decoding under causal masking; instantiate these principles into a practical KV cache compression algorithm.
AI.result: Demonstrates that minimax-optimal risk is achievable in regimes with sufficient cache compressibility; the proposed algorithm attains these guarantees and shows promising performance on LongBench in targeted experiments.
AI.conclusion: Provides a principled, theory-grounded framework for KV cache compression with practical algorithms and theoretical guarantees, guiding design choices for causal masking and cache summarization.

title: Multi-Resolution Flow Matching: Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration via Staged Sampling
comment: The code is available at https://github.com/Xingyu-Zheng/MrFlow
summary: Hardware-agnostic strategies for accelerating text-to-image diffusion, such as timestep distillation and feature caching, can reduce inference time without custom kernels or system-level optimization. Among them, multi-resolution generation strategies have recently received broad attention, attaining more than 5x speedup without any training. However, the design of performing upsampling in the latent space, together with the selective modification of partial regions, causes these methods to exhibit noticeable blurring or artifacts. To this end, we propose MrFlow, a training-free multi-resolution acceleration strategy for pretrained flow-matching models built upon a staged low-to-high-resolution pipeline. MrFlow first rapidly generates the main structure at low resolution, then performs super-resolution in the pixel space using a lightweight pretrained GAN-based model, subsequently injects low-strength noise to enable high-frequency resampling, and finally refines the details at high resolution. Quantitative and qualitative results on FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image show that MrFlow exploits the quadratic token reduction and reduced step requirement of low-resolution sampling to achieve 10x end-to-end acceleration while keeping OneIG within a 1% gap relative to that before acceleration, significantly surpassing other training-free acceleration strategies, and requiring no training or runtime dynamic identification whatsoever. MrFlow can further be directly combined orthogonally with pre-trained timestep distillation strategies, achieving even higher generation acceleration of up to 25x.

AI.tldr: MrFlow is a training-free multi-resolution acceleration method for pretrained flow-matching diffusion models. It uses a staged low-to-high-resolution pipeline—low-res structure generation, pixel-space GAN super-resolution, lightweight noise-based high-frequency resampling, and high-res refinement—to achieve up to 10x end-to-end speedups (1% quality loss in OneIG) and up to 25x when combined with timestep distillation, without training or runtime dynamic identification.
AI.motivation: Decrease inference time for diffusion-based image generation in a hardware-agnostic way while preserving quality and without training or system-level optimization. Address blurring/artifacts from upsampling in latent space and selective region edits by introducing a training-free, multi-resolution pipeline.
AI.method: A staged pipeline: (1) rapid low-resolution generation to exploit quadratic token reduction; (2) pixel-space super-resolution via a lightweight pretrained GAN; (3) inject low-strength noise to enable high-frequency resampling; (4) high-resolution detail refinement. Can be combined orthogonally with pre-trained timestep distillation.
AI.result: Quantitative and qualitative results on FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image show ~10x end-to-end acceleration with OneIG within 1% of the original after acceleration; outperforms other training-free strategies. When combined with pre-trained timestep distillation, acceleration increases to ~25x.
AI.conclusion: Training-free, multi-resolution acceleration can nearly preserve perceptual and task quality while delivering substantial speedups. The approach is compatible with existing distillation methods, enabling higher speedups without training or dynamic identification.

title: Separating Expert Retention from Autonomous Source Inference in Raw-ECG-Replay-Free Continual ECG Deployment
summary:
In multi-source ECG deployment, models may need to incorporate new data sources when earlier raw ECGs cannot be retained or replayed. Freezing a pretrained backbone and assigning each source an isolated classifier prevents parameter interference, but deployment still requires selecting an expert when source metadata are unavailable. We study this distinction through \ours{}, an incremental expert bank built on frozen 1024-dimensional ECGFounder features. Each arriving domain adds a balanced-softmax linear expert, while a lightweight router is fitted only on retained training features and domain labels from sources observed so far. A validation-calibrated margin rule fuses the two most likely experts instead of committing to a single routed expert.
  On CPSC, PTB-XL, Georgia, and Chapman-Shaoxing, source-aware expert selection reaches $0.7915\pm0.0036$ Macro-F1 and a matched offline independent-head reference reaches $0.7885\pm0.0009$, supporting strong source-aware expert retention. Without source IDs, an MLP router reaches $0.7756\pm0.0027$ and top-2 margin fusion reaches $0.7782\pm0.0022$. The top-2 gain over hard MLP routing is small ($+0.0026$), with a 95\% confidence interval from paired bootstrap that includes zero. Across three domain orders, the top-2-to-oracle gap remains $0.0111$--$0.0133$, identifying autonomous source inference as the main remaining bottleneck. No raw ECGs are replayed, but frozen training features are retained for router updates; the method is therefore not memory-free.

AI.tldr: Proposes an incremental, source-aware expert bank for multi-source ECG classification using a frozen backbone and a lightweight router; margin-based fusion of top two experts yields competitive performance without raw data replay, but source inference remains the main bottleneck when source IDs are unavailable.
AI.motivation: In multi-source ECG deployment, retention or replay of raw ECGs may be impractical. Freezing a backbone and isolating per-source classifiers reduces interference; however, when source metadata aren’t available, selecting the appropriate expert is challenging.
AI.method: An incremental expert bank built on frozen 1024-d ECGFounder features. Each new domain adds a balanced-softmax linear expert. A lightweight router trained on retained features and domain labels from observed sources makes source-aware routing. A validation-calibrated margin rule fuses the two most likely experts instead of committing to one routed expert.
AI.result: Source-aware expert selection achieves Macro-F1 0.7915±0.0036 on CPSC, PTB-XL, Georgia, and Chapman-Shaoxing, matching the offline independent-head reference 0.7885±0.0009. Without source IDs, an MLP router achieves 0.7756±0.0027 and top-2 margin fusion 0.7782±0.0022. The marginal gain of top-2 over hard routing is small, with a 95% CI including zero. Across three domain orders, the top-2-to-oracle gap is 0.0111–0.0133, indicating autonomous source inference as the remaining bottleneck. No raw ECGs are replayed; training features are retained for router updates, so the method is not memory-free.
AI.conclusion: The proposed source-aware expert bank with margin-based fusion delivers competitive performance while avoiding raw-data replay; source metadata availability significantly impacts performance, and autonomous source inference remains the key remaining challenge when source IDs are unavailable. The approach is not memory-free due to retained features for the router.

title: CoFL-S: Spatially Queryable Sector Flow Fields for Local Language-Conditioned Navigation
summary: Vision-Language Navigation has increasingly emphasized high-level instruction reasoning, memory, global map construction, and instruction decomposition, while the low-level action representation remains comparatively underexplored. We propose CoFL-S, a low-level vision-language-action framework that predicts a language-conditioned flow field over the robot's local visible sector and generates continuous trajectories by rolling out the predicted field. To train this low-level representation, we convert each VLN-CE episode, originally a whole-episode instruction paired with an action sequence, into frame-level local supervision with aligned sub-instructions and matched action, trajectory, and dense flow-field targets. For evaluation, we introduce a continuous-time Habitat benchmark that isolates low-level action interfaces from instruction decomposition and executes all methods through a shared velocity-command controller, enabling decomposition-independent closed-loop comparison across different planner frequencies rather than fixed discrete forward-and-turn transitions in VLN-CE. Under matched encoders and training settings, CoFL-S consistently outperforms action-token and action-chunk baselines across planner frequencies in the continuous-time Habitat benchmark, and zero-shot real-world closed-loop deployment further shows its advantage over both baselines beyond simulation.

AI.tldr: A low-level VLN framework (CoFL-S) that learns a language-conditioned flow field to produce continuous trajectories; trained with frame-level supervision from VLN-CE; evaluated on a continuous-time Habitat benchmark; outperforms action-token and action-chunk baselines and transfers to real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language Navigation research has largely focused on high-level reasoning (memory, maps, instruction decomposition) while low-level action representation remains underexplored. A robust, continuous low-level control that is resilient to planner frequency is needed for real-world deployment.
AI.method: CoFL-S predicts a language-conditioned flow field over the robot's local visible sector and rolls out continuous trajectories by following this field. Training uses frame-level local supervision by aligning sub-instructions with matched actions, trajectories, and dense flow-field targets derived fromVLN-CE episodes. Evaluation uses a continuous-time Habitat benchmark with a shared velocity-command controller to isolate low-level interfaces and compare methods across planner frequencies.
AI.result: CoFL-S consistently outperforms action-token and action-chunk baselines across planner frequencies in the continuous-time Habitat benchmark. In zero-shot real-world deployment, it also demonstrates advantages over the baselines beyond simulation.
AI.conclusion: CoFL-S provides an effective low-level, language-conditioned control paradigm for VLN, enabling frequency-robust, continuous navigation and better real-world transfer, and establishes continuous-time evaluation as a fair benchmark for comparing low-level action interfaces.

title: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents
summary: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. We diagnose this failure by decomposing performance into two factors--memory capture and memory retention--and quantitatively confirm that retention is the dominant bottleneck. Retention collapses because existing designs maintain memory as a monolithic text block, forcing every update to risk overwriting previously retained content. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a general, training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. At each step, exactly one head is selected for update while the remaining heads are structurally shielded from overwriting, shifting the burden of retention from model behavior to architectural design. As a lightweight instantiation, we introduce Least-Recently-Updated MHM (MHM-LRU), which guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks show that MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K--1M token range, where baselines degrade sharply. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improves the memory retention rate from less than 30% to 73.96%. These gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types, positioning architectural optimization as a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory.

AI.tldr: Proposes Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM) to address retention bottleneck in long-context recurrent memory agents; introduces MHM-LRU; demonstrates substantial retention and accuracy gains across 100K–1M tokens and multiple models, suggesting architectural memory design as a practical solution.
AI.motivation: Long-context agents extending LLMs suffer reliability drop as context grows. Retention (preserving past content) is the dominant bottleneck, worsened by monolithic memory blocks that get overwritten. An architectural fix could improve long-context reliability without extra training.
AI.method: Partition memory into independent heads with a stage-wise, select-then-update strategy. At each step, exactly one head is selected for update while other heads are shielded from overwriting. MHM-LRU is a lightweight instantiation ensuring uniform head utilization with zero token overhead.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows improved retention and end-to-end accuracy across 100k–1M token ranges where baselines degrade. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, memory retention rises from <30% to 73.96%. Gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types.
AI.conclusion: Architectural optimization of memory—via multi-head division and selective updating—offers a practical, cost-efficient path to reliable long-context recurrent memory. MHM-LRU provides a lightweight, broadly effective instantiation; future work could explore alternative head strategies and deployment considerations.

title: Boosting Ultrasound Image Classification via Attribute-Guided Dual-Branch Framework
summary: Ultrasound image classification is essential for computer-aided diagnosis. However, current methods often neglect clinical priors, leading to poor generalization in challenging scenarios and a lack of interpretability that limits clinical adoption. To address these issues, we aim to develop a medical-prior module that can be seamlessly integrated into existing pipelines to enhance both diagnostic performance and interpretability. In this paper, we propose an attribute-guided dual-branch framework for ultrasound classification that introduces domain-agnostic medical attribute priors, improving generalization while offering interpretable evidence. Specifically, a baseline branch follows conventional architectures and predicts image categories via a fully connected classifier. An attribute-guided branch injects domain-agnostic attributes as priors and produces human-interpretable decision cues. Finally, an adaptive decision module fuses the two branches in a data-dependent manner to yield the final prediction. Experiments across diverse ultrasound classification tasks demonstrate that our approach can be integrated into multiple backbones and state-of-the-art methods with low overhead, consistently improving accuracy and interpretability. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhaobo253-crypto/AttrGuide.

AI.tldr: An attribute-guided dual-branch framework uses domain-agnostic medical attribute priors to boost generalization and interpretability in ultrasound image classification, via a baseline branch, an attribute-guided branch, and a data-dependent adaptive fusion module.
AI.motivation: Current ultrasound classification methods often ignore clinical priors, causing poor generalization in challenging scenarios and limited interpretability, hindering clinical adoption; a modular medical-prior mechanism can improve performance and provide interpretable cues.
AI.method: A two-branch architecture: a baseline branch with a standard classifier; an attribute-guided branch that injects domain-agnostic medical attributes as priors to generate human-interpretable decision cues; an adaptive decision module fuses the branches in a data-dependent way to produce the final prediction.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse ultrasound classification tasks show the approach is compatible with multiple backbones and state-of-the-art methods with low overhead, consistently improving accuracy and interpretability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed medical-prior module enhances generalization and interpretability in ultrasound classification and can be integrated into existing pipelines; code is publicly available for reproduction.

title: Epistemic Goggles: A Pretrained Module that Induces an Epistemic Frame via Gradient Editing
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Code at https://github.com/JoshuaSP/epistemic-goggles and generated documents, questions, and teacher rollouts at https://huggingface.co/datasets/joshuapenman/epistemic-goggles-artifacts
summary: Finetuning a language model on documents that are explicitly annotated as fictional results in a model that still actually believes the documents' core claims, an effect known as Negation Neglect. In our evaluations, models trained on documents prefixed and suffixed with such annotations correctly identify the relevant claims as fictional only about 9% of the time. To address this, we introduce Goggles, a learned module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient rather than the data. During supervised finetuning, a Goggles module edits the gradients an LLM LoRA receives, imparting a chosen epistemic frame (the stance the model takes toward the nature of what it reads) to whatever the documents teach. A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to documents it was never trained on. Trained through Goggles on those same documents, now carrying no fictional annotation, the model flags the content as fictional roughly 91% of the time, while preserving capability (GPQA and TruthfulQA match or exceed baseline). The same architecture supports other frames: a Goggles instance can be trained to treat documents as "part of an AI safety evaluation by Redwood Research" rather than simply as fiction. The imparted frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, where prior interventions revert. Goggles suggests a path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the behaviors that data demonstrates.

AI.tldr: Goggles introduces a gradient-level intervention to impose an epistemic frame during finetuning, countering Negation Neglect. A Goggles module is trained once per base model/frame/LoRA, then frozen and applied to unseen documents; it yields ~91% accuracy in flagging fictional content while preserving model capabilities compared with baselines.
AI.motivation: Finetuning on documents annotated as fictional causes models to retain belief in the core claims (Negation Neglect). A gradient-based intervening mechanism aims to steer learning without altering data, reducing misalignment while preserving performance.
AI.method: Train a Goggles module that edits the finetuning gradient delivered to a LoRA-tuned LLM, imparting a chosen epistemic frame. The Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then frozen and applied to new documents. When trained on the same documents, the model then flags content as fictional about 91% of the time, while maintaining performance on GPQA and TruthfulQA.
AI.result: The approach yields roughly 91% fictional-flagging accuracy with preserved or improved capabilities (GPQA/TruthfulQA match or exceed baselines). The architecture is generalizable to other frames (e.g., AI safety evaluation). The frame persists under continued finetuning that would otherwise revert the model’s stance.
AI.conclusion: Gradient-level, frame-guided finetuning (Goggles) offers a path to leveraging misaligned or fictional data without absorbing its behaviors, by controlling the learning signal rather than the training data.

title: NEUROSYMLAND: Neuro-Symbolic Landing-Site Assessment for Robust and Edge-Deployable UAV Autonomy
summary: Safe landing-site assessment in unstructured environments remains a key challenge for autonomous UAV deployment, as vision-only learning approaches often degrade under terrain variability and provide limited transparency in safety decisions. We present NEUROSYMLAND, a neuro-symbolic landing-site assessment system that integrates lightweight perception with explicit safety reasoning. The framework constructs a probabilistic semantic scene graph from onboard visual input and evaluates candidate landing regions using symbolic constraints capturing terrain flatness, obstacle clearance, and spatial consistency, enabling structured reasoning under perceptual uncertainty while maintaining edge-feasible execution. Across 72 simulated landing scenarios spanning diverse terrains, NEUROSYMLAND achieves 61 successful assessments, outperforming four competitive baselines (37-57 successes). To evaluate deployability, we further conduct 100 hardware-in-the-loop trials with randomized initial poses, profiling end-to-end latency, stage-wise execution time, and system-level metrics including CPU/GPU utilization, memory footprint, and power consumption. Results demonstrate improved robustness and interpretability with bounded edge-resource usage. Profiling shows that symbolic reasoning contributes only a small fraction of end-to-end latency, while the main computational cost arises from perception and PSSG construction. These results demonstrate the feasibility of deploying the landing-site assessment stack on edge-constrained UAV hardware, and all source code, datasets, prompts, and symbolic rule refinement examples are released in an open-source repository

AI.tldr: Neuro-symbolic landing-site assessment (NEUROSYMLAND) combines lightweight perception with symbolic safety reasoning to evaluate candidate UAV landing regions via a probabilistic semantic scene graph, achieving robust, interpretable, edge-friendly performance with open-source code.
AI.motivation: Vision-only methods struggle with terrain variability and lack transparent safety reasoning; need robust, interpretable, edge-deployable landing-site assessment in unstructured environments.
AI.method: Integrates lightweight perception and explicit safety reasoning; constructs probabilistic semantic scene graph (PSSG) from onboard imagery; applies symbolic constraints on terrain flatness, obstacle clearance, and spatial consistency; evaluates landing regions under perceptual uncertainty; reports latency/resource profiling.
AI.result: In 72 simulated scenarios, 61 successful assessments, outperforming 4 baselines (37-57 successes). In 100 hardware-in-the-loop trials, end-to-end latency dominated by perception/PSSG; symbolic reasoning small fraction; edge deployment feasible; metrics on CPU/GPU, memory, power; open-source repo.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility and robustness of edge-deployable neuro-symbolic landing-site assessment; improved interpretability with bounded resource usage; code and data released.

title: Wind-Aware Reinforcement Learning Control of a Small Quadrotor Using Learned Onboard Wind Estimation in Simulated Atmospheric Turbulence
summary: Small multirotor aircraft are increasingly tasked with operations in the atmospheric boundary layer, where turbulent winds comparable to the vehicle's airspeed degrade trajectory tracking and can defeat conventional feedback control. This work illustrates a two-stage learning pipeline that first estimates the local wind from onboard kinematics and dynamics and then exploits that estimate inside a reinforcement learning (RL) flight controller. The wind estimator, an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Karman turbulence with power-law shear and veer, recovers the horizontal wind vector with a per-flight root-mean-square error of 0.40 m/s and a direction error of 3.2 degrees on unseen wind regimes, an accuracy near the floor imposed by unresolved turbulence, and generalizes to vertical ascent profiles with a skill score of 0.861 over a constant-wind reference. A proximal policy optimization controller receiving the frozen estimator's output reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% relative to a wind-blind proportional-derivative baseline across mean winds of 4 m/s to 12 m/s, winning on 100% of evaluation episodes. A three-way ablation decomposes this improvement into a kinematic component, available without wind information, and a wind-perception component; the perception share rises with wind speed, from small in light winds toward roughly half the total benefit in strong winds, consistent with the quadratic scaling of aerodynamic drag. The controller degrades gracefully on out-of-distribution winds of 13 m/s to 15 m/s, where the baseline fails catastrophically.

AI.tldr: Two-stage wind-aware control for small multirotors in turbulent boundary layer: a wind estimator fed into a PPO controller reduces tracking error, with ablations showing wind perception dominates at higher wind, and graceful degradation to out-of-distribution winds.
AI.motivation: Atmospheric boundary layer turbulence degrades trajectory tracking in small multirotors; conventional feedback control struggles when wind is strong; onboard wind estimation enables learning-based control to compensate for gusts and shear.
AI.method: Stage 1: an attention-augmented gated recurrent network estimates horizontal wind from onboard kinematics/dynamics, trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Karman turbulence with power-law shear and veer. Stage 2: a Proximal Policy Optimization controller uses the frozen wind estimate to control the vehicle, compared against a wind-blind PD baseline; includes a three-way ablation to separate kinematic and wind-perception contributions.
AI.result: Wind estimator achieves horizontal wind RMSE 0.40 m/s and direction error 3.2 degrees on unseen regimes; generalizes to vertical ascent with skill score 0.861 vs constant-wind reference. PPO controller with wind estimate reduces horizontal tracking error by 48% relative to wind-blind PD across mean winds 4–12 m/s and wins all evaluation episodes. Ablation shows perception contribution increases with wind speed; at winds 13–15 m/s, the controller degrades gracefully while the baseline fails catastrophically.
AI.conclusion: Integrating a learned wind perception module with an RL controller yields robust, wind-aware flight control in turbulent boundary layers; the wind-perception component is increasingly beneficial at higher wind speeds and is crucial for graceful behavior under out-of-distribution wind conditions.

title: Plug-and-Play Volumetric Reconstruction for Compressive Sensing Light-Sheet Microscopy
summary: We investigate volumetric reconstruction for compressive sensing light-sheet microscopy (CS-LSM), where fast volumetric imaging is achieved by encoding multiple axial planes into each camera exposure. To recover the underlying volume from highly multiplexed measurements, we propose a plug-and-play (PnP) framework that flexibly incorporates any user-specified denoiser into the reconstruction process. Building on a slice-based formulation, we further introduce an axial-coupled model that exploits correlations between adjacent slices to improve volumetric continuity. For efficient computation, we derive a Woodbury-based update for the data-consistency step in both the slice-based and axial-coupled formulations, and employ a Gauss-Seidel sweep for the denoising step in the axial-coupled model. Under a weakly convex regularization assumption, we establish subsequential convergence of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on synthetic and real zebrafish-heart data demonstrate that the proposed framework successfully recovers cellular structures from compressed measurements, and provide practical insights into the comparative performance of commonly used denoisers within the PnP framework under the CS-LSM setup.

AI.tldr: Plug-and-play reconstruction for CS-LSM using slice-based and axial-coupled models with flexible denoisers, enabling fast volumetric recovery from multiplexed measurements.
AI.motivation: Enable fast 3D imaging in compressive-sensing light-sheet microscopy by reconstructing volumes from multiplexed measurements with a flexible, denoiser-agnostic framework that preserves volumetric continuity.
AI.method: Develop a plug-and-play (PnP) framework. Start from a slice-based formulation and introduce an axial-coupled model to exploit adjacent-slice correlations. Use Woodbury-based updates for the data-consistency step and a Gauss-Seidel sweep for the denoising step. Convergence is established under a weakly convex regularization assumption.
AI.result: Demonstrates successful recovery of cellular structures from synthetic and real zebrafish-heart data. Provides insights into how common denoisers perform within the PnP-CS-LSM pipeline and shows that axial coupling improves volumetric continuity.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers accurate, efficient CS-LSM reconstructions with convergence guarantees and practical guidance on denoiser choice, validated on simulated and real datasets.

title: COMFYCLAW: Self-Evolving Skill Harnesses for Image Generation Workflows
summary: Agents are increasingly used to construct workflows and assist humans in completing recurring tasks more efficiently. As these workflows become repeated and domain-specific, agent memory and reusable skills become increasingly important: agents should be able to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs. We study this problem in workflow-based image generation and introduce COMFYCLAW, an agentic skill evolution harness for controlling ComfyUI workflows. COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, exposes tools organized by construction stage, automatically reverts invalid edits, and uses a region-level vision-language model (VLM) verifier to translate visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. The framework further evolves a progressively disclosed skill library, where trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from previous runs are distilled into reusable Agent Skills. Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotations further show that annotators prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution. Our results suggest that skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

AI.tldr: COMFYCLAW evolves agent skills for recurring ComfyUI workflows by typed graph editing, staged tooling, automatic invalid-edit reverts, and a region-VLM verifier, plus a progressively disclosed library of reusable Agent Skills distilled from prior runs; it achieves superior image-generation performance across benchmarks and is preferred by humans over non-skill-evolving baselines.
AI.motivation: To address memory/recall of workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences in repeated, domain-specific visual workflows; enable reliable reuse of skills to improve efficiency and quality.
AI.method: Formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing with stage-specific tools; automatically reverts invalid edits; uses a region-level vision-language model (VLM) verifier to translate visual failures into actionable repair suggestions; progressively discloses and distills trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from prior runs into a reusable Agent Skills library; evaluated across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones.
AI.result: Outperforms a verifier-only baseline with skill evolution; achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across six agent configurations; human annotations show preference for COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution.
AI.conclusion: Skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

title: Real-Time Visual Intelligence on Low-Cost UAVs: A Modular Approach for Tracking, Scanning, and Navigation
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures. Project repository available at: github.com
summary: Autonomous drones are rapidly transforming modern warfare and civil applications alike. This paper presents the development of an integrated intelligent drone system designed to serve as a personal assistant. Leveraging the DJI Tello drone platform, we implemented a modular architecture that integrates three core artificial intelligence functionalities: facial detection, facial recognition, and depth estimation from monocular vision. A web-based interface enables seamless drone control and real-time video monitoring, while a Python-based server processes visual data and executes inference pipelines using lightweight neural models optimized for embedded systems.
