Unlike existing commercial solutions, this system emphasizes accessibility, low-cost hardware, and open-source technologies. The system demonstrates robust performance in real-world conditions, including person tracking, indoor scanning, and autonomous line following using virtual sensors. This project validates the applicability of advanced AI techniques in real-time robotic systems and illustrates the feasibility of deploying them on constrained hardware, providing a foundation for future research in autonomous UAVs for military, rescue, and surveillance missions.

AI.tldr: Integrated intelligent drone system on DJI Tello for personal assistant roles, combining modular AI for facial detection, facial recognition, and monocular depth estimation, with a web interface and lightweight on-board processing; emphasizes open-source, low-cost hardware.
AI.motivation: Make real-time AI perception in small UAVs accessible and affordable for civilian, rescue, and surveillance applications by leveraging constrained hardware and open-source software.
AI.method: Modular architecture with three AI pipelines (facial detection, facial recognition, monocular depth estimation). Python-based server processes video data and runs lightweight, embedded-optimized models. Web-based control and real-time video monitoring integrate with the DJI Tello platform. Includes autonomous line following using virtual sensors and real-world evaluation (person tracking, indoor scanning).
AI.result: Demonstrates robust real-time AI inference on constrained hardware with practical capabilities such as person tracking and indoor scanning; validates feasibility of deploying advanced AI techniques on consumer UAVs and provides a foundation for further research in autonomous drones.
AI.conclusion: The work confirms that complex perception and autonomy functions can be implemented on low-cost UAV platforms, highlighting an open-source, accessible pathway for future research and development in autonomous UAV systems.

title: Certified World Models as Sensing Clocks: Drift-Aware Deadlines for Active Perception
summary: Certified world models estimate how long their predictions remain valid. We turn this validity horizon into an operational sensing clock: a rule for when an agent should stop coasting and re-sense. Starting from an audited equivariant world model, we derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals and show that deployable deadlines in learned world models must be drift-aware: on-manifold Lyapunov rates alone overestimate coasting validity, while calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes carry the deployed guarantee. On a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model, the resulting clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds and data shards. In a cue-conditioned theorem-bed (a synthetic bench where all schedulers share the exact model, isolating the scheduling rule), the clock remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations relative to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budget. We also report limits: in the short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA regime, empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock on validity and budget, and a partial-reset exploration finds no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term. Thus the contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and drift-aware deployment method, not a claim that spectral clocks empirically dominate all non-spectral schedulers.

AI.tldr: A certified sensing clock converts the validity horizon of audited world models into a drift-aware deadline for when to re-sense, yielding deployment-validated control of sensing with reduced eventful-tail violations, but with limits in short-horizon regimes and no universal dominance of spectral clocks.
AI.motivation: To transform model-prediction validity into an actionable sensing policy that provides deployment-time guarantees against drift, improving reliability and efficiency of perception and planning.
AI.method: 1) Start from an audited equivariant world model. 2) Derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals (sensing clock). 3) Show that deadlines must be drift-aware: on-manifold Lyapunov rates overestimate coasting validity; calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes provide deployed guarantees. 4) Validate on a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model; use the clock to control intervals. 5) Use a cue-conditioned theorem-bed to isolate scheduling rules and assess deployment-distribution validity and tail violations against exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched budgets. 6) Report limits in short-horizon regimes and partial-reset explorations for spectral terms.
AI.result: The clock achieves hold-out interval-simultaneous certificate satisfaction across seeds and data shards; substantially reduces eventful-tail violations relative to a baseline scheduler; conformal horizons in the short-horizon regime match deployed clock validity and budget; no clear budget-matched advantage found for the spectral term in partial-reset experiments.
AI.conclusion: The work delivers a certified sensing-clock primitive and a drift-aware deployment method, rather than claiming spectral clocks universally dominate non-spectral schedulers.

title: Domain Generalization via Text-Anchored Information Bottleneck
summary: Visual recognition models often fail when deployed in new environments. Domain Generalization (DG) addresses this by learning representations that remain invariant to environment-specific variations. Recent approaches increasingly rely on large vision-language models, assuming that preserving their expressive visual representations improves robustness. However, we show that such visual expressiveness can instead propagate spurious cues that tie representations to the training environments, hindering invariant learning. We therefore discard visual guidance and instead treat the language embedding space as the primary source of domain invariance, naturally acting as an information bottleneck that preserves core semantics while suppressing domain-specific variations. Extensive experiments across diverse backbones exhibit state-of-the-art performance and further analyze what makes guidance effective for robust generalization. These findings shift the focus of DG from improving representations to designing supervision that enforces invariance.

AI.tldr: Reframes domain generalization by using language embedding space as the primary invariant representation, discarding visual guidance from vision-language models to avoid environment-specific cues; achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse backbones.
AI.motivation: Environment-specific variations cause DG failures. Visual expressiveness from large vision-language models can propagate spurious cues tied to training domains, hindering invariant learning.
AI.method: Treat the language embedding space as the main source of domain invariance and an information bottleneck, suppressing domain-specific variations while preserving core semantics by discarding visual guidance.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse backbones show state-of-the-art DG performance; analysis of what makes language-guided supervision effective for robust generalization.
AI.conclusion: Shifts the DG focus from improving representations to designing supervision that enforces invariance via language-space bottlenecks.

title: Generic Expert Coverage for Pruning SparseMixture-of-Experts Language Models
summary: Sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models contain substantial structured redundancy among routed experts, but pruning them without downstream calibration data remains challenging. Existing expert-pruning methods typically rely on a single aggregated importance score, which can bias the retained set toward experts favored by dominant calibration patterns. We propose \textbf{Generic TB-Coverage}, a coverage-aware expert pruning method that uses only generic text corpora (WikiText2 and C4) for calibration. Instead of collapsing expert utility into one score, our method profiles per-expert utility separately on each corpus and enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask. Across Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25\%, 50\%, and 75\% retention budgets, our method improves average accuracy on six common zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, while also reducing perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. The gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25\% and 50\% retain), suggesting that preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning. Our improvements hold with fixed pruning budgets and no downstream calibration data.

AI.tldr: Introduce Generic TB-Coverage for MoE pruning: profile per-expert utility on multiple generic corpora and enforce a cross-corpus coverage constraint under a fixed pruning budget, improving zero-shot accuracy and reducing perplexity without downstream calibration data.
AI.motivation: Sparsely activated MoE models exhibit structured redundancy among routed experts. Pruning using a single aggregated importance score biases toward experts aligned with dominant calibration patterns and often requires downstream calibration data, which may not be available. A robust pruning approach should preserve cross-corpus utility and work without task-specific calibration data.
AI.method: Profile per-expert utility separately on each corpus (e.g., WikiText2, C4) and apply a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from every corpus before constructing the final pruning mask. Then prune to the chosen budget. This yields a cross-corpus, coverage-aware pruning mask rather than a single aggregated score-based mask.
AI.result: On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25%, 50%, and 75% retention, Generic TB-Coverage improves average zero-shot accuracy over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity across six benchmarks; also reduces perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. Gains are largest at aggressive pruning (25% & 50%), demonstrating the value of preserving cross-corpus expert coverage. These improvements hold with fixed pruning budgets and without downstream calibration data.
AI.conclusion: Cross-corpus coverage-aware pruning is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning. It mitigates the biases of single-score pruning and yields robust performance under limited budgets without requiring downstream calibration data.

title: The Moving Eye: Enhancing VLA Spatial Generalization via Hybrid Dynamic Data Collection
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown remarkable promise in generalized robotic manipulation. However, their spatial generalization remains fragile. We argue that simply increasing the number of viewpoints is insufficient. Models often fall into the trap of Shortcut Learning, latching onto spurious correlations (e.g., fixed relative poses between objects or between the camera and robot base) rather than learning true spatial relationships. In this work, we propose a data-centric solution to enhance VLA spatial generalization. We utilize a dual-arm setup where one arm performs manipulation while the other serves as a mobile environmental camera. We systematically evaluate three data distribution patterns: Fixed, Multi-Fixed, and Moving Views. Our findings reveal that a hybrid strategy, combining continuous camera motion with diverse static viewpoints, yields the best performance by substantially reducing spurious correlations while maintaining training stability. Our experiments demonstrate that this strategy mitigates spurious correlations, enabling VLAs to generalize to unseen camera poses and object configurations where simply adding more static viewpoints fails. Crucially, we reveal that the susceptibility to shortcut learning and the struggle with spatial generalization are universal characteristics shared across diverse architectures. Consequently, all evaluated models (ACT, Diffusion, and VLA models including Pi0 and Gr00t) benefit significantly from our mixed data strategy.

AI.tldr: A data-centric mixed-view strategy with a dual-arm setup improves spatial generalization for Vision-Language-Action models by mitigating shortcut learning; continuous camera motion plus diverse static viewpoints outperform fixed-view baselines across architectures.
AI.motivation: Shortcut learning and reliance on spurious correlations hinder spatial generalization in VLA models; merely adding viewpoints is insufficient; a deliberate data distribution strategy can reduce shortcuts and improve generalization to unseen poses and configurations.
AI.method: Introduce a dual-arm setup with one manipulator and a mobile environmental camera; compare three data distributions (Fixed, Multi-Fixed, Moving Views); propose a hybrid strategy combining continuous camera motion with diverse static viewpoints; evaluate across multiple architectures (ACT, Diffusion, Pi0, Gr00t).
AI.result: Hybrid mixed-view strategy substantially reduces spurious correlations and maintains training stability; improves generalization to unseen camera poses and object configurations; all architectures benefit significantly from the approach.
AI.conclusion: Spatial generalization and shortcut susceptibility are common across VLA architectures; data-centric mixed-view sampling is an effective strategy to enhance generalization and should be considered across models and tasks.

title: Evolutionary Feature Engineering for Structured Data
comment: 9 page main content, 41 pages in total
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as open-ended search operators in evolutionary optimization. We introduce Evolutionary Feature Engineering (EFE), a framework for using LLM-based evolution to discover preprocessing transformations for structured data. EFE represents transformations as Python programs with a standardized fit/transform interface, allowing them to be inserted directly into existing machine learning pipelines. During evolution, candidate programs are refined using dataset context, summary statistics, and downstream performance feedback on validation set. We instantiate EFE in two settings. For time-series forecasting, EFE-Time learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations that improve off-the-shelf time-series foundation models. It reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) 3% or more when averaged across datasets and improvements are as much as 19% on the COVID-Deaths dataset. Notably, these improvements occur with recent TSFMs such as Chronos-2. For tabular prediction, EFE-Tab evolves compact feature programs that add useful interpretable features and remove redundant ones, improving or matching existing LLM-based feature-engineering methods. We found EFE-Tab to be particularly effective on classical decision trees, where small sets of evolved features yield competitive accuracy while preserving interpretability. Overall, EFE demonstrates that LLM-based evolution can improve both accuracy and interpretability when automatically tackling structured data.

AI.tldr: EFE uses LLM-guided evolution to discover Python-based preprocessing transformations for structured data, with two instantiations: EFE-Time for time-series normalization and EFE-Tab for tabular features, yielding better accuracy and interpretability in pipelines.
AI.motivation: To automate feature engineering and preprocessing for structured data by leveraging LLMs to explore and refine transformations within ML pipelines, guided by dataset context and validation feedback.
AI.method: Represent transformations as Python programs with fit/transform interfaces and evolve them using dataset context, summary statistics, and downstream validation performance. Two instantiations: (1) EFE-Time learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations for time-series; (2) EFE-Tab evolves compact, interpretable feature programs that augment or prune features, improving tree-based models.
AI.result: EFE-Time reduces forecasting errors by 3%+ on average (MASE, WQL, MAE) across datasets, with up to 19% improvement on COVID-Deaths, and compatibility with Chronos-2 TSFMs. EFE-Tab yields improvements or parity with existing LLM-based FE methods and is particularly effective for classical decision trees, producing competitive accuracy with interpretable features.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven evolution, as instantiated by EFE, can enhance both accuracy and interpretability in structured-data pipelines by automatically discovering effective preprocessing transformations and feature programs.

title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models What to See and Where to Look
comment: The paper has been accepted by ECCV 2026
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing VLAs' training relies heavily on text-centric visual question answering and chain-of-thought reasoning data, which emphasizes linguistic reasoning rather than action-grounded planning. As a result, the learned representations capture semantic knowledge but lack spatial dependencies crucial for reliable trajectory prediction. We propose DriveTeach-VLA, a framework that explicitly teaches VLAs what to see and where to look. Driving-aware Vision Distillation (DVD) injects driving-specific perceptual priors into the vision encoder, while 2D Trajectory-Guided Prompts (2D-TGP) provide spatial conditioning aligned with feasible driving trajectories. Together, they form a vision-guided learning pipeline: what to see (DVD pretraining) - where to look (TGP-guided SFT) - how to act (TGP-guided GRPO). DriveTeach-VLA achieves the state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM and nuScenes. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ShivaTeam/DriveTeach-VLA.

AI.tldr: DriveTeach-VLA introduces a three-stage vision-language-action framework that teaches a VLA to see and look in driving contexts, using driving-aware vision distillation (DVD) and 2D trajectory-guided prompts (2D-TGP) for spatial conditioning, forming a pipeline: what to see (DVD pretraining) - where to look (TGP-guided SFT) - how to act (TGP-guided GRPO), achieving state-of-the-art results on NAVSIM and nuScenes.
AI.motivation: VLAs in autonomous driving have relied on text-centric VQA and chain-of-thought data, which emphasize linguistic reasoning rather than action-grounded spatial planning. There is a need to inject driving-specific perceptual priors and spatially aligned guidance to improve trajectory prediction and control.
AI.method: Introduce Driving-aware Vision Distillation (DVD) to inject driving priors into the vision encoder. Introduce 2D Trajectory-Guided Prompts (2D-TGP) to provide spatial conditioning aligned with feasible driving trajectories. Implement a three-stage pipeline: (1) what to see via DVD pretraining; (2) where to look via TGP-guided supervised fine-tuning (SFT); (3) how to act via TGP-guided GRPO (policy optimization).
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM and nuScenes datasets.
AI.conclusion: DriveTeach-VLA offers a principled pathway to align vision-language-action models with driving dynamics by combining perception priors and spatially grounded prompts, improving trajectory-grounded decision making in autonomous driving; code is publicly available.

title: Distributionally Robust Listwise Preference Optimization
summary: Existing robust preference optimization for language-model alignment mainly studies pairwise supervision and places robustness at the dataset, prompt, or preference-pair level. We instead study listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty: given a prompt and a candidate list, the observed ranking over that list may be ambiguous due to annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy rankwise feedback, or reward-model noise. We propose a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett--Luce objective that directly robustifies the ranking label conditional on the candidate list. The robust loss admits an exact decomposition into the nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction, and the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order, reducing the inner maximization from $K!$ enumeration to $O(K\log K)$. This tractable structure yields strong offline and online optimization guarantees. In the offline fixed-list setting, the robust objective is convex and projected stochastic subgradient reaches global $ε$-suboptimality with $O(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity. In the online policy-induced setting, where candidate lists are generated by the current policy, we establish weak convexity and $\widetilde O(ε^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity. Experiments in offline LLM alignment show that the proposed robust correction largely preserves performance under clean labels and improves robustness under noise. In online alignment, it makes reward-model-ranked candidate expansion more reliable and improves both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge metrics.

AI.tldr: A robust, listwise ranking objective for LLM alignment under ranking-label uncertainty. It uses a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett–Luce loss with an exact decomposition into a nominal loss plus a worst-case correction; worst-case ranking is efficiently computed in O(K log K). The framework provides offline convex guarantees and online weak convexity with Moreau-envelope stationarity, with empirical gains in robustness to label noise and improved reward-model-based ranking in online settings.
AI.motivation: Existing robust preference optimization largely targets pairwise supervision and is limited to dataset, prompt, or pair-level robustness. There is a need for robust listwise optimization under ranking-label uncertainty to handle annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy feedback, and reward-model noise in LLM alignment.
AI.method: Introduce a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett–Luce objective that conditions on the candidate list; derive an exact decomposition into nominal PL loss and a worst-case PL correction; compute the worst-case ranking by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order, reducing inner maximization from factorial to quasi-linear time (O(K log K)); analyze offline and online optimization properties, establishing convexity in offline fixed-list setting and weak convexity with Moreau-envelope stationarity in online policy-induced setting.
AI.result: The robust objective retains nominal performance under clean labels and improves robustness under label noise in offline LLM alignment experiments; in online alignment, it stabilizes reward-model-ranked candidate expansion and improves metrics for both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge evaluations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed robust listwise-Plackett–Luce framework provides tractable, provably good optimization with strong offline and online guarantees, delivering practical robustness gains in LLM alignment without incurring factorial computation of worst-case rankings.

title: HEFT: Heavy-Payload Full-size Humanoid Teleoperation with Privileged Motion Guidance and Windowed Payload Curriculum
summary: General motion tracking and teleoperation offer a promising path to scalable humanoid skill acquisition, yet most existing frameworks are validated on compact platforms or without real payload interaction, leaving full-size humanoids with real payloads largely unexplored. Scaling to full-size humanoids introduces two compounding challenges: their larger inertia and tighter balance margins make tracking highly sensitive to noise, drift, and retargeting errors from commodity VR trackers, while their payload potential remains largely underutilized. We present HEFT, a heavy-payload full-size humanoid teleoperation framework that addresses both challenges. HEFT learns from deployable noisy VR references with physically plausible reconstructed references through Privileged Motion Guidance (PMG), and uses a Windowed Payload Curriculum (WPC) with expert-guided payload caps to acquire robust heavy-payload tracking. We deploy HEFT on L7, a 175cm, 65kg humanoid. The robot tracks motions including turns, forward/backward locomotion, and squats under payloads up to 24kg.

AI.tldr: HEFT enables robust heavy-payload full-size humanoid teleoperation by integrating Privileged Motion Guidance and Windowed Payload Curriculum, enabling tracking under payloads up to 24 kg on a 1.75 m humanoid.
AI.motivation: Scale full-size humanoids to utilize payload potential while maintaining stable, accurate tracking despite high inertia, tight balance margins, and noise from commodity VR trackers.
AI.method: Privileged Motion Guidance reconstructs physically plausible references from noisy VR data; Windowed Payload Curriculum teaches tracking under progressively heavier payloads with expert-guided caps; deployed on L7 (175 cm, 65 kg).
AI.result: Demonstrates tracking of turns, forward/backward locomotion, and squats under payloads up to 24 kg on the L7 humanoid.
AI.conclusion: HEFT addresses inertia and balance-related sensitivity and underutilized payloads through PMG and WPC, enabling reliable heavy-payload teleoperation for full-size humanoids.

title: X-LogSMask: Expand Transformer for Graph-Structured Data
summary: Transformers have become general-purpose architectures, but their all-to-all self-attention is poorly matched to graph data, whose interactions are sparse, structured and multi-scale. Existing Graph Transformers address this mismatch through structural encodings, hybrid message-passing modules or learned attention constraints, often introducing additional complexity and limited interpretability. Here we introduce X-LogSMask, an explainable multi-head logarithmic structural mask that injects symmetrically normalized graph topology directly into attention logits. The logarithmic transform converts structural connectivity into a topology-aware gating signal, suppressing unsupported node interactions while preserving feature-dependent attention. By assigning different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix to different attention heads, X-LogSMask gives each head a defined structural radius and supports multi-hop information propagation within a single layer. We further show that a standard Transformer encoder can be interpreted as one-step message passing on a complete graph, motivating X-LogSMask as a topology-constrained alternative to unrestricted self-attention. Across 20 node-, edge- and graph-level benchmarks, Transformers equipped with X-LogSMask achieve state-of-the-art performance on 13 datasets and remain competitive in a lightweight one-layer configuration. These results show that simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without changing the Transformer architecture. The code is available at https://github.com/LiLeyan-0120/X-LogSMask.

AI.tldr: Introduce X-LogSMask: an explainable, multi-head logarithmic structural mask that injects normalized graph topology into Transformer attention to enable topology-aware, multi-hop graph learning within a single layer, achieving strong performance on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Graph data have sparse, structured interactions that are not well served by dense, all-to-all self-attention. There is a need for a simple, interpretable mechanism to enforce topology constraints in attention without architectural changes.
AI.method: Propose X-LogSMask: apply symmetric normalization of the adjacency matrix and a logarithmic transform to attention logits to create a topology-aware gating signal. Each attention head uses a different power of the normalized adjacency to assign a distinct structural radius, enabling multi-hop information propagation within a single layer. Interpret a standard Transformer encoder as one-step message passing on a complete graph to motivate this topology-constrained alternative. Implementable within the standard Transformer architecture.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on 20 node/edge/graph benchmarks shows state-of-the-art performance on 13 datasets and competitive results in a lightweight, one-layer configuration.
AI.conclusion: Simple, interpretable structural masks can adapt self-attention to graph learning without changing the Transformer architecture, offering a topology-constrained alternative to unrestricted self-attention.

title: Unified Panoramic-Gaussian Representation for Monocular 4D Scene Synthesis
summary: 4D scene synthesis from monocular videos has made significant progress in recent years. However, existing methods are typically constrained by view interpolation. As a result, they struggle to infer unseen regions beyond the observed views. In this paper, we reformulate the task as 4D scene synthesis with unseen regions, which extends beyond traditional interpolation settings. Camera-conditioned video generation enables unseen region synthesis by guiding generation along specified cameras. However, these methods lack explicit 3D priors and are optimized with random camera trajectories. This design leads to severe inconsistencies under large trajectory deviations. To address this limitation, we build a unified training and inference framework with panoramic trajectory guidance. While this design improves cross-view consistency, the panoramic representation alone fails to model dynamic content effectively. Object motion in panoramic space introduces scale and shape distortions. To address this, we propose PanoGaussian, a unified Panoramic-Gaussian representation that distills the panoramic representation into an explicit dynamic Gaussian representation to capture dynamic physical priors of the 4D scene. Experiments demonstrate that PanoGaussian achieves consistent 4D scene synthesis even under large viewpoint variations.

AI.tldr: Unified panoramic-guided 4D scene synthesis with unseen regions via PanoGaussian, combining panoramic trajectory guidance and a dynamic Gaussian representation to enforce physical priors and cross-view consistency under large camera variations.
AI.motivation: Current monocular 4D scene synthesis is constrained by view interpolation and lacks robust 3D priors, leading to inconsistencies when viewpoints deviate. There is a need to handle unseen regions and dynamic content more faithfully beyond observed views.
AI.method: Introduce a unified training/inference framework with panoramic trajectory guidance and Panoramic-Gaussian (PanoGaussian) representation. The panoramic space guides camera-conditioned generation, while the Gaussian component distills the panorama into an explicit dynamic prior to model motion and scale, addressing distortions inherent to panoramic representations.
AI.result: Empirical results show improved cross-view consistency and robust 4D scene synthesis under large viewpoint variations, outperforming panorama-only approaches by mitigating distortions from dynamic content in panoramic space.
AI.conclusion: PanoGaussian successfully integrates panoramic guidance with an explicit dynamic Gaussian prior to enable consistent, unseen-region 4D scene synthesis across wide camera trajectories.

title: DRL-CLBA: A Clean Label Backdoor Attack for Speech Classification via DDPG Reinforcement Learning
summary: Deep learning models for speech classification are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where malicious triggers cause misclassification at inference time. While sample-specific attacks can bypass many defenses, they often rely on poisoned label attack, making them detectable via manual data defense. In this paper, we propose DRL-CLBA, a novel clean label backdoor attack for speech classification that leverages Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) reinforcement learning. We also utilize deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers into source audio, creating feature-space anchors. The proposed reinforcement learning framework effectively optimizes target samples toward trigger-bearing anchor points in the model's deep latent space, enabling label-migration-free poisoning of target samples. Experimental results across three datasets and four different DNNs demonstrate that DRL-CLBA achieves a high attack success rate, effectively bypassing some backdoor defenses. The attack demonstrates strong resistance against fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral signature defenses, exposing critical vulnerabilities in speech-controlled systems.

AI.tldr: A clean-label backdoor attack for speech classification using DDPG reinforcement learning and deep audio steganography to craft sample-specific triggers in latent space, achieving high attack success and bypassing several defenses across multiple datasets and DNN architectures.
AI.motivation: To overcome detectability of poisoning-based backdoors by avoiding label corruption and leveraging clean-label techniques, while ensuring robust, targeted misclassification through latent-space trigger anchors.
AI.method: Train a DRL agent (DDPG) to steer target samples toward trigger-bearing anchor points in the model’s deep latent space. Embed sample-specific triggers into source audio via deep audio steganography to create feature-space anchors. The framework aims for label-migration-free poisoning by aligning targets with anchor representations.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on three datasets and four DNNs showing high attack success and bypassing some defenses. The attack demonstrates resilience against fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral-signature defenses, highlighting vulnerabilities in speech-controlled systems.
AI.conclusion: DRL-CLBA demonstrates that clean-label backdoor attacks using latent-space anchor optimization and steganographic triggers can be highly effective and difficult to defend against, underscoring the need for robust defense mechanisms in speech classification.

title: ACID: Action Consistency via Inverse Dynamics for Planning with World Models
summary: Decision-time planning with action-conditioned world models has become a popular paradigm for embodied control. However, the standard planning cost judges a candidate solely by how close its predicted terminal state lies to the goal, leaving the realizability of the intermediate transitions unchecked -- a predicted trajectory can look convincing while the environment rollout drifts away from it. In this paper, we propose ACID, a decision-time planning framework that introduces cycle action consistency: the action inferred backward from a predicted transition by an inverse dynamics model should recover the one that was conditioned on. We fold this per-step residual into the planning cost via a scale-invariant adaptive weight. Across four action-conditioned world models and six tasks spanning rigid and deformable manipulation, articulated control, and visual navigation, ACID consistently improves planning and matches the baseline's accuracy with substantially less planning compute.

AI.tldr: ACID adds cycle action consistency to decision-time planning with action-conditioned world models by enforcing recoverability of the conditioned action via inverse dynamics, integrated as a scale-invariant per-step residual in the planning objective; this yields more realistic trajectories and reduces compute.
AI.motivation: Existing planning costs only optimize terminal state proximity, ignoring the realism of intermediate transitions; this can produce convincing predictions that drift in reality. ACID targets realism of per-step transitions to improve planning reliability.
AI.method: Introduce cycle action consistency: compute the action inferred from a predicted transition using an inverse dynamics model and penalize deviations from the originally conditioned action. Incorporate the per-step residual into the planning cost with a scale-invariant adaptive weighting. Evaluate across four action-conditioned world models and six tasks (rigid/deformable manipulation, articulated control, visual navigation).
AI.result: ACID consistently improves planning and achieves baseline accuracy with substantially less planning compute across diverse models and tasks.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing cycle action consistency anchors imagined trajectories to real action-conditioned dynamics, yielding more reliable planning with reduced computational cost.

title: Geometric Signatures of Reasoning: A Spectral Perspective on Task Hardness
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables large language models (LLMs) to solve complex problems by generating intermediate reasoning steps. While much attention has been paid to the length and content of these reasoning chains, far less is known about their internal geometry. We study the \emph{geometry} of CoT trajectories in the hidden state space of transformer models, formalizing each reasoning chain as a discrete curve in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and characterizing it through spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals. We introduce the effective dimension $d_ρ$ as a measure of trajectory complexity and show theoretically that trajectories with flatter eigenvalue spectra correspond to harder tasks, as they explore more of the hidden dimensions. Lastly, we explore how kinematic features of the trajectory, mean position, positional dispersion, initial and current hidden states, mean velocity, mean speed, and speed dispersion, can be used to predict solution correctness before generation is complete, and may inform future early-stopping strategies. Experimentally, on mathematical reasoning problems from the MATH500 dataset, $d_ρ$ achieves $0.93$ AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems, while kinematic features potentially can predict correctness from only the first $20\%$ of generated tokens. These correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty, establishing that the shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory is a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality.

AI.tldr: Formalizes Chain-of-Thought reasoning as trajectories in hidden state space; defines geometric functionals including an effective dimension d_ρ; links flatter eigenvalue spectra to harder tasks; shows kinematic features enable early prediction of correctness; achieves 0.93 AUC on MATH500 for hard/easy discrimination and potential early-stopping cues.
AI.motivation: To understand the internal geometry of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in transformer models, relating hidden-state trajectory shape to task hardness and solution quality beyond surface-level metrics like chain length or token content.
AI.method: Model the CoT reasoning path as a discrete curve in R^d; characterize it via spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals. Define effective dimension d_ρ as a trajectory complexity measure. Prove that flatter eigenvalue spectra correlate with harder tasks (broader exploration of hidden dimensions). Extract kinematic features (mean position, positional dispersion, initial/current states, mean velocity, mean speed, speed dispersion) from hidden states and evaluate their ability to predict solution correctness before generation completes. Validate on mathematical reasoning tasks from the MATH500 dataset and test transferability across varying difficulty questions.
AI.result: The effective dimension d_ρ achieves 0.93 AUC in distinguishing easy vs. hard problems. Kinematic features show potential to predict correctness from only the first 20% of generated tokens. The correctness signatures transfer across questions of differing difficulty, suggesting the internal trajectory shape is a principled indicator of task hardness and solution quality.
AI.conclusion: Internal geometry of CoT trajectories offers a principled lens into task difficulty and solution quality, with practical implications for early-stopping and monitoring of LLM reasoning. The framework links spectral properties to task hardness and demonstrates robust predictive cues from hidden-state dynamics across problems.

title: Temporal and Cross-Modal Alignment for Enhanced Audiovisual Video Captioning
summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have advanced video understanding, achieving precise temporal and cross-modal alignment in audiovisual video captioning remains a formidable challenge. Most existing approaches suffer from modality detachment and temporal incoherence, failing to accurately bind auditory events to visual entities or capture complex causal dynamics. To address these deficiencies, we propose TCA-Captioner, a framework specifically engineered to enhance Temporal and Cross-Modal Alignment for audiovisual video captioning. We first introduce the Observer-Checker-Corrector (OCC) framework, an iterative refinement strategy that generates high-fidelity, meticulously grounded training data. Leveraging a curated high-density human interaction dataset, TCA-Captioner is optimized to model sophisticated audiovisual interactions. Furthermore, we present TCA-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark utilizing a Decoupled Evaluation Protocol to isolate and quantify model proficiency in audiovisual binding and temporal relational reasoning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TCA-Captioner sets a new standard for temporally-coherent and synchronized audiovisual narratives.

AI.tldr: Introduces OCC-driven iterative data refinement (Observer-Checker-Corrector) and a high-density interaction dataset to improve temporal and cross-modal alignment in audiovisual captioning; also provides TCA-Bench for decoupled evaluation, achieving superior temporal coherence.
AI.motivation: Current MLLMs struggle with precise temporal binding of audio events to visual entities and with modeling causal audiovisual dynamics; existing methods suffer modality detachment and incoherence.
AI.method: OCC framework to generate high-fidelity, grounded training data via iterative refinement; uses high-density human interaction data to train model to capture audiovisual interactions; TCA-Bench with Decoupled Evaluation Protocol to separately evaluate audiovisual binding and temporal relational reasoning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show TCA-Captioner achieves temporally-coherent and synchronized audiovisual narratives, setting a new standard.
AI.conclusion: The OCC data-refinement pipeline and decoupled benchmark provide a robust path to improve temporal and cross-modal alignment in audiovisual captioning; future work could extend to broader modalities and real-world noisy data.

title: Reformalization of the Jordan Curve Theorem
summary: We present a case study in reformalization, a variant of autoformalization in which the input proof is not natural language but a formal development in a different proof assistant. Concretely, we report three reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem: from Mizar to Lean, from HOL Light to Lean, and from HOL Light to Agda. We analyse the results and identify pipeline design choices that matter for practical reformalization tasks.

AI.tldr: Three cross-system reformalizations of Jordan Curve Theorem (Mizar→Lean, HOL Light→Lean, HOL Light→Agda) with analysis of pipeline choices affecting practical reformalization.
AI.motivation: Investigate practical aspects of reformalization, exploring interoperability between proof assistants and how translation pipelines affect outcomes.
AI.method: Case-study translations of a formal theorem across proof assistants, examining representations, libraries, proof styles, automation, and evaluation of translatability and performance.
AI.result: Preliminary observations on which pipeline design choices matter in reformalization: foundational representations (set theory vs type theory), library alignment, handling of implicit/structured proofs, and translation of tactics vs terms; identification of pain points and potential strategies to improve cross-system reformalization.
AI.conclusion: Pipeline design choices significantly shape reformalization success; results inform best practices and guide future tooling to support cross-system formalization.

title: LIME: Learning Intent-aware Camera Motion from Egocentric Video
summary: Autonomous robots often need to move their camera before they can act: to inspect an object, reveal an occluded region, or obtain a view that responds to a user's intent. While vision-language navigation translates instructions to base motion and vision-language-action policies map instructions to manipulation actions, language-conditioned camera motion remains comparatively underexplored as a first-class action. We formulate language-conditioned camera motion generation: given a current RGB observation and a free-form natural-language intent, predict a relative target camera pose for the next observation. This task is inherently non-trivial: viewpoint changes are driven by latent perceptual intentions, and a valid motion may operate at different semantic granularity, from entering a room to looking around a corner, inspecting a visible object, or revealing an occluded detail. To model this structure, we mine multi-intention camera-motion supervision from egocentric video, pairing plausible intents and observation-gain descriptions with relative SE(3) target poses. We propose LIME, a vision-language camera-motion generator that combines an auto-regressive observation-gain output with a continuous flow-matching pose head. This design lets the model jointly predict what the next view should reveal while representing multi-hypothesis target views. Across experiments and downstream robotic tasks, we show that LIME can learn to actively choose camera poses from passive human video, turning ordinary egocentric recordings into supervision for intent-aware active perception.

AI.tldr: A vision-language camera-motion generator (LIME) predicts next camera pose from a current RGB observation and a free-form natural-language intent, using autoregressive observation-gain output and a flow-matching pose head, trained on mined intents from egocentric video to enable multi-hypothesis, intent-driven active perception.
AI.motivation: Language-conditioned camera motion as a first-class action in robotics is underexplored. Viewpoint changes are driven by latent perceptual intents and can occur at varying granularities; leveraging egocentric data can provide supervision for intent-aware view planning.
AI.method: Introduce LIME, an architecture with an autoregressive observation-gain module and a continuous-flow pose head. Mine multi-intention camera-motion supervision from egocentric video by pairing plausible intents and description of observation gains with relative SE(3) poses. The model jointly predicts the next view content and a distribution over target poses, enabling multi-hypothesis outputs.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show LIME can learn to actively choose camera poses from passive human video and improve downstream robotic tasks, demonstrating effective intent-aware active perception from egocentric supervision.
AI.conclusion: Language-conditioned camera motion is feasible and beneficial. LIME provides a unified framework to couple language, perception, and pose prediction, and can exploit passive egocentric data to train intention-aware active perception policies.

title: BOUNDARY_SYNC: Measuring Communication-Induced Representational Coupling in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed as communicating agents, does inter-agent communication cause outputs to converge? We introduce BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol measuring representational coupling via the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline), where CAF < 1 indicates homogenization and CAF > 1 indicates diversification. In controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9,900 API calls), we measure coupling in text and image communication. Key findings: (1) text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803 [0.740, 0.873], d=1.30, p<0.001), confirmed by no-communication ablation and prompt-perturbation controls; (2) image communication also homogenizes under within-modality baselines (CAF=0.834 [0.811, 0.858]), with comparable proportional effect; (3) group size moderates coupling direction -- K=5 produces homogenization while K=3 yields CAF > 1.0 (point estimates 1.14 and 1.06, CI pending), suggesting a directional shift toward diversification; (4) cross-model replication shows extreme variation (CAF 0.034-0.803), with DeepSeek dominated by format artifacts; (5) coupling is stateless -- driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating, with continuous consensus producing monotonic convergence. These results establish LLM agent coupling as real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level, with direct implications for multi-agent system design.

AI.tldr: BOUNDARY_SYNC introduces Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline) to quantify representational coupling in inter-agent LLM communication. Across text and image modalities, results show homogenization under most settings, with group size modulating the direction of coupling. Cross-model replication reveals substantial variability, and the coupling is largely driven by prompt context (stateless) rather than cumulative updates. Implications: coupling is real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level for multi-agent system design.
AI.motivation: As LLMs increasingly operate as communicating agents, it is vital to quantify whether inter-agent communication causes outputs to converge (homogenize) or diversify, and to establish a metric and experimental protocol that isolates and controls this coupling for robust multi-agent system design.
AI.method: Controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9,900 API calls). Define CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline to measure coupling. Evaluate text and image communication against within-modality baselines, with ablations (no-communication, prompt perturbation) to validate coupling. Systematically vary group size K (e.g., 3 vs 5) and replicate across models (including DeepSeek). Assess whether coupling is stateless (prompt-context driven) or accumulates over time, and report confidence intervals and effect sizes (d) where reported.
AI.result: (1) Text communication yields significant homogenization (CAF=0.803 [0.740,0.873], d=1.30, p<0.001); confirmed by ablation controls. (2) Image communication also homogenizes under within-modality baselines (CAF=0.834 [0.811,0.858]), similar magnitude. (3) Group size shifts coupling: K=5 yields homogenization; K=3 yields CAF>1 (diversification); point estimates 1.14 and 1.06 with CI pending. (4) Cross-model replication shows wide variation (CAF 0.034–0.803); DeepSeek dominated by format artifacts. (5) Coupling is stateless; driven by prompt context; continuous consensus yields monotonic convergence.
AI.conclusion: LLM agent coupling is real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level. Findings have practical implications for designing multi-agent systems, enabling deliberate adjustment of coupling via prompt strategies and prompting structure to balance homogenization and diversification as task demands dictate.

title: HistoSeg++: Delving deeper with attention and multiscale feature fusion for biomarker segmentation
comment: Published in the Proceedings of ICBBE 2025. The Version of Record is available at https://doi.org/10.1145/3794209.3794211
summary: Segmentation of biomarkers in medical images is frequently viewed as a first step towards medical image analysis in any bioinformatics or biomedical application. Despite progress, existing methods still struggle to capture information at multiple scales and to perform upsampling effectively across different datasets. These shortcomings often result in suboptimal generalization capabilities. Recently, architectures belonging to the Nested-UNet family excel in capturing multiscale contextual information and upsample them effectively. In this work, We propose a novel Nested-UNet architecture that effectively captures multi-scale contextual information. It includes inner and outer attention units to enhance focus during upsampling, along with channel-wise feature recalibration using squeeze-and-excitation modules, leading to improved segmentation performance. Additionally, the architecture integrates an edge-aware loss to emphasize boundary accuracy by assigning greater importance to edge regions. Tested extensively on three publicly available benchmark datasets. Our method demonstrates a generalization performance superior to existing Nested-UNet methods. Code: https://github.com/saadwazir/histosegplusplus

AI.tldr: A Nested-UNet-based architecture with inner/outer attention, squeeze-and-excitation recalibration, and edge-aware loss improves multi-scale biomarker segmentation and generalization across public datasets; code released.
AI.motivation: Address the difficulty of capturing multi-scale contextual information and effective upsampling in medical image segmentation, which hampers generalization across datasets.
AI.method: Proposes a novel Nested-UNet architecture augmented with (i) inner and outer attention modules to refine upsampling, (ii) channel-wise recalibration via squeeze-and-excitation (SE) blocks, and (iii) an edge-aware loss to emphasize boundary accuracy. Tested on three public benchmarks, with comparisons to existing Nested-UNet variants.
AI.result: Demonstrates superior generalization and segmentation performance over existing Nested-UNet methods across three datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed architecture enhances multi-scale feature aggregation, boundary precision, and cross-dataset generalization, and is accompanied by publicly available code.

title: Meta-Benchmarks for Financial-Services LLM Evaluation
summary: Public LLM leaderboards optimise for global average performance and do not capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work: a model that leads on MMLU-Pro may underperform on document-grounded compliance reasoning, and a coding leader may handle multi-turn customer interactions poorly. We present a meta-benchmarking framework that organises 452 publicly reported benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and aggregates those into 38 BIAN banking business domains spanning sales, operations, risk, and support work. A multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination x coverage x recency), computed over a rolling model window, rewards benchmarks that still separate the best models, are widely reported, and remain in active use, suppressing saturated legacy tests automatically. These weights scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, producing cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalisation; business-domain scores are weighted averages of the constituent work-activity Elos. We demonstrate the framework on a point-in-time public snapshot covering 288 models across 25 organisations as of June 2026, and describe the methodology, full taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations with the aim of making the approach reproducible for institutions facing similar selection and governance challenges.

AI.tldr: A meta-benchmarking framework reclassifies 452 public benchmarks into 41 O*NET activities and 38 BIAN banking domains, applying a multiplicative discrimination x coverage x recency weighting within a rolling window to scale Elo-based work-activity scores and derive domain scores; demonstrated on 288 models across 25 organisations (as of June 2026) with documented methodology for reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Public LLM leaderboards optimize for global averages and miss the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work. A domain-aware, governance-friendly benchmarking framework is needed to reflect real-work tasks, adapt to evolving benchmarks, and avoid saturating legacy tests.
AI.method: Map 452 benchmarks to 41 O*NET generalized work activities, aggregate to 38 BIAN banking domains; implement a multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination × coverage × recency) over a rolling model window; apply these weights to scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament to produce cross-benchmark work-activity Elos; compute business-domain scores as weighted averages of work-activity Elos; present a point-in-time snapshot (288 models, 25 organisations, June 2026) and provide full taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations for reproducibility.
AI.result: Framework demonstrated on a public snapshot, yielding cross-benchmark comparable work-activity scores without raw-score normalization and domain-level scores as averages of constituent Elos; supports reproducible evaluation suitable for governance contexts.
AI.conclusion: The approach offers a reproducible, domain-aware benchmarking methodology for financial-services LLM evaluation, mitigating legacy-test saturation and enabling governance-oriented model selection and comparison; limitations are openly discussed to guide adoption.

title: WorldSample: Closed-loop Real-robot RL with World Modelling
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can overcome the demonstration-coverage limitation of imitation learning (IL) by allowing robots to improve through trial-and-error interaction beyond the states observed in demonstrations. However, deploying RL on real robots remains constrained by high interaction costs, since each physical rollout is costly and reflects only one realized action-outcome path. To address this challenge, we propose WorldSample, a physically grounded data augmentation framework for real-robot RL that closes a real-synthetic loop between physical rollouts, world-model generation, and policy improvement. Grounded on real rollouts, WorldSample generates high-fidelity synthetic transitions through a post-trained world model, which greatly lowers the visual hallucination. Specifically, rather than simply using these transitions as real-world experience, WorldSample introduces Policy-Paced Learning (PPL) to regulate the training process through sample selection and scheduling, balancing useful augmentation against value overestimation and mitigating the hallucination-induced noise. Experiments on robot manipulation tasks involving contact-rich and precise tasks show that WorldSample improves policy success rate by 28% while reducing training steps by 59% compared with baselines. Furthermore, WorldSample improves world model visual fidelity by 19.4dB in PSNR and 0.47 in SSIM over demonstration-only post-training, validating the effectiveness of the real-synthetic loop for both policy and world model performance.

AI.tldr: WorldSample uses a real-synthetic loop for real-robot RL: real rollouts feed a post-trained world model to generate high-fidelity synthetic transitions, regulated by Policy-Paced Learning to balance augmentation and overestimation. This yields better policy performance and faster training, with improved world-model fidelity.
AI.motivation: Reduce real-robot reinforcement learning data collection costs by leveraging a grounded world model to augment experience while controlling hallucination and value overestimation.
AI.method: 1) Collect real-rollout data to learn a policy and initialize a grounded world model. 2) Post-train a high-fidelity world model that can generate synthetic transitions from states. 3) Use Policy-Paced Learning (PPL) to selectively incorporate augmented synthetic data via sample selection and scheduling to mitigate hallucination and value overestimation. 4) Evaluate on manipulation tasks with contact-rich and precision requirements, comparing against baselines.
AI.result: WorldSample improves policy success rate by 28% and reduces training steps by 59% relative to baselines. It also improves world-model visual fidelity by 19.4 dB (PSNR) and 0.47 (SSIM) over demonstration-only post-training.
AI.conclusion: A real-synthetic loop with policy-paced data augmentation can substantially enhance both policy learning efficiency and world-model fidelity for real-robot RL in contact-rich manipulation tasks.

title: SINA: A Fully Automated Circuit Schematic Image to Netlist Generator Using Artificial Intelligence
summary: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have revolutionized Electronic Design Automation (EDA), particularly through Large Language Models (LLMs) for circuit design tasks. However, their application to analog and mixed-signal domains remains limited by the lack of machine-readable representations of existing circuit design knowledge. Circuit schematic images found in research manuscripts, textbooks, and websites constitute a vast repository of validated designs; however, these visual representations cannot be directly processed by EDA tools. Converting them into machine-readable netlists is essential for enabling simulation, verification, and building comprehensive databases for AI-based models. Current conversion methods lack generalization across both Integrated Circuit (IC) and Printed Circuit Board (PCB) level schematics. Moreover, they struggle with component recognition and connectivity inference, and fail to distinguish between connected junctions and crossing wires. In this paper, we propose SINA, an open-source circuit schematic image-to-netlist generator. SINA is a fully automated pipeline that integrates deep learning for robust component detection, connected-component labeling for accurate connectivity inference, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for component reference designator extraction, and a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for reliable reference designator assignment. SINA handles both IC- and PCB-level schematics and incorporates dedicated crossing-wires detection to differentiate wire intersections from connections. We validate the correctness of the generated netlists using graph isomorphism techniques. Our experiments demonstrate an overall netlist generation accuracy of 96.67%, which is 2.72x higher compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: SINA is an open-source image-to-netlist generator for IC and PCB schematics that uses DL-based component detection, connected-component labeling, OCR, and a vision-language model to assign reference designators, with crossing-wire detection and graph-isomorphism validation, achieving 96.67% netlist accuracy and 2.72x improvement over baselines.
AI.motivation: To convert visual schematic representations (from papers, textbooks, and websites) into machine-readable netlists, enabling simulation, verification, and AI-driven database construction for analog/mixed-signal design.
AI.method: An end-to-end pipeline: (1) robust component detection via deep learning, (2) connected-component labeling for accurate connectivity inference, (3) OCR for extracting component reference designators, (4) a vision-language model for reliable reference designator assignment, (5) dedicated crossing-wires detection to distinguish wire intersections from connections, (6) validation of netlists using graph isomorphism techniques; supports both IC- and PCB-level schematics and is open-source.
AI.result: Reported netlist-generation accuracy of 96.67%, claimed to be 2.72× higher than state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: SINA provides a robust, generalizable solution for converting schematic images to netlists across IC and PCB domains, addressing connectivity inference and wire crossing issues and enabling reliable downstream EDA tasks.

title: ICDepth: Taming Video Diffusion Models for Video Depth Estimation via In-Context Conditioning
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project page: https://xuanhuahe.github.io/ICDepth/
summary: Monocular video depth estimation requires temporal consistency, geometric accuracy, and generalization across diverse scenarios, yet existing methods struggle to achieve all three simultaneously. Discriminative models excel at per-frame accuracy but suffer from temporal drift due to limited context windows, while generative methods improve consistency and generalization at the cost of extensive training data (10M+ samples) and lack of geometric precision. In response to these issues, we introduce \textbf{ICDepth}, a framework that adapts pre-trained text-to-video diffusion transformers for video depth estimation via In-Context Conditioning (ICC), leveraging their rich spatial-temporal priors. To address key challenges in transferring ICC from generation to dense prediction, we propose: (1)~\textbf{SAND-Attention}, which ensures precise spatial-temporal alignment via shared RoPE and enforces unidirectional attention to prevent noise contamination; (2)~\textbf{SRFM}, which injects DINOv2 semantic and resolution priors to enhance geometric precision. ICDepth achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks with remarkable data efficiency, trained on only 0.8M frames ($6$--$13\times$ less than competing generative methods), while demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization to diverse domains.

AI.tldr: ICDepth adapts pre-trained text-to-video diffusion transformers for video depth estimation via In-Context Conditioning (ICC), with SAND-Attention and SRFM, achieving state-of-the-art results with high data efficiency (0.8M frames) and strong zero-shot generalization.
AI.motivation: Bridging discriminative per-frame accuracy and generative temporal consistency without requiring massive training data; existing methods struggle to optimize for temporal consistency, geometry, and generalization simultaneously.
AI.method: Adapts ICC from text-to-video diffusion models for dense prediction; introduces SAND-Attention—shared RoPE and unidirectional attention to maintain spatial-temporal alignment and avoid noise propagation; SRFM uses DINOv2 semantic and resolution priors to improve geometric precision.
AI.result: SOTA on multiple benchmarks; trained on 0.8M frames (< training data than competing generative methods by 6–13x); strong zero-shot generalization across domains.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates effective transfer of ICC to dense prediction; achieves a favorable balance among temporal consistency, geometric accuracy, and generalization with data efficiency.

title: Path-level Hindsight Instructions for Semantic Exploration in Vision-Language Navigation
summary: On-policy exploration is a crucial component for training robust Vision-Language Navigation agents, as it exposes the policy to a broader state distribution. However, such exploration inevitably leads to trajectories that deviate from expert demonstrations, resulting in a semantic mismatch between the executed visual stream and the original language instruction. In this work, we address this challenge by introducing Phi-Nav, a unified on-policy framework that leverages hindsight reasoning to align instructions with the agent's actual exploratory journey. Specifically, Phi-Nav operates through a three-stage dual-supervision cycle: 1) the agent performs oracle-guided on-policy exploration, sampling a trajectory while learning from expert action feedback, 2) a hindsight speaker synthesizes a path-level hindsight instruction grounded in the collected visual observations, and 3) the agent conducts a second imitation pass, treating the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration. Through this process, Phi-Nav bridges the critical semantic supervision gap inherent in on-policy methods, transforming semantically unlabeled movement into dense training signals. Evaluations on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks show that Phi-Nav yields competitive performance while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines. These results underscore the necessity of semantic exploration in VLN, positioning Phi-Nav as an effective solution for training embodied agents with limited data.

AI.tldr: Phi-Nav introduces a three-stage on-policy framework with hindsight reasoning to align executed VLN trajectories with instructions, enabling semantic supervision via a hindsight speaker and a second imitation pass; it achieves competitive results on R2R-CE and RxR-CE with substantially fewer expert demonstrations.
AI.motivation: On-policy exploration in Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) creates semantic mismatches between the agent’s observed visual stream and the original language instruction. Without aligned supervision, learning from exploratory trajectories is inefficient and error-prone.
AI.method: A three-stage dual-supervision cycle: (1) oracle-guided on-policy exploration with expert action feedback; (2) a hindsight speaker synthesizes a path-level hindsight instruction from accumulated observations; (3) a second imitation pass treats the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as additional expert data, thereby closing the semantic supervision gap.
AI.result: Phi-Nav yields competitive VLN performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks while using only a fraction of the expert demonstrations required by existing baselines, demonstrating the value of semantic exploration in on-policy VLN training.
AI.conclusion: Semantic exploration is essential for robust VLN training; Phi-Nav provides an effective, data-efficient framework that leverages hindsight reasoning to re-label exploratory trajectories and reinforce learning with dense, semantically aligned supervision.

title: Learning to Move Before Learning to Do: Task-Agnostic pretraining for VLAs
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are fundamentally bottlenecked by the scarcity of expert demonstrations -- triplets of observations, instructions, and actions that are costly to collect at scale. We argue that this bottleneck stems from conflating two distinct learning objectives: acquiring physical competence (how to move) and acquiring semantic alignment (what to do). Crucially, only the latter requires language supervision. Building on this Decomposition Hypothesis, we propose Task-Agnostic Pretraining (TAP), a two-stage framework that first learns transferable motor priors from cheap, unlabeled interaction data -- including discarded off-task trajectories and autonomous robot play -- via a self-supervised Inverse Dynamics objective. A lightweight second stage then grounds these priors in language using minimal expert data. On the SIMPLER benchmark, TAP matches models trained on over 1M expert trajectories while using orders of magnitude less labeled data, yielding a 10% absolute gain over standard behavior cloning. On a real-world WidowX platform, TAP retains 25% success under camera perturbations where internet-scale baselines collapse to 0%, demonstrating that task-agnostic pretraining produces robust, transferable physical representations and offers a scalable path forward for Embodied AI.

AI.tldr: Two-stage Task-Agnostic Pretraining (TAP) decouples physical competence from semantic alignment: learn transferable motor priors via self-supervised inverse dynamics from unlabeled interaction, then ground them in language using minimal expert data. Results show strong label efficiency and robustness on SIMPLER and WidowX.
AI.motivation: VLA models suffer from scarce expert demonstrations (observation-instruction-action triplets). The paper argues that learning physical motor skills and semantic task alignment are distinct: the former needs no language supervision, while the latter does. Decomposition suggests leveraging cheap unlabeled data to learn motor priors, reducing reliance on expensive language-labeled data.
AI.method: Stage 1: self-supervised learning of motor priors through an inverse dynamics objective on unlabeled interaction data (including discarded off-task trajectories and autonomous play). Stage 2: minimal expert data to ground the priors in language, effectively aligning action semantics with instructions. This Task-Agnostic Pretraining (TAP) aims to produce transferable physical representations that are robust to perturbations and scalable across tasks.
AI.result: On the SIMPLER benchmark, TAP matches models trained on over 1M expert trajectories while using orders of magnitude less labeled data, and achieves a 10% absolute gain over standard behavior cloning. On the real-world WidowX platform, TAP maintains 25% success under camera perturbations where internet-scale baselines collapse to 0%, demonstrating robust, transferable physical representations.
AI.conclusion: Task-agnostic pretraining yields robust, transferable physical representations and offers a scalable path forward for Embodied AI by separating physical competence learning from semantic alignment and leveraging cheap unlabeled data to pretrain motor priors.

title: MKGR: Multimodal Knowledge-Graph Representation Learning for Cold-Start Protein-Protein Interaction Prediction
summary: Accurate protein-protein interaction (PPI) prediction is central to functional genomics, disease mechanism discovery, and drug development. A difficult setting arises when candidate interactions include proteins that have no observed PPI edges during training, where models relying on network topology alone often lose useful context. This paper presents \method, a multimodal representation framework for cold-start PPI prediction. \method\ combines region-aware protein sequence encoding with four protein-centered biomedical knowledge graphs, including protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, and protein-lncRNA associations. The sequence branch extracts contextual representations from structurally informed sequence regions, while graph attention encoders learn modality-specific protein embeddings from sparse biomedical associations. A bridge reconstruction objective regularizes graph learning by recovering shared protein-entity associations, and a pair-level gating module adaptively integrates sequence and graph evidence for each candidate protein pair. Experiments on two benchmark datasets under novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings show that \method\ consistently outperforms competitive sequence, network, and knowledge-graph baselines across ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC.

AI.tldr: Multimodal cold-start PPI predictor that fuses region-aware protein sequences with four protein-centered knowledge graphs, using a bridge reconstruction objective and pair-level gating to outperform baselines on cold-start settings.
AI.motivation: Tackle cold-start PPI prediction when training lacks observed edges for certain proteins, where topology-based methods lose predictive power; leverage sequence context and rich biomedical associations to generalize.
AI.method:
- Sequence branch: region-aware encoding using structurally informed sequence regions.
- Graph branch: four protein-centered KG encoders (protein–drug, protein–disease, protein–miRNA, protein–lncRNA) with graph attention.
- Bridge reconstruction objective: recovers shared protein–entity associations to regularize graph learning.
- Pair-level gating: adaptively fuses sequence and graph evidence for each candidate protein pair.
AI.result:
On two benchmark datasets under novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings, 
	i) outperforms competitive baselines (sequence, network, KG) across accuracy, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC.
AI.conclusion: Integrating region-aware sequence information with multiple, sparse biomedical knowledge graphs via a bridge objective and pair-level gating improves cold-start PPI prediction and demonstrates effective cross-modality fusion.

title: Structure-Aware Gaussian Splatting for Large-Scale Scene Reconstruction
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting has demonstrated remarkable potential in novel view synthesis. In contrast to small-scale scenes, large-scale scenes inevitably contain sparsely observed regions with excessively sparse initial points. In this case, supervising Gaussians initialized from low-frequency sparse points with high-frequency images often induces uncontrolled densification and redundant primitives, degrading both efficiency and quality. Intuitively, this issue can be mitigated with scheduling strategies, which can be categorized into two paradigms: modulating target signal frequency via densification and modulating sampling frequency via image resolution. However, previous scheduling strategies are primarily hardcoded, failing to perceive the convergence behavior of scene frequency. To address this, we reframe the scene reconstruction problem from the perspective of signal structure recovery and propose SIG, a novel scheduler that synchronizes image supervision with Gaussian frequencies. Specifically, we derive the average sampling frequency and bandwidth of 3D representations, and then regulate the training image resolution and the Gaussian densification process based on scene frequency convergence. Furthermore, we introduce Sphere-Constrained Gaussians, which leverage the spatial prior of initialized point clouds to control Gaussian optimization. Our framework enables frequency-consistent, geometry-aware, and floater-free training, achieving state-of-the-art performance by a substantial margin in both efficiency and rendering quality in large-scale scenes. The code is available at: https://github.com/weiyixue999/Signal_Structure_Aware_Gaussian

AI.tldr: Proposes SIG, a frequency-aware scheduler for 3D Gaussian Splatting that aligns image supervision with Gaussian frequencies and introduces Sphere-Constrained Gaussians to improve large-scale scene reconstruction; achieves notable gains in efficiency and rendering quality.
AI.motivation: Large-scale 3D scenes exhibit regions with sparse observations. Naïve supervision from low-frequency points to high-frequency images causes uncontrolled densification and redundant primitives, hurting efficiency and quality. Existing schedulers are hardcoded and ignore convergence behavior of scene frequency.
AI.method: Introduce SIG (Signal-Structure Aware Gaussian) scheduler that (1) derives average sampling frequency and bandwidth of 3D representations, (2) regulates training image resolution and Gaussian densification based on scene frequency convergence, and (3) proposes Sphere-Constrained Gaussians utilizing initial point-cloud priors to constrain optimization.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance in both efficiency and rendering quality for large-scale scenes, with frequency-consistent, geometry-aware, and floater-free training.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-aware training guided by scene structure improves large-scale 3D reconstruction quality and efficiency; Sphere-Constrained Gaussians further stabilize optimization.

title: Mastermind: Strategy-grounded Learning for Repository-Scale Vulnerability Reproduction
summary: Repository-level vulnerability reproduction is a demanding software engineering (SE) task: an agent must inspect a codebase, infer the input grammar that reaches a vulnerable path, construct a proof-of-conceptv(PoC), and verify that the crash disappears on the patched build. Recent LLM agents can often execute these steps when the approach is correct, yet they still fail by choosing the wrong strategy. This paper argues that strategy, rather than the full action trajectory, is the right learning unit for such SE agents: it is compact enough to optimize, concrete enough to guide execution, and stable enough to store and reuse across attempts. We present Mastermind, a dual-loop framework that separates transferable strategy learning from task-specific experience. A trainable planner learns reusable vulnerability-reproduction strategies through SFT and milestone-based GRPO, while an experience loop maintains task-local strategy records that guide subsequent attempts. The planner is trained independently of the executor, allowing strategy learning to improve multiple frozen executors without modifying their action-generation capability. We evaluate Mastermind on CyberGym using 260 training tasks and 200 held-out evaluation tasks.
