AI.result: Experiments with leading general-purpose and medical vision-language models show a substantial drop in performance when moving from offline recognition to streaming and proactive settings, exposing a gap between conventional accuracy and temporally grounded decision-making.
AI.conclusion: Time-aware evaluation is essential for clinically deployable systems. MedStreamBench provides the benchmarks and framework to assess and drive progress in temporally grounded medical video understanding, highlighting limitations of current models in timing and alerting behaviors.

title: Pre-Flight: A Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Aviation Operational Knowledge
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Benchmark available in inspect_evals (UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_evals)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for aviation business operations, from documentation and training generation to customer facing assistants. General purpose benchmarks do not measure whether a model reasons safely and correctly about aviation specific operational knowledge, and the high stakes, regulated nature of the domain makes that gap consequential. We present Pre-Flight, an open source benchmark of 300 multiple choice questions drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material, covering international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, aviation general knowledge and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners with experience in air traffic management, ground operations and commercial flying. We evaluate a range of contemporary commercial and open weight models using the Inspect evaluation framework, scoring by accuracy under a standard multiple choice protocol, and we maintain the leaderboard on a rolling basis as new models are released. Against an informal expert reference of around 95%, obtained from a low sample quiz of aviation professionals at a conference, even the strongest model evaluated (released in 2026) reaches 82.7%, having improved only gradually from roughly 75% in early 2025. A substantial and persistent gap below expert level reliability therefore remains. We release the dataset, the evaluation harness and the results, and the benchmark is available within the community evaluations package distributed with inspect_evals. We argue that domain specific evaluation of this kind is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non safety critical aviation operations.

AI.tldr: Open-source Pre-Flight benchmark for aviation LLMs: 300 MCQs from ICAO/FAA/Ground ops; evaluated with Inspect; strongest model ~82.7% accuracy (2026) vs informal expert ~95%; persistent gap; dataset and harness released.
AI.motivation: High-stakes, regulated aviation requires reliable evaluation of model reasoning on domain knowledge and safety; general benchmarks fail to capture aviation-specific operational reasoning.
AI.method: 300 multiple-choice questions drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material; authored/reviewed by practitioners in air traffic management, ground ops, and commercial flying; evaluation using Inspect framework with accuracy-based scoring; rolling leaderboard; open-source dataset and evaluation harness.
AI.result: Strongest model (2026 release) achieves 82.7% accuracy; ~75% in early 2025; informal expert baseline around 95%; substantial gap to expert reliability persists; results and dataset released via inspect_evals package.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in aviation operations, including non-safety-critical tasks.

title: PixGS: Pixel-Space Diffusion for Direct 3D Gaussian Splat Generation
summary: Recent advances in 3D content generation from text or images have achieved impressive results, yet view inconsistency from 2D generators and the scarcity of high-quality 3D data remain significant bottlenecks. Existing solutions typically adapt large-scale pre-trained text-to-image latent diffusion models to generate 3D Gaussian Splats (3DGS). However, these approaches often rely on training complex cascade pipelines that are computationally expensive and scalability-limited. Most critically, the quality of generated 3D assets is inherently constrained by each component capacity and compressed latent space, leading to decoding artifacts and accumulated errors. To address these limitations, we propose PixGS, a single-stage pipeline for direct high-quality 3DGS generation, which leverages recent advances in pixel-space diffusion to bypass lossy latent compression while still benefiting from the vast 2D generative priors. By directly denoising 3D Gaussian attributes at each timestep, our method enables precise, splat-level regularization of both appearance and geometry. Furthermore, we introduce a comprehensive supervision strategy that incorporates surface normals, depth, and high-frequency structural information, which is often overlooked in prior works. Experiments demonstrate that PixGS outperforms current state-of-the-art methods while maintaining a fast inference speed (1s on a single A100 GPU), offering a robust and efficient alternative to multi-stage generation pipelines.

AI.tldr: Single-stage pixel-space diffusion for direct high-quality 3D Gaussian splat generation, bypassing latent compression to improve quality and speed; achieves state-of-the-art results with 1s inference on an A100.
AI.motivation: 3D content generation from text/images suffers from view inconsistency inherent to 2D generators and limited high-quality 3D data. Existing latent-diffusion-based 3DGS approaches rely on costly multi-stage pipelines and suffer from cascading errors and artifact accumulation due to compressed latent spaces.
AI.method: Direct 3D Gaussian attributes denoising at each diffusion step in pixel space (no latent compression). Uses a single-stage pipeline with splat-level regularization for appearance and geometry. Employs comprehensive supervision signals including surface normals, depth, and high-frequency structure to guide learning.
AI.result: PixGS outperforms current state-of-the-art methods while maintaining fast inference speed (approximately 1 second on a single A100 GPU), indicating improved quality and efficiency over multi-stage pipelines.
AI.conclusion: PixGS demonstrates that pixel-space diffusion can effectively generate high-quality 3D Gaussian splats, offering a robust and efficient alternative to multi-stage generation pipelines and reducing accumulated artifacts through direct, per-splat supervision.

title: Model Merging as Probabilistic Inference in Fine-Tuning Parameter Space
comment: Accepted for Publication at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI), 2026
summary: Model merging aims to combine existing single-task solutions into a multi-task solution without additional data-driven fine-tuning.~Most existing approaches achieve this using geometric properties of local solution spaces. However, such geometric views provide limited guidance for scoring how statistically useful each task-specific update direction is across tasks during merging. To address this, we formulate model merging from a new perspective of probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts (PoE) scenario where each single-task solution defines an energy-based expert model (EBM) over the merged parameters. We show that several existing model merging methods arise as special cases of our framework under energy designs that impose implicit Gaussian assumptions on directional residuals between merged and task-specific models. Empirically, we find that these residuals are often heavy-tailed which exposes a mismatch with the imposed light-tailed Gaussian structures. We address this with a heavy-tailed PoE design based on Cauchy experts, which better captures the observed residual behavior while admitting a provably convergent inference procedure. Experiments across multiple tasks and architectures show significant improvements over state-of-the-arts baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/MinhLong210/PoE-EBM-Merging.git.

AI.tldr: A probabilistic framework for model merging using a product-of-experts energy-based model (PoE-EBM) is proposed, with heavy-tailed Cauchy experts to capture task residuals, improving over Gaussian-based methods and yielding convergence guarantees.
AI.motivation: Geometric views of model merging poorly quantify how useful task-specific update directions are across tasks. A probabilistic, inference-based formulation can score updates by their contribution to each task, accounting for residual statistics.
AI.method: Each single-task solution defines an energy-based model (EBM) over the merged parameters. The merged model is the product of experts (PoE) where each task-specific EBM acts as an expert. Existing methods are shown to be special cases under Gaussian residual assumptions. The authors observe heavy-tailed residuals and introduce a heavy-tailed PoE using Cauchy experts, enabling provably convergent inference.
AI.result: Empirical results across multiple tasks and architectures show significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. The code is released at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: A unifying probabilistic framework for model merging is established, with heavy-tailed (Cauchy) PoE-EBMs better capturing residual behavior and providing convergence guarantees, outperforming Gaussian-based mergers.

title: The Turning Point of 3D Plant Phenotyping: 3D Foundation Models Enable Minute-to-Second Cross-Crop Reconstruction and Beyond
summary: 3D plant phenotyping is notoriously known to be procedure-complicated and of low throughput due to the extensive multi-view imaging, the fragile 3D reconstruction pipeline, and the additional cost from reconstructed geometry to phenotypic extraction. These limitations are further amplified in low-cost data acquisition, where smartphone videos or sparsely sampled multi-view images provide limited view overlap and self-occlusion. In this work, we show that the conventional 3D plant phenotyping pipeline could be streamlined and significantly accelerated with 3D Foundation Models (3DFMs), and particularly, present one of the first cross-crop 3D phenotyping frameworks powered by 3DFMs. The framework replaces COLMAP-style sparse initialization with 3DFM-based feed-forward geometric recovery, combines geometry-constrained 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense reconstruction, enables few-view reconstruction through iterative view synthesis and refinement, and converts reconstructed geometry into measurable organs through 2D-to-3D semantic transfer, metric scale recovery, and organ instance separation. We further construct a cross-crop dataset with smartphone-based image acquisition, diverse plant morphologies, and manual annotations for segmentation and phenotypic evaluation. Experiments across 26 plant sequences show that 3D Foundation Models reduce the average reconstruction time from 6.52 minutes to 1.58 seconds while maintaining high reconstruction quality and phenotyping accuracy. These results suggest a fresh technical route for high-throughput 3D plant phenotyping, from low-cost image acquisition to fast reconstruction, perception, scale recovery, and phenotypic measurement.

AI.tldr: Cross-crop 3D phenotyping via 3D foundation models enables fast, low-cost reconstruction and accurate phenotypic measurement from smartphone data.
AI.motivation: 3D plant phenotyping is slow and fragile due to multi-view imaging and densely reconstructed pipelines; low-cost data further reduces view overlap and causes self-occlusion; a faster, robust, cross-crop pipeline is needed.
AI.method: Replace COLMAP-style sparse initialization with 3DFM-based feed-forward geometric recovery; apply geometry-constrained 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense reconstruction; enable few-view reconstruction via iterative view synthesis and refinement; perform 2D-to-3D semantic transfer, metric scale recovery, and organ instance separation; build a cross-crop smartphone-based dataset with annotations.
AI.result: Reconstruction time drops from 6.52 minutes to 1.58 seconds while maintaining high reconstruction quality and phenotyping accuracy across 26 plant sequences.
AI.conclusion: 3D Foundation Models enable high-throughput, cross-crop 3D plant phenotyping from low-cost imagery by fast reconstruction, perception, scale recovery, and phenotypic measurement.

title: Actual causality in fault trees
summary: Fault trees are a widely used as effective risk models for complex systems, answering the question "what can go wrong?", especially through minimal cut set analysis. We study fault trees from the perspective of Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality. This allows us to use fault trees to answer the question "why has it gone wrong?", which is fundamental to failure diagnostics. We give a complete classification of each of the different notions of actual causality in terms of the fault tree's graph structure and logical structure, and show how minimal cut sets give rise to actual causes.

AI.tldr: Links fault-tree analysis with Halpern–Pearl actual causality to explain failures, providing a complete classification of causality notions via the fault-tree graph and logic, and showing how minimal cut sets correspond to actual causes.
AI.motivation: Fault trees answer what can go wrong; the paper extends this by answering why it went wrong using actual causality, enabling better failure diagnostics and explanations.
AI.method: Formal mapping between fault-tree structures (graphs and logical gates) and Halpern–Pearl notions of actual causality; classifies each causality notion in terms of the fault-tree topology; analyzes how minimal cut sets instantiate actual causes.
AI.result: A complete classification of the various Halpern–Pearl actual-causality notions in the context of fault trees; demonstration that minimal cut sets yield actual causes; framework for diagnostic reasoning based on causal explanations.
AI.conclusion: Fault trees can provide not only risk estimates but also causal explanations for failures; the approach offers a systematic basis for failure diagnostics and theoretical bridge between risk modeling and causal reasoning.

title: Robust Image Processing Techniques for Construction Environment Monitoring Using Underwater Robots
summary: This paper proposes a robust image processing framework for underwater robot-based construction environment monitoring, targeting complex degradations observed in real marine environments. Unlike conventional approaches that mainly consider absorption and backscattering, real underwater imagery is strongly affected by depth-dependent forward scattering blur and particle-induced degradations such as marine snow. To address this, we introduce a staged processing pipeline that sequentially models background degradation via depth-aware forward scattering and foreground degradation using realistic marine snow patterns extracted from real images. The resulting synthetic data are used to retrain an existing Joint-ID network without modifying its architecture, enabling an isolated evaluation of dataset realism. In addition, a lightweight post-processing scheme is applied to enhance contrast and structural clarity. Experiments on real underwater datasets collected in Korean coastal environments demonstrate consistent improvements in visual quality and UIQM scores. The results indicate that explicitly modeling forward scattering and realistic particle effects effectively reduces the synthetic-to-real gap and improves practical applicability in real-world underwater robotic operations.

AI.tldr: A depth-aware forward scattering plus marine-snow-aware pipeline synthesizes realistic underwater data, retrains a Joint-ID network without architectural changes, and yields improved visual quality (UIQM) and reduced simulated-to-real gap for robotic monitoring tasks.
AI.motivation: Underwater imagery is degraded not only by absorption and backscatter but also by depth-dependent forward scattering and particle-induced degradations (e.g., marine snow). Existing methods insufficiently capture these effects, limiting real-world deployment of underwater robots.
AI.method: A staged pipeline: (1) model background degradation via depth-aware forward scattering; (2) model foreground degradation using realistic marine snow patterns extracted from real images; (3) synthesize data and retrain an existing Joint-ID network without changing its architecture to isolate dataset realism; (4) apply a lightweight post-processing step to boost contrast and structural clarity. Evaluation on real underwater datasets from Korean coasts, using UIQM as a primary metric.
AI.result: The approach achieves consistent improvements in visual quality and UIQM scores, indicating a reduced synthetic-to-real gap and enhanced applicability for real underwater robotic operations.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling depth-dependent forward scattering and marine-snow degradations yields more realistic data, enabling better transfer of learned perception models to real underwater environments.

title: A Mathematical Introduction to Diffusion Models
comment: Lecture notes for the John Tukey Summer Graduate School on Mathematics of Generative Models at SLMath (June 22nd, 2026 -- July 2nd, 2026)
summary: These notes give a proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from the viewpoint of sampling, tracing a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, their error analysis, and inference-time control. Throughout, the material is layered into core definitions and identities proved in full, representative estimates proved under simplifying assumptions, and research-level theorems stated with a proof roadmap. The intended audience is beginning graduate students with a background in probability but no prior exposure to stochastic differential equations, stochastic numerics, or diffusion models.

AI.tldr: A proof-oriented, classroom-style introduction to diffusion models from sampling dynamics, tracing the evolution from classical sampling to modern diffusion samplers, with error analysis and inference-time control, organized into core definitions, simplifying estimates, and proof-roadmapped theorems, aimed at beginning grad students with probabilistic backgrounds but no SDE/diffusion prior.
AI.motivation: Provide a rigorous, pedagogy-driven bridge between classical sampling methods and diffusion-based samplers; equip probabilists and numerically inclined readers with foundational definitions, identities, and a roadmap to research-level results; address the learning gap in SDEs and stochastic numerics related to diffusion models.
AI.method: Expository structure with layered content: fully proved core definitions/identities, representative estimates under simplifying assumptions, and statements of research-level theorems with proof roadmaps; follows a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to contemporary diffusion samplers; includes error analysis and inference-time control aspects.
AI.result: Produces a cohesive, proof-oriented introduction that is accessible to the target audience, offering a conceptual framework for diffusion models via sampling dynamics, and laying groundwork for more advanced results and research directions.
AI.conclusion: The notes function as a didactic resource that demystifies diffusion models for beginners, enabling rigorous understanding of sampling-based diffusion processes, error behavior, and control during inference, while outlining paths toward more advanced theorems.

title: ProSAC-CT: Progressive Spectral-Anatomical Co-Guided Multi-Stage Diffusion Model for Low-Dose CT Denoising
summary: Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces radiation exposure but introduces stronger quantum noise, streak artifacts, and local texture degradation, which can obscure anatomical boundaries and weaken low-contrast structures. Diffusion models are promising for LDCT denoising by progressively recovering normal-dose CT (NDCT) images from degraded LDCT inputs, but existing methods often suffer from insufficient anatomical guidance, uncertain frequency-dependent recovery, and uniform reverse-process modeling. We propose ProSAC-CT, a progressive spectral-anatomical co-guided multi-stage diffusion model for image-domain LDCT denoising. ProSAC-CT integrates an anatomical-prior-guided conditioning (APGC) module, a residual frequency-domain decoupling stage (RFDDS), and a time-step-decoupling denoising decoder (TD3). APGC extracts LDCT-derived structural guidance, RFDDS enhances frequency-aware representations, and TD3 assigns them to different reverse-diffusion stages for anatomical stabilization, boundary refinement, and fine-detail recovery. Experiments on four LDCT degradation benchmarks show that ProSAC-CT improves image fidelity, structural similarity, perceptual quality, and information preservation over representative methods while better preserving boundary-sensitive anatomical details. Downstream anatomical-region classification on Mayo-2020 further indicates that ProSAC-CT retains task-relevant anatomical information, supporting its practical use for low-dose CT denoising.

AI.tldr: A multi-stage diffusion model (ProSAC-CT) for LDCT denoising using anatomical priors and frequency-aware, stage-wise denoising to improve fidelity and preserve anatomy; validated on four LDCT benchmarks and Mayo-2020 for downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: LDCT reduces radiation but introduces noise, artifacts, and texture degradation that obscure anatomy. Diffusion-based denoising is promising but often lacks strong anatomical guidance, clear frequency-dependent recovery, and non-uniform reverse-process modeling.
AI.method: ProSAC-CT integrates three components: APGC (anatomical-prior-guided conditioning) for LDCT-derived structural guidance; RFDDS (residual frequency-domain decoupling stage) for frequency-aware representation enhancement; TD3 (time-step-decoupling denoising decoder) to assign features to different reverse-diffusion stages, enabling anatomical stabilization, boundary refinement, and fine-detail recovery.
AI.result: On four LDCT degradation benchmarks, ProSAC-CT improves image fidelity, SSIM, perceptual quality, and information preservation over representative methods, with better preservation of boundary-sensitive anatomical details. Mayo-2020 downstream anatomical-region classification shows retention of task-relevant anatomical information, supporting practical clinical use.
AI.conclusion: ProSAC-CT effectively combines spectral-anatomical priors with stage-specific diffusion denoising to enhance LDCT image quality while maintaining critical anatomical information, demonstrating potential for clinical LDCT denoising.

title: CLAP: Closed-Loop Training, Evaluation, and Release Control for Domain Agent Post-training
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Accepted to CRAE 2026; to appear in SPIE Proceedings. Best Poster Award
summary: Domain agents often face noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk. This paper presents CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training), a closed-loop method that converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. CLAP combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide whether an adapter is suitable for the target application chain. On five anonymized manufacturing-scenario batches, QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT yields modest average gains: overall score increases by 0.0098, pass rate by 0.0240, and evidence accuracy by 0.0280, while hallucination and wrong facts decrease. Yet only 3 of 5 batches improve, some batches regress, and GRPO exposes high KL risks. Application-chain replay further shows that RAG is necessary for factual extraction; under the same 3B backbone and 100 replay cases, an application-RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over base+RAG, but increases latency. These results support managing domain-agent post-training through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying on training completion or a single offline score.

AI.tldr: A closed-loop post-training framework (CLAP) for domain agents converts business data into structured SFT/evidence/holdout/release records to guide adapter selection, with offline gates and application-chain replay. It yields mixed but sometimes positive gains across five anonymized manufacturing datasets; RAG helps factual extraction but adds latency; advocates an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop over single offline scores.
AI.motivation: Tackle noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and release risk in domain-agent adapters by creating a closed-loop workflow that jointly validates data, calibrates targets, diagnoses risk, and replays across application chains to decide adapter suitability.
AI.method: CLAP integrates data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gating, and application-chain replay to generate: structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. Evaluation uses QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT on five anonymized manufacturing batches with a 3B backbone and 100 replay cases; compares base+RAG vs application-RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapters across application chains.
AI.result: Average performance gains are modest: overall score +0.0098, pass rate +0.0240, evidence accuracy +0.0280, with reduced hallucinations and factual errors. However, only 3/5 batches improve; some regress; GRPO uncovers high KL risks. Application-chain replay shows RAG is needed for factual extraction; with 100 replay cases and same backbone, an application-RAG LoRA-SFT improves value, core-field coherence, and answer-evidence alignment vs base+RAG, but increases latency.
AI.conclusion: An integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop better manages domain-agent post-training than relying on training completion or a single offline score, albeit with tradeoffs in consistency and latency; results highlight the need for closed-loop governance in post-training adapter deployment.

title: NeoMap: Training-free Novel-View Synthesis from Single Images and Videos
comment: ECCV 2026. Jinxi and Tianyi are co-first authors. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/vLAR-group/NeoMap
summary: We study the challenging problem of novel view video synthesis from single images or monocular videos. Existing methods, which operate under the assumption that pre-trained video models lack native novel view synthesis capability and enforce view alignment via camera conditioning, task-specific fine-tuning, or stepwise hard denoising guidance, often suffer from artifacts and compromised global scene consistency. In this paper, we introduce NeoMap, a novel training-free framework designed to locate high-fidelity, view-consistent novel view solutions from general pre-trained video models. The key to our approach is the core insight that promising novel view solutions are inherently encoded within the natural video data manifold learned by pre-trained models, and the core challenge is simply to locate this optimal solution. We solve this via our core mechanism: convergent manifold alternating projection iterations that optimize the initial noise. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NeoMap significantly outperforms all existing methods across 3 standard novel view synthesis benchmarks, including the challenging Tanks-and-Temples, LLFF and DAVIS datasets, achieving state-of-the-art generation fidelity and top-tier view consistency.

AI.tldr: NeoMap is a training-free framework that locates high-fidelity, view-consistent novel views from pre-trained video models by optimizing initial noise via convergent manifold alternating projection iterations.
AI.motivation: Current pre-trained video models struggle to synthesize novel views without artifacts and global inconsistency, often requiring task-specific fine-tuning or denoising guidance; a training-free approach to exploit the model's data manifold is desirable.
AI.method: Uses convergent manifold alternating projection iterations to optimize initial noise, effectively navigating the model's learned video data manifold to retrieve a suitable novel-view solution without additional training.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on Tanks-and-Temples, LLFF, and DAVIS show NeoMap achieves state-of-the-art generation fidelity and top-tier view consistency, outperforming existing methods.
AI.conclusion: NeoMap demonstrates that promising novel-view solutions are encoded in the natural video data manifold of pre-trained models and can be efficiently located without training, enabling robust, high-quality novel-view video synthesis.

title: Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine for Solving High-Frequency Partial Differential Equations
summary: Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency solutions remains a central challenge in physics-informed machine learning due to spectral bias -- the tendency of neural networks to learn low-frequency components preferentially. This paper proposes a Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine (FS-PIELM) framework that addresses this limitation through an additive mechanism for weight initialization. Rather than multiplying random weights by a scaling factor, the method translates the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping the variance fixed at unity, thereby avoiding the variance amplification inherent in scaling-based methods. Two variants are developed: FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes to individual neurons, while FS-PIELM-G groups neurons for improved robustness. Theoretical analysis shows that the frequency variance under the proposed framework remains bounded and approaches unity regardless of target frequency, in contrast to the quadratic growth of conventional approaches. The method preserves the computational efficiency of extreme learning machines, requiring only a single linear solve. Experiments on seven benchmark problems spanning six equation types -- Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, and advection-diffusion -- on both regular and complex geometries show that the linear variant achieves the best accuracy in six of seven cases, with improvements of one to nearly five orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants. The code and data accompanying this manuscript will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xgxgnpu/Physics-informed-vibe-coding/tree/main/FS-PIELM.

AI.tldr: FS-PIELM introduces a frequency-shift weight initialization that keeps weight variance bounded, enabling high-frequency PDE solutions with an ELM-like framework; it delivers large accuracy gains (up to several orders) across multiple PDEs while preserving efficiency.
AI.motivation: High-frequency PDE solutions suffer from spectral bias in neural networks, limiting accuracy of physics-informed ML approaches. An efficient method that can achieve high-frequency accuracy without extensive training is needed.
AI.method: Additive frequency shift to Gaussian weight initialization for extreme learning machines (FS-PIELM), with variance fixed at unity. Two variants: FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes per neuron; FS-PIELM-G groups neurons for robustness. Theoretical analysis shows bounded frequency variance (approaching unity) independent of target frequency, unlike quadratic growth in traditional scaling. Only a single linear solve is required for training.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across seven PDE benchmarks (Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, advection-diffusion) on regular and complex geometries shows FS-PIELM-L (and FS-PIELM-G) achieve top accuracy in most cases; the linear variant attains best results in 6 of 7 problems with accuracy improvements ranging from 1 to nearly 5 orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants.
AI.conclusion: The frequency-shift initialization in FS-PIELM mitigates spectral bias for high-frequency PDEs while preserving the computational efficiency of ELM-based PINNs, applicable across diverse equation types and geometries; code will be publicly available for reproducibility.

title: Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement
summary: Safety training for large language models (LLMs) is conducted predominantly in English, leaving uncertain how well safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages and mixed-language code-switching. We show that this creates an epistemic gap in which models confidently generate harmful responses for inputs that fall outside the distribution of their safety training. To study this phenomenon, we introduce STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement), a gradient-guided attack that identifies words contributing most strongly to the model's refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent. Across six open-source 8B-parameter models, STEER achieves attack success rates of up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG). The resulting prompts also transfer to GPT-4o-mini, achieving a 35.5% attack success rate without requiring access to the target model, suggesting that the underlying weakness is not specific to a single architecture. These findings demonstrate that safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. We argue that improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and mechanisms that explicitly detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

AI.tldr: Introduces STEER, a gradient-guided code-switching attack that suppresses LLM safety refusals in multilingual inputs, revealing English-centric safety gaps across models and architectures; high attack success on open-source models and GPT-4o-mini; calls for multilingual alignment and OOD detection.
AI.motivation: Safety protocols for LLMs are predominantly trained in English, leaving uncertainty about generalization to low-resource languages and code-switching. This creates an epistemic risk where models may confidently generate harmful outputs outside their safety training distribution.
AI.method: Identify words contributing to the model's refusal via gradient analysis, then iteratively translate those tokens into low-resource languages to induce code-switching and suppress refusal while retaining harmful intent; evaluate on six open-source 8B-parameter models across JailbreakBench and AdvBench; compare to random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG); test transferability to GPT-4o-mini without access to the target model.
AI.result: Attack success rates reach up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, substantially outperforming baselines; prompts transfer to GPT-4o-mini with a 35.5% attack rate without target-model access, suggesting the weakness is not architecture-specific.
AI.conclusion: Safety mechanisms primarily aligned to English do not reliably generalize to multilingual inputs; improving multilingual safety requires broader alignment coverage and explicit detection/abstention on out-of-distribution inputs.

title: Episodic-to-Semantic Consolidation Without Identity Drift
summary: Long-running adaptive intelligent agents face a structural tension between knowledge consolidation and information integrity. Memory consolidation is conventionally treated as an agent-changing operation: a model is fine-tuned, a prompt rewritten, a policy distilled, or a reflection appended to the context that governs future behaviour. In regulated autonomic deployment this is a liability because the agent operates under commitments and audit contracts that bind to a specific, cryptographically certified identity. We propose to treat consolidation not as a mutation of the planner or the identity manifest, but as a deterministic function f: M^ep -> M^sem over episodic memory whose output is a separately addressable semantic knowledge layer; the identity hash does not read M^sem, so consolidation updates knowledge without changing the agent's certified identity. We give a formal account of the agent representation, prove identity invariance through a structural lemma on the manifest's hash-input set, specify a deterministic aggregation algorithm whose outputs are auditable database rows with explicit confidence and supporting-event provenance, and validate the construction with synthetic experiments demonstrating per-field correctness, byte-equal identity across consolidation passes, and a mean 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%] across 10 seeds) against a calibrated Bayesian-shrunk baseline. The construction is a knowledge-update discipline for autonomic agents in which lessons accumulate as queryable facts while the agent's certified identity remains byte-equal across its operational lifetime, with an embodied service agent as the running case study.

AI.tldr: A memory consolidation scheme for autonomous agents that updates a separate semantic layer deterministically without altering the agent's certified identity, with formal invariants and auditable provenance, validated on synthetic data showing major reductions in unproductive planner attempts.
AI.motivation: In regulated deployments, agents must maintain a cryptographically certified identity and auditable behavior. Conventional memory update—tuning models or rewriting prompts—risks violating commitments and auditability. The work seeks to detach knowledge updates from identity to preserve accountability.
AI.method: Define a deterministic memory consolidation function f: M^ep → M^sem that writes to a separate semantic knowledge layer. The agent's identity hash does not read M^sem, ensuring identity invariance. Provide a formal representation of the agent and prove invariance via a structural lemma on the manifest’s hash-input set. Propose a deterministic aggregation algorithm that outputs auditable database rows with explicit confidence and provenance. Validate with synthetic experiments showing per-field correctness, byte-equal identity across passes, and a mean reduction in unproductive planner attempts (79.82%, 95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%]) against a calibrated Bayesian-shrunk baseline; illustrated on an embodied service agent as running case study.
AI.result: Formal identity invariance guarantees; an auditable, provenance-producing consolidation pipeline; empirical evidence of substantial efficiency gains and stable identity over time; per-field correctness and byte-level identity retention across consolidation passes demonstrated on synthetic seeds.
AI.conclusion: The work introduces a knowledge-update discipline that accumulates lessons as queryable facts without altering the agent’s certified identity, enabling safe long-horizon autonomous operation with auditable memory updates. It is validated on synthetic experiments and demonstrated with an embodied service agent.

title: Predicting Closed-Loop Performance of Latent World Models: Offline Checkpoint Selection for MPC and Model-Based RL Under Non-Markovian Rewards in LunarLander
comment: Preprint, 19 pages (16 main text + 3 pages appendix), 7 figures, 4 tables. Video: https://youtu.be/4PxHFW_TYUw , Code: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM
summary: We study how to predict the downstream closed-loop performance of a learned latent world model from validation-time diagnostics alone. Choosing the right checkpoint from a world-model training run is difficult: validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE keep improving long after closed-loop performance has collapsed. We present a suite of structural validation-time diagnostics drawn from optimal-control theory and apply them to Gymnasium's LunarLander v3, which features shaped rewards. We train an RSSM [5, 4] world model on it and treat per checkpoint CEM-MPC return as the oracle for closed-loop quality. By evaluating 40 metrics against this oracle, we find that the strongest single predictor is the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF), which measures the reward predictor's dependence on the observable subspace. We combine ROF with three structural regularizers into a single-number offline checkpoint selection score, the Composite Reward Observability Fraction (CROF). The CROF-selected world model trains a model-based A2C policy that beats a fairly evaluated model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions, and the same world model also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy. Code and data: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM.

AI.tldr: Validation-time diagnostics from optimal-control theory can predict closed-loop performance of a learned latent world model; CROF (combining Reward Observability Fraction with regularizers) selects checkpoints that enable strong model-based control and data efficiency.
AI.motivation: Checkpoint selection for latent world models is difficult because validation losses and multi-step prediction errors do not reliably predict closed-loop performance. There is a need for diagnostics that align with control performance.
AI.method: Train an RSSM world model on LunarLander v3 with shaped rewards. Use per-checkpoint CEM-MPC return as the oracle for closed-loop quality. Evaluate 40 metrics and identify ROF (reward predictor's dependence on observable subspace) as the strongest predictor. Build CROF by combining ROF with three structural regularizers into a single offline checkpoint score. Select the best checkpoint by CROF, train a model-based A2C policy, compare to a model-free A2C baseline, and demonstrate zero-shot CEM-MPC with the same world model. Provide code and data at the linked repository.
AI.result: ROF emerged as the strongest single predictor of closed-loop performance. CROF, the composite score, enabled effective offline checkpoint selection. The CROF-selected world model yielded a model-based A2C policy that outperformed a fairly evaluated model-free A2C by about 24.5 return points, while requiring roughly 65x fewer real-environment interactions. The same world model also supported a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy.
AI.conclusion: Offline, validation-time physics-inspired diagnostics can reliably forecast closed-loop quality and guide checkpoint selection for latent world models. The CROF metric provides a robust, single-number criterion that enhances sample efficiency and policy performance, with applicability to both model-based planning and zero-shot control.

title: ProCal: Inference-Time Proposal Calibration for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
summary: Open-vocabulary object detection aims to localize and classify objects beyond the fixed set of categories seen dur ing training. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods improve localization and classification for unseen categories by leveraging a frozen VLM as a detector backbone. However, VLM classification score lacks recognizing position and scale of the object in an image. We observe that pretrained VLMs en able to classify foreground and background regions. According to this observation, we propose a simple inference-time Pro posal Calibration (ProCal) that improves localization quality of the classification score. ProCal computes a proposal prior by combining two scores: localization-aware foreground score and background-aware suppression score. Localization-aware foreground score captures whether a proposal contains an object area. Background-aware suppression score measures the extent to which the proposal resembles background. We analyze that ProCal suppresses false novel activation on background proposals and consistently ranks true novel proposals above background and partial novel proposals. Applied to CLIPSelf ViT-L/14, ProCal improves APr +2.5 on OV-LVIS. The analyses show that proposal-level localization-aware reranking effects to mitigate ranking miscalibration for novel objects.

AI.tldr: ProCal is an inference-time proposal calibration that improves localization in open-vocabulary object detection by ranking proposals with a localization-aware foreground score and a background-suppression score, yielding significant gains on OV-LVIS.
AI.motivation: VLM-based detectors provide strong classification but lack robust localization cues; open-vocabulary detection requires reliable localization and discrimination between novel objects and background. ProCal leverages foreground/background signals to recalibrate proposals.
AI.method: Compute a proposal prior by combining two scores: a localization-aware foreground score (objectness) and a background-aware suppression score (background similarity). Use this to re-rank proposals at inference time. Demonstrated with CLIPSelf ViT-L/14 as backbone.
AI.result: On OV-LVIS with CLIPSelf ViT-L/14, ProCal achieves APr +2.5; suppresses false novel activations on background proposals; ranks true novel proposals above background and partial novel ones; analyses show proposal-level localization-aware reranking mitigates ranking miscalibration for novel objects.
AI.conclusion: A simple, effective inference-time calibration that improves localization quality for open-vocabulary detectors by exploiting localization-aware foreground signals and background suppression, without retraining.

title: CamoNAS: Neural Architecture Search for Enhanced Camouflaged Object Detection
comment: Published in The Visual Computer. Author manuscript version
summary: Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) aims to locate and segment objects that blend into their surroundings, presenting challenges due to weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries. Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and multi-scale feature fusion, which are often guided by intuition rather than systematic search. This paper introduces CamoNAS, a frequency-aware multi-resolution Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework for COD. CamoNAS automatically searches both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, forming a hierarchical search space tailored to detect camouflaged objects. Additionally, it adopts an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture, where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream. CamoNAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks (CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, CHAMELEON), highlighting the effectiveness of NAS for COD. Our code is available at https://github.com/rendaweiSIMIT/CamoNAS.

AI.tldr: CamoNAS is a NAS-based framework for camouflaged object detection that jointly searches cell-level operations and downsampling paths while employing a frequency-aware RGB dual-stream with a learnable wavelet transform, achieving state-of-the-art results on four COD benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Camouflaged objects have weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries, making detection hard with hand-designed architectures. NAS can automatically tailor architectures to COD by exploring a hierarchical search space and leveraging frequency-domain cues.
AI.method: Proposes a hierarchical NAS search space that optimizes both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths for COD. Introduces an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture in which a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream, enabling frequency-aware feature extraction for camouflaged objects.
AI.result: Reported state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks (CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, CHAMELEON) and provides code at the project repository.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that NAS, combined with frequency-aware multi-resolution design and wavelet-based dual streams, is effective for camouflaged object detection and can surpass hand-crafted architectures.

title: Finite-Lag Operator Geometry of Recurrent Representations
summary: Recurrent representations are trajectories, but representation geometry is often measured from static snapshots. We develop finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent hidden states from observed source-successor pairs $(X_t,X_{t+Δ})$. The primitive is the conditional transport law $Q_Δ(dy\mid x)$, estimated by a dense Gaussian source-smoothing operator. From this directed finite-lag law we derive a source-centered transport tensor $G_Δ$, which decomposes exactly into conditional spread and coherent displacement, and an antisymmetric coordinate circulation $W_Δ^ρ$, which summarizes directed lagged flow. We prove affine covariance with explicit metric dependence of scalar summaries, dense estimator stability on bounded trajectory clouds, and a finite-lag separation result showing that source-centered transport detects deterministic recurrent motion not recorded by infinitesimal carre-du-champ geometry. A linear-Gaussian closed form calibrates the quantities in terms of the update $A_Δ$, source covariance, and innovation covariance. Controlled experiments validate the decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability predictions. In performance matched repeat-copy networks, the framework reveals architecture dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, while coherent displacement fraction is metric and resolution dependent.

AI.tldr: Finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent representations using conditional transport (Q_Δ) from source–successor pairs. It yields a source-centered transport tensor G_Δ and an antisymmetric circulation W_Δ^ρ, with affine covariance, stability, and finite-lag separation results. A linear-Gaussian closed form calibrates the quantities; experiments validate the framework and reveal architecture-dependent transport characteristics and metric/resolution effects on coherent displacement fraction.
AI.motivation: Static snapshot geometry inadequately characterizes the dynamics of recurrent representations. The work introduces a finite-lag, source-centered transport framework to capture lagged, directed motion and separate deterministic recurrent dynamics from instantaneous geometric notions, enabling robust, affine-covariant summaries.
AI.method: Estimate the conditional transport law Q_Δ(dy|x) from observed (X_t, X_{t+Δ}) via a dense Gaussian source-smoothing operator. Derive the source-centered transport tensor G_Δ that decomposes into conditional spread and coherent displacement, and define an antisymmetric coordinate circulation W_Δ^ρ to summarize lagged flow. Prove affine covariance with metric dependence of summaries, establish estimator stability for bounded trajectory clouds, and prove a finite-lag separation result showing detection of deterministic motion not captured by infinitesimal carré-du-champ geometry. Provide a linear-Gaussian closed form calibrated in terms of update A_Δ, source covariance, and innovation covariance. Conduct controlled experiments to validate decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability; compare performance-matched repeat-copy networks to reveal architecture-dependent transport characteristics and metric/resolution effects on coherent displacement fraction.
AI.result: The framework yields a precise decomposition of lagged transport into spread and coherent displacement, and a compact antisymmetric circulation capturing directed lag flow. Estimator stability and affine covariance are established, with finite-lag separation proving sensitivity to deterministic recurrent motion beyond infinitesimal geometry. A linear-Gaussian calibration relates quantities to model updates and covariances. Experiments confirm predictions and show architecture-dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace; coherent displacement fraction depends on metric and resolution.
AI.conclusion: The finite-lag operator-geometry framework provides a principled, affine-covariant toolkit for analyzing recurrent representations, enabling detection of lagged, deterministic motion and unveiling architecture-dependent transport properties. It yields practical, linear-Gaussian calibrations and stable estimators, with clear implications for understanding and comparing recurrent architectures across metrics and scales.

title: JointHOI: Jointly Generating Contact Maps Enhances Hand Object Interaction Generation
summary: Text driven hand object interaction (HOI) generation is gaining attention for immersive applications and robotics, yet producing physically plausible interactions remains challenging. Even when individual motions appear natural, small contact errors can cause conspicuous artifacts such as floating and interpenetration. Prior methods mitigate these issues using explicit contact cues or implicit grasp priors, but typically rely on multi stage pipelines and fail to model temporally evolving contact. We present JointHOI, a single stage diffusion framework that jointly generates 3D hand object motion and dynamic, distance based contact maps from text. By treating contact as an auxiliary inner modality, joint generation enables the model to learn contact motion coupling during training. At inference, contact guided sampling enforces consistency between generated contact maps and motion implied geometry, improving temporal stability and reducing penetration and floating. Experiments on GRAB and ARCTIC demonstrate consistent improvements in text adherence and physical plausibility over prior methods.

AI.tldr: JointHOI introduces a single-stage diffusion model that jointly generates 3D hand-object motion and dynamic, distance-based contact maps from text, improving temporal consistency and physical plausibility in hand-object interactions.
AI.motivation: To address artifacts like floating and interpenetration arising from poor contact modeling in text-driven HOI, and to move beyond multi-stage pipelines with static or implicit priors.
AI.method: A diffusion-based framework that treats contact as an auxiliary modality, enabling joint training of motion and distance-based contact maps; at inference, contact-guided sampling enforces consistency between generated contact maps and motion-implied geometry to enhance temporal stability and reduce penetration.
AI.result: Demonstrated improvements in text adherence and physical plausibility on GRAB and ARCTIC benchmarks compared to prior methods, with better temporal stability and fewer contact artifacts.
AI.conclusion: JointHOI provides a unified, end-to-end approach for text-driven hand-object interaction that couples motion with dynamic contact, reducing artifacts and simplifying pipelines while enhancing realism.

title: SkillCoach: Self-Evolving Rubrics for Evaluating and Enhancing Agentic Skill-Use
summary: Skills are becoming a reusable operational layer for LLM agents, encoding SOPs, domain rules, tool workflows, scripts, and validation routines. In realistic skill repositories, overlapping skills make reliable skill-use difficult. Final verifier success is too coarse for both evaluation and training, since an agent may pass through trial and error while selecting distractor skills, skipping required steps, composing workflows incorrectly or omitting final checks. We introduce SkillCoach, a self-evolving rubric framework for evaluating and enhancing agentic skill-use. SkillCoach derives skill-grounded process rubrics from real rollouts and evaluates trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection. It keeps the external verifier as a separate outcome signal, allowing process quality to be distinguished from accidental task success. The evolved rubrics further serve as process supervision for selecting high-quality training trajectories. Experiments show that evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.

AI.tldr: SkillCoach introduces a self-evolving rubric framework to evaluate and improve agentic skill-use by deriving skill-grounded rubrics from real rollouts and evaluating trajectories across four dimensions, with an external verifier as a separate signal.
AI.motivation: In realistic skill repositories, overlapping skills and coarse final success impede reliable skill-use and effective training. There is a need for process-level evaluation and supervision beyond outcome validity to guide learning and diagnose failures.
AI.method: Derive skill-grounded process rubrics from real rollouts and evaluate agent trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection. Maintain an external verifier as a separate outcome signal. Use the evolved rubrics to supervise selection of high-quality training trajectories.
AI.result: Evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, reveal failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.
AI.conclusion: Evolving process rubrics enable more reliable evaluation and more effective supervision for agentic skill-use, potentially improving training efficiency and robustness.

title: Efficient Temporal Point Processes via Monotone Alternating Splines
summary: Temporal point processes (TPPs) have widespread applications across various domains. Compared to modeling the conditional intensity of a TPP, modeling its cumulative conditional intensity function (CCIF) improves computational efficiency and eliminates numerical approximation errors. However, current CCIF parameterizations uniformly rely on Monotone Neural Networks (MNNs), which we identify as suffering from three structural deadlocks--convexity restrictions, saturation limits, and violations of CCIF modeling requirements--that fundamentally restrict their representational capacity for complex temporal dynamics. To resolve these bottlenecks, this paper proposes a novel framework called Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS). By leveraging distinct interpolation and extrapolation components, MAS provides a flexible and efficient framework for modeling CCIFs. Theoretically, MAS's interpolation provides strong fitting accuracy, while its extrapolation supports robust generalization, reducing the irreducible approximation gaps of MNNs. Extensive experiments show that MAS achieves superior performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: Introduce Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS) to model the CCIF of temporal point processes, overcoming the three limitations of Monotone Neural Networks and achieving superior performance on synthetic and real data.
AI.motivation: Current CCIF parameterizations rely on Monotone Neural Networks (MNNs), which impose convexity restrictions, face saturation limits, and violate certain CCIF modeling requirements, limiting expressiveness for complex temporal dynamics. MAS aims to provide a flexible, efficient alternative that improves both fitting and generalization.
AI.method: Propose MAS framework that separates interpolation and extrapolation components using monotone alternating spline constructions to model CCIFs. Provide theoretical analysis showing strong interpolation accuracy and robust extrapolation generalization. Empirically evaluate on synthetic and real-world datasets, comparing against MNN-based baselines.
AI.result: MAS achieves superior performance relative to MNN-based models on both synthetic and real-world datasets, with improved fitting accuracy and better generalization, indicating reduced irreducible approximation gaps of prior approaches.
AI.conclusion: MAS offers a flexible, efficient approach to CCIF modeling in TPPs, overcoming the structural limitations of MNNs and delivering strong empirical performance across diverse datasets.

title: LLM-Empowered Multimodal Fusion Framework for Autonomous Driving: Semantic Enhancement and Channel-Adaptive Design
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Accepted by 2026 IEEE 37th International Symposium on Personal, Indoor and Mobile Radio Communications (PIMRC)
summary: Vision-radar fusion is central to robust autonomous driving, combining dense visual semantics with precise range and velocity measurements from radar. However, real-world fusion quality is fundamentally challenged by dynamically varying input quality, stemming from occlusion, adverse weather, and channel noise. To address this, we re-frame the problem from static data fusion to channel-aware semantic reasoning and propose a Large Language Model-centric Semantic-layer Channel-aware Integrated Perception (LM-SCIP) framework. It places a Large Language Model (LLM) as a central reasoning core to fuse a local visual stream with a quality-varying external radar stream used to cover perception-blind spots. Concretely, LM-SCIP couples a hierarchical radar-vision encoder with a Channel-Adaptive Semantic Module (CASM) that maps link indicators into a "Channel Prompt" to dynamically gate external radar features. A parameter-efficient, LoRA-tuned LLM, in conjunction with a heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts (H-MoE), then arbitrates between local visual cues and the channel-conditioned radar context. Finally, a decoupled multi-task decoder outputs localization, trajectory forecasting, and image reconstruction. Experiments on nuScenes and VIRAT validate our approach. On nuScenes, under a controlled toggle of radar input, LM-SCIP reduces localization RMSE by 40.0% versus a vision-only baseline. On VIRAT, the model attains a 0.214m localization RMSE and 0.179m minFDE (k=1). These results reveal that the proposed LM-SCIP enables a robust vision-dominant fallback at low SNR and synergistic fusion at high SNR.

AI.tldr: LM-SCIP introduces an LLM-centric, channel-aware fusion framework for vision-radar perception, using a Channel-Adaptive Semantic Module to gate radar features and a LoRA-tuned LLM with a heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts to arbitrate between visual and radar cues, achieving notable localization improvements on nuScenes and VIRAT.
AI.motivation: Robust autonomous driving requires reliable fusion under dynamically varying input quality due to occlusion, weather, and channel noise. Static fusion can fail when one sensor degrades; a channel-aware, semantic reasoning approach can adaptively weigh sources.
AI.method: A hierarchical radar-vision encoder couples with a Channel-Adaptive Semantic Module (CASM) that maps link indicators into a Channel Prompt to gate external radar features. A parameter-efficient, LoRA-tuned LLM, together with a heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts (H-MoE), arbitrate between local visual cues and channel-conditioned radar context. A decoupled multi-task decoder outputs localization, trajectory forecasting, and image reconstruction.
AI.result: On nuScenes, under a controlled toggle of radar input, LM-SCIP reduces localization RMSE by 40.0% versus a vision-only baseline. On VIRAT, it achieves 0.214m localization RMSE and 0.179m minFDE (k=1). These results suggest robust vision-dominant fallback at low SNR and synergistic fusion at high SNR.
AI.conclusion: The LM-SCIP framework demonstrates that an LLM-centric, channel-aware integration strategy can robustly fuse vision and radar, leveraging semantic reasoning to adapt to quality variations and improve localization and trajectory tasks across datasets.

title: Spec-AUF: Accept-Until-Fail Training under Train-Inference Misalignment for Masked Block Drafters
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting a block of tokens that the target model verifies left-to-right, committing only the longest accepted prefix. Block (DLM-style) drafters predict the whole block in parallel, which is fast but trained with a full-block cross-entropy that supervises every position against the gold continuation -- even though inference discards every token after the first rejection. Recent acceptance-aware objectives patch this by reweighting the full-block loss; we instead use teacher-forced learning as a motivation for how supervision should concentrate on the accepted prefix. A mask-only block drafter has no input-side channel for gold-prefix conditioning, so AUF approximates that prefix-sensitive supervision on the loss side by keeping the cross-entropy support only through the drafter's first predicted failure. AUF is a single, detached change to the CE support -- no auxiliary objective, no verifier rollouts, and no change to the inference pipeline or the exactness contract. Within fixed drafter backbones and serving settings on Qwen3-8B, AUF raises the DFlash drafter's average emitted length $τ$, averaged over six benchmarks, from 2.40 to 2.61, with a gain on every benchmark, and transfers to Domino's two-branch head (2.56 to 2.68). Two findings sharpen the picture: the decay-only baseline reaches higher token accuracy on the shared block mask yet decodes worse, and on DFlash, once AUF truncates the support, the standard exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert.

AI.tldr: AUF is a simple, prefix-focused adjustment to cross-entropy supervision for mask-only block drafters in speculative decoding, improving average emitted length and token accuracy without altering inference, by concentrating loss on the accepted prefix and truncating support after first failure.
AI.motivation: Block-draft training uses full-block CE or reweighting-based, prefix-insensitive losses. The authors aim to align supervision with the actual inference behavior (accepting only the longest accepted prefix) while keeping the inference pipeline unchanged.
AI.method: Introduce AUF as a single, detached change to CE support for mask-only drafter. AUF concentrates CE only on the drafter’s first predicted failure, approximating prefix-sensitive supervision without extra objectives or verifier rollouts. No changes to inference or exactness contract. Evaluate on Qwen3-8B backbones (DFlash and Domino two-branch heads) across six benchmarks, measuring average emitted length τ and token accuracy.
AI.result: AUF increases the average emitted length τ: DFlash from 2.40 to 2.61 (six benchmarks); Domino two-branch head from 2.56 to 2.68. Findings: (1) decay-only baseline yields higher token accuracy yet decodes worse; (2) for DFlash, once AUF truncates the support, exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert.
AI.conclusion: A minimal, loss-focused modification to cross-entropy support suffices to better align supervision with accepted-prefix decoding, improving efficiency (longer emitted blocks) without changing inference, and with predictable interactions with prefix conditioning and position weighting.

title: Role-Aware Neural Convex Divergence Heads for Asymmetric Representation Learning
summary: Many representation learning problems involve directed relations, such as lexical entailment, sentence entailment, ontology hierarchy, and citation links. Standard Euclidean, cosine, and Mahalanobis heads are symmetric, while generic neural scorers can model directionality but provide limited geometric structure. This paper proposes a role-aware neural convex divergence head for asymmetric representation learning. The head applies source- and target-role projections before evaluating an input-convex neural Bregman divergence, yielding a nonnegative structured score in the role-projected space. We characterize its projected-space identity, source-role convexity, directional-gap decomposition, and Hessian-based local curvature. Experiments on lexical, sentence, ontology, and directed graph benchmarks compare symmetric distances, unstructured asymmetric scorers, order/hyperbolic baselines, plain ICNN-Bregman heads, and the proposed role-aware variant. Across ten random seeds on the main semantic and ontology benchmarks, role-aware projections consistently improve directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads while preserving zero observed negative divergence rate. The results also identify a boundary case: on large fixed-feature citation prediction, specialized symmetric or hyperbolic baselines remain stronger in ranking accuracy. Overall, the proposed head is best understood as a structured and interpretable plug-in distance module for tasks where directional relations matter.

AI.tldr: Introduces a role-aware neural convex divergence head for asymmetric representation learning, combining source/target role projections with an ICNN-based Bregman divergence to capture directional relations across NLP/graph tasks; shows improved directional accuracy and zero negative divergence rate, with a boundary case where some symmetric/hyperbolic baselines perform best on large citation data; presents the head as a structured, plug-in distance for directional tasks.
AI.motivation: Address the limitations of symmetric similarity measures for directed relations (e.g., entailment, ontology, citations) by providing a geometrically interpretable, convex, directional distance.
AI.method: Project embeddings via source- and target-role projections, evaluate an input-convex neural network (ICNN) Bregman divergence in the projected space, analyze properties such as projected-space identity, source-role convexity, directional-gap decomposition, and Hessian curvature; compare to symmetric distances, unstructured asymmetric scorers, order/hyperbolic baselines, plain ICNN-Bregman heads across lexical, sentence, ontology, and directed-graph benchmarks, with ten random seeds.
AI.result: Role-aware projections consistently improve directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads on main semantic and ontology benchmarks, while preserving zero observed negative divergence rate; a boundary case shows that on large fixed-feature citation prediction, specialized symmetric or hyperbolic baselines can outperform in ranking.
AI.conclusion: The proposed head is best understood as a structured, interpretable plug-in distance module for tasks where directional relations matter, offering improved directional discrimination with interpretable geometry while maintaining convexity properties.

title: SpaceEra++: A Unified Framework Towards 3D Spatial Reasoning in Video
summary: Visual-spatial understanding, defined as the ability to infer object relationships and scene layouts from visual inputs, is fundamental to downstream tasks such as robotic navigation and embodied interaction. However, pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) remain constrained by spatial uncertainty stemming from inherently 2D observations and by the scarcity of data for 3D spatial understanding. To address these limitations, we proposed a novel framework, SpaceEra, in the NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight paper. Although it achieved significant performance gains, we further observed that its effectiveness is hindered by insufficient input from scanning videos and weak reasoning constraints. To tackle these newly emerged challenges, we extend the original framework into a comprehensive system, termed SpaceEra++, which spans data construction, model design, training optimization, and prompting inference. Specifically, to alleviate input insufficiency, we introduce ScenePick, a frame sampling strategy that balances spatial coverage with object semantics to produce compact yet comprehensive scene representations. In addition, to enhance spatial reasoning, we develop SpaceAlign, which enforces pairwise object constraints by jointly exploiting absolute coordinates and relative spatial relations, thereby aligning optimization with spatial accuracy. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines, while ablation studies validate both the individual and joint contributions of each component, and further analyses provide guidance for future research.

AI.tldr: SpaceEra++ extends SpaceEra to address input insufficiency and weak spatial reasoning with ScenePick sampling and SpaceAlign constraints, achieving consistent improvements across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Pre-trained vision-language models suffer from spatial uncertainty due to 2D observations and limited 3D data; SpaceEra showed gains but is hampered by insufficient scanning inputs and weak reasoning constraints, motivating a more complete system.
AI.method: Data construction and model design enhancements: ScenePick frame sampling balances spatial coverage with object semantics to produce compact scene representations; SpaceAlign enforces pairwise object constraints using absolute coordinates and relative spatial relations, aligning optimization with spatial accuracy; training optimization and prompting inference are integrated into SpaceEra++.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines; ablation studies validate the individual and joint contributions of ScenePick and SpaceAlign; analyses provide practical guidance for future work.
AI.conclusion: SpaceEra++ offers a comprehensive framework that mitigates input insufficiency and strengthens spatial reasoning in vision‑language models for robust 3D spatial understanding in embodied tasks.

title: Rethinking Complexity Metrics for LLM-Integrated Applications: Beyond Source Code
summary: LLM-integrated applications blend natural language prompts with program code, and much of their runtime behavior originates in the prompt layer rather than in the code itself. Existing complexity metrics, however, operate solely at the code level and therefore overlook this behavioral logic entirely. We present HECATE, the first tool designed to assess complexity in both the prompt and code layers of such applications. Central to HECATE is Prompt-as-Specification, a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism that interprets every prompt as a specification of intended behavior. Grounded in 25 complexity dimensions identified across published taxonomies, the tool generates 52 candidate metrics. We assess each metric against 118 components collected from 18 open-source repositories, relying on maintenance activity derived from version history as an empirical proxy for complexity, and discard any metric that loses significance once code size is accounted for. Only ten metrics withstand this test. Seven belong to our newly introduced set; rather than measuring sheer volume, each tallies structurally distinct elements, such as LLM call sites, memory attributes, and prompt templates, an attribute we call structural breadth. Of the three surviving conventional metrics, RFC exhibits a similar breadth-oriented character, while Halstead N and V survive only as a residual effect of size; our top-performing metrics exceed all three. Crucially, the prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when the strongest code-level metric is added as a covariate, establishing prompt complexity as a dimension in its own right. A final validation on 20 components spanning six held-out repositories shows that the two best-performing metrics continue to predict maintenance effort, supporting their generalizability beyond the training set.

AI.tldr: HECATE is a tool to measure and compare complexity in both the prompt and code layers of LLM-driven applications. It introduces Prompt-as-Specification, combines new structural-breadth metrics with conventional metrics, and demonstrates that prompt complexity independently predicts maintenance effort beyond code complexity, validated on multiple repositories.
AI.motivation: Traditional program complexity metrics ignore the prompt layer in LLM-integrated apps, yet prompts significantly influence runtime behavior. There is a need for metrics that capture prompt-layer complexity to better predict maintenance effort.
AI.method: Develop HECATE and a Prompt-as-Specification formalism. Identify 25 complexity dimensions from published taxonomies and derive 52 candidate metrics. Evaluate these metrics on 118 components from 18 open-source repositories using version-history maintenance activity as a proxy for complexity. Discard metrics that lose significance after controlling for code size. Distill to 10 robust metrics, including 7 novel structural-breadth metrics (e.g., LLM call sites, memory attributes, prompt templates) and 3 conventional metrics (RFC, Halstead N, Halstead V). Validate on 20 components from 6 held-out repositories to test predictive power for maintenance effort.
AI.result: Ten metrics survive the significance test after accounting for code size. Seven of these are novel structural-breadth metrics focusing on distinct prompt/code structures; three are conventional metrics with varying relevance (RFC breadth-like; Halstead N/V largely tied to size). The top-performing metrics exceed conventional baselines and maintain significance when a strong code-size metric is added. Final validation shows the two best metrics reliably predict maintenance effort on held-out data, indicating generalizability beyond the training set.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-layer complexity is a measurable, independent contributor to maintenance burden in LLM-integrated apps. HECATE provides a validated framework to quantify and compare prompt and code complexity, enabling better maintenance planning and design decisions for hybrid software systems.

title: Denser $\neq$ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training
summary: Continual post-training enables foundation models to acquire new knowledge while preserving existing capabilities. Recent work suggests that on-policy learning can mitigate forgetting, with on-policy self-distillation emerging as a particularly attractive approach. In this work, we revisit this optimistic view through self-distillation policy optimization (SDPO). Our experiments show that SDPO can accelerate in-domain specialization when teacher signals are stable and well aligned, but it struggles to generalize to out-of-distribution scenarios. In continual post-training, SDPO exhibits stronger forgetting and can even collapse, whereas on-policy reinforcement learning methods such as GRPO adapt more conservatively and better preserve prior capabilities. Further analyses reveal that denser self-distillation induces larger drift in both parameter space and response space, and can amplify high-frequency formatting artifacts through a self-reinforcing teacher--student loop. These findings suggest that on-policy data alone is insufficient for continual learning. Dense self-distillation can accelerate specialization when teacher targets are stable and token-level supervision is reliable, but it should not be treated as a default stabilizer for continual post-training. Our code is available at https://github.com/Moenupa/SDPO-CL.

AI.tldr: SDPO can speed up in-domain specialization when teacher signals are stable and aligned, but generalization to out-of-distribution data is poor. In continual post-training, SDPO forgets more and can collapse, whereas on-policy RL methods like GRPO preserve prior capabilities more reliably. Denser self-distillation causes larger drift in parameter/response space and amplifies high-frequency formatting artifacts via a self-reinforcing loop. On-policy data alone is insufficient for continual learning; dense distillation is not a default stabilizer. Code available at the provided GitHub link.
