To bridge this gap, we benchmark representative token compression and structural pruning methods for ViT-based semantic segmentation under matched FLOPs on ADE20K and Cityscapes, together with their common-corruption variants ADE20K-C and Cityscapes-C. Our results reveal a consistent trend on both clean and corrupted inputs: token compression is highly effective at mild reductions but degrades sharply when compression becomes severe, consistent with substantial information loss from overly aggressive token reduction. In contrast, structural pruning exhibits a smoother degradation curve and is more stable at high compression. Motivated by these findings, we study a prune-then-merge pipeline that applies moderate token compression on top of a moderately pruned backbone. At comparable FLOPs, this combined strategy consistently achieves a better accuracy-robustness trade-off at high compression, offering a practical recipe for deployment-oriented ViT segmentation. Code is available at https://github.com/phatnguyencs/vit-seg-compression.

AI.tldr: Token compression and structural pruning offer different efficiency-accuracy curves for ViT-based semantic segmentation. Under aggressive compression, pruning is more stable than token compression. A prune-then-merge approach (moderate token compression on a moderately pruned backbone) yields the best accuracy-robustness trade-off at high FLOPs, suggesting a practical deployment recipe. Code is provided in the repo.
AI.motivation: Evaluate and compare token compression and structural pruning for ViT-based semantic segmentation under matched FLOPs and corrupted inputs, addressing the lack of a unified protocol and understanding behavior under aggressive compression.
AI.method: Benchmark representative token-compression and structural-pruning methods for ViT-based semantic segmentation under matched FLOPs on ADE20K and Cityscapes, including common corruptions ADE20K-C and Cityscapes-C; analyze performance vs. compression level and robustness; propose a prune-then-merge strategy and compare it to baselines.
AI.result: Token compression is highly effective at mild reductions but degrades sharply under aggressive compression due to information loss; structural pruning shows a smoother degradation and greater stability at high compression; the prune-then-merge pipeline (moderate token compression on a moderately pruned backbone) achieves a better accuracy-robustness trade-off at high compression; this provides a practical deployment strategy for ViT segmentation across clean and corrupted inputs.
AI.conclusion: For deployment under tight FLOPs constraints, prioritize structural pruning for high compression; augment with moderate token compression in a prune-then-merge scheme to balance accuracy and robustness; the work offers a unified benchmarking protocol and actionable insights for ViT segmentation.

title: Neuron-Aware Data Selection for Annotation-Free LLM Self-Distillation
summary: Post-training large language models (LLMs) without real-world interaction feedback or human-labeled supervision remains challenging, particularly in specialized domains where expert annotations are costly to obtain. Recent annotation-free self-evolution methods address this by using the model's own outputs as supervision signals, constructing a teacher via additional context and aggregating predictions across multiple rollouts through majority voting to produce pseudo-labels. However, these approaches are not without drawbacks: SFT- and GRPO-based variants suffer out-of-domain performance degradation, while reward-based on-policy RL inflates calibration error. In this paper, we propose Neuron On-Policy Self-Distillation (Neuron-OPSD), a data-centric framework for annotation-free self-distillation that leverages internal neuron activations to guide both training-data selection and teacher context construction. The model is then trained via on-policy distillation from the teacher distribution, requiring no ground-truth labels at any stage. Across specialized-domain benchmarks, Neuron-OPSD improves in-domain task performance while preserving cross-domain generalization and mitigating calibration collapse over prior annotation-free baselines. This framework is particularly relevant to settings where online interaction or external supervision is costly or infeasible, and is conceptually distinct from offline RL approaches that rely on logged, reward-labeled trajectories.

AI.tldr: Neuron-OPSD is a data-centric, annotation-free self-distillation framework for post-training LLMs in specialized domains. It uses internal neuron activations to guide training-data selection and teacher-context construction, and performs on-policy distillation from the teacher distribution without any ground-truth labels. It improves in-domain performance while preserving cross-domain generalization and reducing calibration collapse compared to prior annotation-free baselines.
AI.motivation: Post-training LLMs face the challenge of learning without real-world interaction feedback or labeled data, especially in specialized domains where expert annotations are costly. Prior annotation-free self-evolution methods rely on self-generated signals or rewards but can degrade out-of-domain performance or inflate calibration error. A data-centric, neuron-guided approach aims to align data, supervision signals, and model behavior without external labels.
AI.method: The framework leverages internal neuron activations to select training data and to construct the context for the teacher. It then trains the model via on-policy distillation from the teacher distribution, with no ground-truth labels at any stage. This contrasts with SFT-/GRPO-based methods and reward-based RL, by using neuron-informed data curation and on-policy, context-aware distillation.
AI.result: Across specialized-domain benchmarks, Neuron-OPSD yields improved in-domain task performance, maintains cross-domain generalization, and mitigates calibration collapse relative to prior annotation-free baselines.
AI.conclusion: Neuron-OPSD provides a data-centric pathway for annotation-free self-distillation, particularly when online interaction or external supervision is costly or infeasible, and it is conceptually distinct from offline RL approaches that rely on reward-labeled trajectories.

title: ArcAD: Anomaly-Rectified Calibration for Cold-Start Supervised Anomaly Detection
comment: Accepted to European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV) 2026
summary: The deployment of Industrial Anomaly Detection (IAD) in real-world manufacturing frequently encounters a challenging cold-start bottleneck, in which limited normal samples fail to represent the full normal distribution and only a few anomalies are available. Under such a regime, existing methods struggle to form compact normal boundaries and fail to effectively exploit supervised signals from rare defects. To address this challenge, we propose Anomaly-Rectified Cold-start AD (ArcAD), a plug-and-play calibration framework for reconstruction-based IAD baselines. ArcAD follows a push-pull learning paradigm to construct a compact and discriminative normal boundary under data scarcity. On the one hand, ArcAD projects limited normal samples onto a hypersphere and pulls them into multiple compact clusters to maximize coverage of the normal manifold. On the other hand, it synthesizes pseudo-anomalies on the hypersphere and leverages real anomalies to push the boundary inward and sharpen anomaly discrimination. Extensive experiments on MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, and MANTA demonstrate that ArcAD significantly outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and unsupervised methods in both single-class and multi-class settings under cold-start conditions. Code is available at: https://github.com/LGC-AD/ArcAD.

AI.tldr: ArcAD is a plug-and-play calibration framework for reconstruction-based industrial anomaly detection under cold-start conditions. It uses push-pull learning on a hypersphere to densely cover the normal data manifold while leveraging real and synthesized anomalies to sharpen the decision boundary, yielding strong gains on multiple benchmarks; code available.
AI.motivation: Industrial anomaly detection often suffers from cold-start: few normal samples fail to represent the full normal distribution and only a few anomalies are available. Existing methods struggle to form a compact normal boundary and exploit scarce defect signals.
AI.method: ArcAD is a plug-and-play calibration framework that uses a push-pull learning paradigm. It projects limited normal samples onto a hypersphere and clusters them into compact regions to maximize normal manifold coverage. It then synthesizes pseudo-anomalies on the hypersphere and uses real anomalies to push the boundary inward, sharpening anomaly discrimination. It is designed to be compatible with reconstruction-based IAD baselines.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, and MANTA show that ArcAD significantly outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and unsupervised methods in both single-class and multi-class settings under cold-start conditions.
AI.conclusion: ArcAD provides an effective, plug-and-play calibration for reconstruction-based industrial anomaly detection under data scarcity, achieving strong empirical gains and offering code for reuse.

title: Beyond Adam: SOAP and Muon for Faster, Label-Efficient Training of Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
summary: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have become a hallmark of AI for scientific simulation. While efforts on new architectures and datasets have led to increasingly accurate and general models, the choice of optimizer for training has largely remained unexplored, defaulting to Adam and its variants in the community. Here, we implement and systematically compare a class of recently proposed matrix-structured optimizers, including Muon, SOAP, and the hybrid SOAP-Muon, for training NequIP and Allegro MLIP models. We find that these optimizers can substantially outperform Adam in both convergence speed and final accuracy. SOAP and SOAP-Muon emerge as robust and consistently strong methods, while Muon only provides partial gains relative to Adam. The improvements are particularly pronounced under partial force supervision. Our results indicate that optimizer choice is an overlooked yet impactful design axis for MLIPs.

AI.tldr: Matrix-structured optimizers (SOAP, SOAP-Muon) outperform Adam in training MLIPs (NequIP, Allegro); Muon helps less; best under partial force supervision.
AI.motivation: Explore optimizer choices as a design axis for MLIPs and evaluate matrix-structured optimizers against Adam.
AI.method: Implement and compare Muon, SOAP, and hybrid SOAP-Muon optimizers for NequIP and Allegro; assess convergence speed and final accuracy under full and partial force supervision.
AI.result: SOAP and SOAP-Muon consistently deliver faster convergence and higher accuracy; Muon yields limited gains; benefits amplified with partial force supervision.
AI.conclusion: Optimizer choice is impactful for MLIPs; matrix-structured optimizers, particularly SOAP and SOAP-Muon, are robust and recommended; Muon offers more limited improvements.

title: AnyGroundBench: A Specialized-Domain Benchmark for Video Grounding in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated immense promise in Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding (STVG). However, current evaluation protocols are largely confined to zero-shot assessments on general, daily-life benchmarks. This creates a critical disconnect from real-world applications in specialized fields, where models inevitably encounter rare visual concepts and complex spatio-temporal dynamics. Since exhaustive pre-training across infinite data distributions is infeasible, the ability to adapt to novel domains is essential. To bridge this gap, we introduce AnyGroundBench, a domain-adaptation benchmark designed to shift the STVG evaluation paradigm from static zero-shot testing to rigorous domain adaptation. Targeting five specialized domains (animal, industry, sports, surgery, and public security), AnyGroundBench pairs newly captured videos such as expert-annotated mouse behaviors with established datasets, unifying them through dense, high-fidelity spatio-temporal annotations. Crucially, the benchmark provides dedicated training subsets to systematically measure domain adaptability. We extensively evaluate 15 state-of-the-art VLMs, assessing their zero-shot generalization and In-Context Learning (ICL) capabilities under practical computational constraints. Ultimately, our findings reveal that current models fail in both zero-shot and ICL-based adaptation when confronted with specialized domains, exposing critical flaws in spatio-temporal reasoning that future research must address.

AI.tldr: A domain-adaptation benchmark for Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding (STVG) called AnyGroundBench, evaluating five specialized domains with dedicated training subsets; 15 SOTA VLMs show poor zero-shot and In-Context Learning adaptation, highlighting gaps in spatio-temporal reasoning.
AI.motivation: Current STVG evaluation relies on zero-shot general benchmarks, failing to reflect performance in specialized real-world domains. Domain adaptation is essential due to infeasibility of exhaustive pre-training across infinite distributions.
AI.method: Construct AnyGroundBench with five domains (animal, industry, sports, surgery, public security) by pairing new expert-annotated videos with existing datasets, providing dense spatio-temporal annotations and explicit training subsets; evaluate 15 state-of-the-art VLMs under zero-shot and In-Context Learning within practical compute constraints.
AI.result: 15 VLMs underperform in both zero-shot and ICL adaptation on these domains, revealing critical deficiencies in spatio-temporal reasoning and generalization to novel concepts.
AI.conclusion: AnyGroundBench provides a targeted benchmark for domain adaptability in STVG and exposes the need for improved spatio-temporal reasoning in VLMs to handle specialized domains.

title: DemoPSD: Disagreement-Modulated Policy Self-Distillation
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a practical method for training large language models (LLMs) to reason, where a single model acts as both the teacher and the student with different levels of information access. However, recent studies have found that the teacher's dense token-level supervision, conditioned on privileged information, can lead to overfitting to in-domain patterns, suppress exploration, and hurt cross-domain generalization, while also introducing a more fundamental issue: *privileged information leakage*, where the student encodes answer-dependent shortcuts that are unavailable at test time. We introduce **DemoPSD**, a novel framework that resolves such problems through the idea of *selective adoption of teacher guidance*. Instead of fitting the full teacher distribution, DemoPSD steers the student toward a *reverse-KL barycenter target*, a weighted geometric combination of the teacher and student distributions, that naturally balances learning from the teacher with preserving the student's own reasoning capacity. We measure the difference between their distributions and use such a discrepancy to adaptively control the blending at each token position. We provably show that DemoPSD achieves **(1)** *leakage attenuation*, i.e., effective mitigation of privileged information leakage; and **(2)** *exploration preservation*, i.e., preservation of exploration capacity under dense token-level distillation. Extensive experiments on SciKnowEval across four scientific fields show that DemoPSD outperforms both GRPO and SDPO while maintaining higher training entropy and robustly generalizing to out-of-distribution GPQA benchmarks.

AI.tldr: DemoPSD introduces selective on-policy self-distillation by blending teacher and student distributions via a reverse-KL barycenter, adaptively controlled by token-level distribution discrepancy to mitigate privileged information leakage and preserve exploration, achieving better cross-domain generalization and higher training entropy on SciKnowEval.
AI.motivation: Teacher-driven dense token-level supervision in on-policy self-distillation risks overfitting to in-domain patterns, reduces exploration, harms cross-domain generalization, and leaks privileged information that helps test-time answers but is unavailable then.
AI.method: Replace full teacher guidance with a weighted geometric combination (reverse-KL barycenter) of teacher and student distributions at each token, where the blending weight is adaptive based on the discrepancy between teacher and student distributions; provide theoretical guarantees for leakage attenuation and exploration preservation; demonstrate selective adoption of teacher guidance instead of plain distillation.
AI.result: Empirical results on SciKnowEval across four scientific fields show DemoPSD outperforms GRPO and SDPO, maintains higher training entropy, and robustly generalizes to out-of-distribution GPQA benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: DemoPSD resolves privileged information leakage while preserving exploration and maintaining competitive performance, supported by theoretical properties and experimental validation.

title: AGVBench: A Reliability-Oriented Benchmark of Data Augmentation for Vein Recognition
summary: Vein recognition is a secure biometric technology often constrained by limited annotated data and imaging variations. While data augmentation mitigates this, strategies designed for natural images may disrupt the fine-grained topology and textures essential for identity discrimination. We present AGVBench, which evaluates 30 representative augmentation strategies on five public palm- and finger-vein datasets with seven backbone architectures, covering classic CNNs, vision transformers, and vein-specific recognition models. Our results show that multi-image mixing methods (e.g., MixUp, PuzzleMix, StarMixup) generally provide the strongest recognition performance. However, they are often poorly calibrated and vulnerable to adversarial perturbations, revealing a clear inconsistency between clean accuracy and adversarial security. We also find that severe geometric transformations frequently degrade recognition, which is potentially due to feature misalignment or spatial cropping, and that augmentation effectiveness varies across palm and finger vein datasets. These findings prove that accuracy-centric evaluation is insufficient for biometric augmentation. AGVBench provides standardized protocols to support reproducible research and guide the design of reliable, secure, and robust vein recognition systems. Our codebase is available at https://github.com/Advance-VeinTech-Innovators/AGVBench.

AI.tldr: AGVBench systematically benchmarks 30 augmentation strategies for vein recognition across five datasets and seven backbones, revealing accuracy–robustness trade-offs, dataset- and transform-specific effects, and the need for standardized evaluation.
AI.motivation: Data augmentation can mitigate limited vein data, but augmentation strategies from natural images may disrupt vein-specific features; a standardized evaluation is needed to guide robust, secure vein recognition.
AI.method: Evaluate 30 augmentation strategies on five public palm- and finger-vein datasets using seven backbone architectures (CNNs, Vision Transformers, and vein-specific models); analyze accuracy, calibration, and adversarial robustness; study geometric transforms and dataset differences; provide reproducible protocols and code.
AI.result: Multi-image mixing methods (e.g., MixUp, PuzzleMix, StarMixup) yield strongest recognition accuracy but are poorly calibrated and vulnerable to adversarial perturbations; severe geometric transformations degrade recognition; augmentation effectiveness varies across palm vs finger vein datasets; clean accuracy and adversarial security are inconsistent; standardized protocols proposed to guide reliable vein recognition design.
AI.conclusion: Accuracy-centric evaluation is insufficient for biometric augmentation; AGVBench offers standardized protocols for reproducible research and to guide reliable, secure vein recognition systems; code available at the provided GitHub URL.

title: Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions
summary: Many everyday programming tasks resist clean rule-based implementation, such as alerting on important log lines, repairing malformed JSON, or ranking search results by intent, and are increasingly outsourced to large language model APIs at the cost of locality, reproducibility, and price. We propose fuzzy-function programming: compiling such a function from a natural-language specification into a compact, locally-executable neural artifact. We instantiate this paradigm with Program-as-Weights (PAW), in which a 4B compiler trained on FuzzyBench, a 10M-example dataset we release, emits parameter-efficient adapters for a frozen, lightweight interpreter. A 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter executing PAW programs matches the performance of direct prompting of Qwen3-32B, while using roughly one fiftieth of the inference memory and running at 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3. PAW reframes the foundation model from a per-input problem solver into a tool builder: invoked once per function definition, it produces a small reusable artifact whose subsequent calls per function application are cheap and offline.

AI.tldr: A new paradigm, fuzzy-function programming, compiles a natural-language specification into a small, locally-executable neural artifact. It is instantiated as Program-as-Weights (PAW), which emits parameter-efficient adapters for a frozen interpreter.
AI.motivation: Many common programming tasks resist rule-based solutions and are increasingly outsourced to large language model APIs, harming locality, reproducibility, and cost. A local, reusable artifact could preserve locality and efficiency while leveraging LLMs for specification.
AI.method: Train a 4B compiler on the FuzzyBench dataset (10M examples) to produce adapters for a frozen, lightweight interpreter. Use a 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter that executes PAW programs, producing compact, reusable artifacts per function definition.
AI.result: PAW-enabled Qwen3 (0.6B) matches direct prompting performance while using about 1/50 the inference memory and running ~30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3. The approach yields reusable artifacts whose per-call cost is cheap and offline.
AI.conclusion: PAW reframes the foundation model as a tool-builder: a single compilation step per function definition creates a reusable artifact; later calls are cheap and offline, enabling efficient, local function execution.

title: FlowCIR: Semantic Transport via Flow Matching for Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval
summary: Zero-shot composed image retrieval (ZS-CIR) aims to retrieve a target image by editing a reference image with a natural-language instruction, without relying on domain-specific annotated triplets. Most existing ZS-CIR methods rely on textual inversion to translate the reference image into pseudo-text tokens and then compose them with the instruction via simple concatenation in the text space, which can be lossy and brittle for fine-grained semantics. In this work, we propose a new paradigm, namely FlowCIR, that casts ZS-CIR as conditional semantic transport between reference and target embeddings. Leveraging \emph{conditional flow matching}, our model learns a lightweight transport field that maps the instruction representation toward a target-aligned query embedding conditioned on the reference image. Since FlowCIR operates on pre-extracted VLM embeddings and trains only a small transport module without updating the image or text encoder, it offers a computationally efficient training protocol compared with prior textual-inversion-based approaches. The resulting framework is training-efficient, requiring roughly $10\times$ fewer training resources than prior textual-inversion-based approaches. We further identify negation and removal as a major failure mode of VLM-based composition. To address this, we propose an inference-only Multi-Negative Steering strategy that steers a negation-containing relative instruction away from its negated semantics, mitigating the limited negation handling of VLMs and improving robustness on negation-heavy queries. Extensive experiments on standard CIR benchmarks demonstrate that FlowCIR achieves strong and competitive performance compared with recent ZS-CIR methods.

AI.tldr: FlowCIR reframes zero-shot composed image retrieval as conditional semantic transport via conditional flow matching, enabling efficient training with a lightweight transport module and improved negation handling through Multi-Negative Steering.
AI.motivation: Traditional ZS-CIR relies on textual inversion and text-space concatenation, which can be lossy for fine-grained semantics and require substantial resources. A more efficient, robust approach is needed that preserves semantics and handles negation.
AI.method: Introduce conditional flow matching to learn a transport field that maps the instruction embedding toward a target-aligned query embedding conditioned on the reference image. Operates on pre-extracted VLM embeddings and trains only a small transport module (no updates to image/text encoders). Inference-only Multi-Negative Steering mitigates negation-related failures by steering negation-containing instructions away from negated semantics.
AI.result: Demonstrates competitive performance on standard CIR benchmarks with roughly 10x reduction in training resources compared to textual-inversion-based approaches. Shows improved robustness on negation-heavy queries due to the Multi-Negative Steering strategy.
AI.conclusion: FlowCIR offers a training-efficient, robust ZS-CIR framework by reframing composition as conditional flow transport and addressing negation at inference time, achieving strong results while reducing training resource requirements.

title: DisciplineGen-1M: A Large-Scale Dataset for Multidisciplinary Visual Generation and Editing
summary: Recent image generation and editing models can produce visually appealing natural images, yet they remain unreliable when the target image is a knowledge-intensive diagram whose correctness depends on disciplinary concepts, symbolic structure, and precise spatial relations. We introduce DisciplineGen-1M, a million-scale multidisciplinary dataset that supports text-to-image generation and image editing. It contains 1.2M samples spanning mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, geography, computer science, economics, history, music, and sports. To construct the dataset, we design a scalable framework that combines vector-graphics rendering, OCR-based editing, curated programmatic synthesis, and large-scale text-to-image filtering. These pipelines produce captions, editing instructions, structured annotations, and paired images with controllable semantic differences. Building on DisciplineGen-1M, we further introduce a discipline-informed reasoning-generation model for both text-to-image generation and image editing. Experiments on discipline-related benchmarks, GenExam and GRADE, show substantial improvements over open-source baselines, while evaluations on general reasoning-informed benchmarks, WISE and RISE, further indicate broader transfer. The results suggest that large-scale structured academic visual data is a key ingredient for moving image generation from aesthetic plausibility toward verifiable knowledge-grounded visual creation. We will publicly release our dataset, model, and source code of the data curation pipeline to ensure reproducibility and benefit future research.

AI.tldr: Introduces DisciplineGen-1M, a million-scale multidisciplinary dataset and a discipline-informed reasoning-generation model for text-to-image generation and editing, achieving improvements on domain-specific benchmarks and transfer to general reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Knowledge-intensive diagrams require discipline-specific concepts, symbolic structures, and precise spatial relations; existing models struggle with such content, highlighting the need for large-scale, structured academic visual data to ground visual generation in verifiable knowledge.
AI.method: A 1.2M-sample multidisciplinary dataset built via vector-graphics rendering, OCR-based editing, curated programmatic synthesis, and large-scale text-to-image filtering, producing captions, editing instructions, structured annotations, and paired images with controllable semantic differences; plus a discipline-informed reasoning-generation model for generation and editing.
AI.result: Significant improvements over open-source baselines on discipline-related benchmarks GenExam and GRADE; observed transfer to broader benchmarks WISE and RISE; supports the potential of knowledge-grounded visual creation and plans for public release of dataset, model, and code.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale structured academic visual data is a key ingredient to shift image generation from aesthetic plausibility toward verifiable knowledge-grounded visual creation; the work provides reproducible data and methods for future research.

title: Dual-Selective Network for Domain-Incremental Change Detection
comment: International Conference on Artificial Neural Networks, ICANN-2026
summary: Domain-incremental change detection (DICD) continuously adapts models to new geographic domains while preserving prior knowledge. However, a structural mismatch exists: the label space remains fixed while domain characteristics vary drastically. Consequently, incremental models struggle to maintain stable spatial change representations across domains. Existing strategies, such as replay-based or regularization-based methods, often fail to scale to long domain sequences, leading to knowledge degradation or increased computational cost. We propose Dual-Selective Incremental Network (DSINet), a unified framework built on visual state space models. DSINet leverages Mamba's input-dependent selective mechanism through a selective spatial state unit (S3U). This unit preserves stable spatial change structures while filtering domain-specific variations during feature propagation. As a result, spatial representations remain stable across domains, preventing the accumulation of feature confusion over incremental steps. Additionally, we employ a concentration-balanced distillation (CBD) strategy to stabilize knowledge transfer across domains. It balances hardness and confidence concentration effects during incremental updates. This ensures reliable probability mass allocation and prevents over-smoothing or mode collapse during distillation. Together, these mechanisms maintain stable learning dynamics throughout incremental stages. Experimental results demonstrate that DSINet mitigates knowledge degradation across long domain sequences while maintaining the linear computational efficiency of state space models.

AI.tldr: DSINet introduces a Dual-Selective Incremental Network for domain-incremental change detection, using a Selective Spatial State Unit (S3U) and Concentration-Balanced Distillation (CBD) to preserve stable spatial change representations across long domain sequences, achieving scalable linear-complexity performance.
AI.motivation: Domain-incremental change detection faces fixed label spaces amidst drastic domain shifts, leading to unstable spatial representations and knowledge degradation; existing replay/regularization methods struggle to scale to long domain sequences.
AI.method: DSINet is built on visual state space models and employs Mamba's input-dependent selective mechanism via a Selective Spatial State Unit (S3U) to filter domain-specific variations while preserving stable spatial change structures. It also introduces Concentration-Balanced Distillation (CBD) to balance hard and soft (confidence) signals during incremental updates, preventing over-smoothing or mode collapse.
AI.result: Empirical results show reduced knowledge degradation across long domain sequences while maintaining the linear computational efficiency of state space models.
AI.conclusion: DSINet provides stable learning dynamics for domain-incremental change detection, scalable to long domain sequences with preserved spatial representations and efficient computation.

title: Search-based Testing of Vision Language Models for In-Car Scene Understanding
comment: Accepted at the Industry Track of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: In the automotive domain, in-car scene understanding (ISU) enables the detection of safety-critical events, such as driver distraction, and supports drivers or passengers by analyzing the in-car scene and adapting the environment (e.g., ambient lighting). The industry is increasingly exploring vision-language models (VLMs) to interpret camera-recorded in-car scenes and extract information for downstream reasoning tasks. However, VLMs may generate incomplete, erroneous, or misleading scene descriptions, highlighting the need for systematic testing. Collecting real in-vehicle data is costly, difficult to scale, and often infeasible, particularly in early design stages. In this paper, we present ISU-Test, an automated testing approach that combines rendering-based scene generation with search-based testing to evaluate ISU systems. By framing testing as an optimization problem and systematically modifying scene parameters, our method generates diverse in-car scenarios and explores a wide range of configurations. We evaluate ISU-Test on both an industrial prototype and open-source VLMs across two case studies: question answering and captioning, comparing against randomized scenario generation. Results show that ISU-Test significantly outperforms the baseline, achieving up to 10 times higher failure rates and up to 3.6 times higher failure coverage.

AI.tldr: ISU-Test combines rendering-based scene generation with search-based testing to systematically test in-car scene understanding (ISU) VLMs, achieving higher failure detection and coverage than randomized generation in QA and captioning tasks.
AI.motivation: In-car ISU models can produce incomplete or misleading scene descriptions; collecting real in-vehicle data is costly, restricted, and infeasible in early design stages, necessitating scalable automated testing to uncover weaknesses.
AI.method: Frame testing as an optimization problem by using rendering-based scene generation and search-based (optimization-guided) exploration to create diverse, targeted in-car scenarios; evaluate on both an industrial prototype and open-source VLMs across two tasks (question answering and captioning) and compare against randomized scenario generation.
AI.result: ISU-Test significantly outperforms the baseline, achieving up to 10× higher failure rates and up to 3.6× higher failure coverage across industrial and open-source VLMs in two case studies.
AI.conclusion: A systematic, optimization-driven testing approach with rendering-based scene generation is effective for validating ISU VLMs in automotive contexts and should be adopted during early-stage development to reliably expose weaknesses that random sampling may miss; findings likely generalize to other VLM-based perception tasks.

title: InvSplat: Inverse Feed-Forward Scene Splatting
summary: Inverse rendering aims to recover both 3D geometry and physically meaningful material properties from images, enabling applications such as relighting and novel view synthesis. Optimization-based methods achieve high fidelity but require costly per-scene fitting, while image-space learning-based approaches often suffer from multi-view inconsistencies and lack an explicit 3D representation for stable novel view rendering. We present a feed-forward multi-view reconstruction framework for inverse rendering that directly predicts a structured 3D Gaussian representation with intrinsic material attributes. Each Gaussian primitive is parameterized by mean, normal, opacity, rotation, scale, albedo, metallic, and roughness, enabling a disentangled and physically grounded scene representation. Our model integrates priors from a material estimation network with a multi-view 3D reconstruction backbone, allowing joint prediction of geometry and reflectance parameters in a single forward pass. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate improved multi-view consistency compared to 2D baselines, accurate material recovery, and stable novel view rendering. Our representation further supports physically-based relighting and more faithful modeling of view-dependent effects compared to existing RGB-based feed-forward reconstruction methods. Our project webpage is: $\href{https://poliik.github.io/invsplat/}{\text{https://poliik.github.io/invsplat/}}$.

AI.tldr: Proposes a feed-forward multi-view inverse rendering framework using structured 3D Gaussian primitives with intrinsic material attributes to jointly recover geometry and material properties in one pass, improving multi-view consistency and enabling relighting.
AI.motivation: Optimization-based inverse rendering yields high fidelity but is costly per-scene; image-space methods lack explicit 3D structure and struggle with multi-view consistency and stable novel-view rendering.
AI.method: Predicts a set of Gaussian primitives with parameters: mean, normal, opacity, rotation, scale, albedo, metallic, roughness; integrates material-estimation priors with a multi-view 3D reconstruction backbone to jointly predict geometry and reflectance in a single forward pass.
AI.result: On synthetic and real data, achieves improved multi-view consistency over 2D baselines, accurate material recovery, and stable novel view rendering; enables physically-based relighting and better modeling of view-dependent effects than RGB-based feed-forward methods.
AI.conclusion: Structured 3D Gaussian representation is effective for inverse rendering, offering explicit 3D structure and physically grounded decomposition that supports reliable rendering and relighting.

title: NEvo: Neural-Guided Evolutionary Video Synthesis for Dynamic Visual Selectivity
summary: The human brain processes dynamic visual input through hierarchically organized, functionally specialized regions. While recent in silico brain encoding models can synthesize optimal stimuli to probe selectivity in different brain regions, prior work has been largely limited to static images, leaving dynamic visual processing underexplored. We introduce a novel neural-guided video synthesis framework that generates stimuli optimized for target brain regions across visual cortex. Our method performs evolutionary search over a structured prompt space, guided by a dynamic encoding model that predicts voxel-level responses to video inputs. By maximizing predicted activity for a target ROI, the framework efficiently discovers hyper-activating dynamic stimuli that consistently surpass handcrafted localizer videos. The synthesized videos recover known selectivities across ventral, dorsal, and lateral pathways, and further reveal systematic differences in sensitivity to temporal dynamics. A searchlight analysis provides new insight into the progression toward increasingly complex social-dynamic features along the lateral stream, further supported by probing with synthesized abstract, non-naturalistic stimuli. Taken together, our framework enables in silico exploration of dynamic visual selectivity, with new predictions for in vivo experiments

AI.tldr: A neural-guided video synthesis framework optimizes dynamic stimuli to probe region-specific visual processing across the cortex, using evolutionary search over a structured prompt space guided by a dynamic encoding model; it reveals region-specific temporal dynamics and social-dynamic feature progression, enabling in silico predictions for future in vivo experiments.
AI.motivation: To extend brain-encoding and stimulus-design methods from static images to dynamic video, enabling efficient probing of dynamic selectivity across ventral, dorsal, and lateral visual pathways and to uncover temporal dynamics in neural responses.
AI.method: An evolutionary search over a structured prompt space generates dynamic videos. A dynamic encoding model predicts voxel-level responses to video inputs; optimization targets maximizing activity in a chosen ROI. The method compares synthesized stimuli against handcrafted localizers, uses searchlight analyses, and probes with abstract, non-naturalistic stimuli to map dynamic selectivity.
AI.result: Synthesized stimuli reproduce known selectivities across ventral, dorsal, and lateral pathways and reveal systematic differences in sensitivity to temporal dynamics. The lateral stream shows progression toward more complex social-dynamic features; searchlight analysis and abstract probes provide new insights. The framework outperforms handcrafted localizers in activating target ROIs and offers a scalable avenue for exploring dynamic visual selectivity in silico.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables in silico exploration of dynamic visual selectivity, generating testable predictions for in vivo experiments and offering a scalable tool to map temporal dynamics and feature complexity along visual pathways.

title: GAP-GDRNet: Geometry-Aware Monocular Visual Pose Sensing on a Single-Target Synthetic Spacecraft Dataset
summary: Monocular relative pose sensing is a central perception problem in non-cooperative rendezvous and on-orbit servicing. In spacecraft images, however, weak surface texture, thin appendages, illumination changes, and partial occlusion often leave only sparse and unstable geometric evidence. This article presents GAP-GDRNet, a geometry-aware attention-enhanced framework for monocular RGB-based 6D pose sensing. The method follows the geometry-guided direct regression paradigm of GDR-Net and modifies two points in the pipeline: an attention-based feature refinement (AFR) module is placed before dense geometric prediction, and a patch-level geometric self-attention (PGSA) module is inserted into Patch-PnP. AFR reinforces global spacecraft structure together with local weak-texture cues; PGSA then relates downsampled geometric patches before final pose regression. A Blender-based annotation process supplies target masks, visible-region masks, dense model-coordinate maps, camera intrinsics, and 6D pose labels for supervised training.

AI.tldr: A geometry-aware, attention-enhanced monocular RGB approach (GAP-GDRNet) extends GDR-Net with an AFR module for global-local refinement and a PGSA module for patch-level self-attention in Patch-PnP, using Blender-based supervision to improve 6D pose estimation of spacecraft under weak texture and occlusion.
AI.motivation: To overcome sparse geometric cues, weak surface texture, illumination changes, and occlusion in monocular spacecraft pose estimation, improving robustness and accuracy.
AI.method: Introduce AFR before dense geometry prediction to reinforce global structure and local textures; insert PGSA into Patch-PnP to relate downsampled geometric patches with self-attention; train with Blender-generated supervision including target masks, visible-region masks, dense model-coordinate maps, intrinsics, and 6D pose labels.
AI.result: Abstract provides no quantitative results; claims improved robustness via attention-guided refinement and patch-level self-attention for monocular 6D pose sensing.
AI.conclusion: GAP-GDRNet demonstrates a geometry-guided, attention-enhanced framework for monocular 6D pose estimation on spacecraft, benefiting from explicit geometric supervision and patch-level reasoning; Blender-based annotation enables supervised training.

title: VisionAId: An Offline-First Multimodal Android Assistant for People with Visual Impairment, Featuring Personalized Object Retrieval
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Project repository available at: github.com
summary: Over 285 million people worldwide live with a visual impairment, for whom everyday tasks such as avoiding obstacles, locating personal belongings, recognizing familiar faces, or handling cash remain persistent obstacles to personal autonomy. Existing assistive applications are typically limited to recognizing predefined categories, depend heavily on cloud connectivity, or require dedicated hardware. We present VisionAId, an Android application that turns a commodity smartphone into a real-time visual assistant. The system integrates six on-device deep learning models (metric monocular depth estimation, instance segmentation, visual and facial embeddings, face detection, and a custom banknote detector) running entirely through ONNX Runtime, with an optional cloud large language model (Google Gemini Flash) used only for narrative scene description and automatic object labeling. A distinctive contribution is a few-shot pipeline for personal objects: the user photographs an object from several angles, and the system later locates that specific instance in the environment, guiding the user toward it with augmented-reality markers, spatial audio, and distance-proportional haptics. All feedback is multimodal (Romanian speech synthesis, voice commands, vibration). On a reference device (Samsung Galaxy S21 Ultra), INT8 quantization reduces depth latency from ~1200 ms to ~491 ms, the custom banknote detector reaches an mAP@50 of 0.986, and metric depth is calibrated to below 1 cm of error within 3 m.

AI.tldr: VisionAId is an Android app that turns a commodity smartphone into a real-time visual assistant for visually impaired users, using on-device ONNX models (depth, segmentation, embeddings, face/eye detection, banknote detector) with optional cloud LLM for scene narration, plus a few-shot personal-object locator offering AR cues, spatial audio, and haptics.
AI.motivation: To improve autonomy and safety for the visually impaired by enabling real-time perception and navigation on-device, avoiding cloud dependency and hardware constraints of existing apps.
AI.method: Six on-device models run via ONNX Runtime (depth estimation, instance segmentation, visual and facial embeddings, face detection, and a banknote detector) with an optional cloud LLM (Gemini Flash) for narrative scene description and object labeling. A few-shot pipeline lets users photograph an object from multiple angles to locate that instance later, guiding the user with AR markers, spatial audio, and distance-proportional haptics. Multimodal feedback includes Romanian speech synthesis, voice commands, and vibration.
AI.result: On a Samsung Galaxy S21 Ultra, INT8 quantization reduces depth latency from ~1200 ms to ~491 ms; banknote detector achieves mAP@50 of 0.986; metric depth error is <1 cm within 3 m calibrated range.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a practical, privacy-preserving, on-device multimodal visual assistant with personalized object search and multimodal feedback. The integration of multiple on-device models and optional LLM balances immediacy and description quality, though performance, energy use, and generalization to more objects and languages warrant further study.

title: Learning Spectral and Polarimetric Clues for One-to-Multimodal Novel View Synthesis
summary: Neural rendering techniques allow for accurate reconstruction of the geometry and color appearance of 3D scenes. Some methods have extended their use to additional imaging modalities, such as multispectral, infrared, or polarimetric data. However, all of these approaches require expensive sensors and calibrated setups to capture new multimodal frames for each new scene. We propose Spectral and Polarimetric Implicit Learned Representation (SPoILeR), a novel method to obtain multi-view consistent renderings of unconventional modalities for scenes where either only RGB frames or very few of the additional modalities are available. Thanks to a multimodal pre-training phase, the model learns the mutual correlation between different modalities. This step allows predicting accurate renderings of unconventional modalities during a fine-tuning phase supervised only by RGB images. Experimental results show that the approach can accurately render infrared, polarimetric, and multispectral frames for scenes where no input sample captured by these types of sensors is provided.

AI.tldr: A multimodal pre-trained implicit representation enables rendering infrared, polarimetric, and multispectral views from RGB-only inputs via cross-modal learning and RGB-supervised fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: High cost and calibration burden of capturing multimodal data; need accurate renderings of unconventional modalities for scenes where only RGB (or few modalities) are available.
AI.method: Train an implicit neural representation with a multimodal pre-training phase to learn cross-modal correlations across RGB, infrared, polarimetric, and multispectral data. During fine-tuning, only RGB supervision is used, but the model can predict other modalities (via modality-specific heads) by leveraging learned cross-modal relations, enforcing multi-view consistency.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate accurate rendering of infrared, polarimetric, and multispectral frames for scenes with no direct samples of these modalities, indicating strong cross-modal generalization and consistency.
AI.conclusion: SPoILeR reduces the need for costly multimodal sensors, enabling cross-modal rendering from RGB data; potential extensions include additional modalities, dynamic scenes, and robustness analyses; limitations may include dependence on the multimodal pre-training data distribution.

title: Representation Distribution Matching for One-Step Visual Generation
summary: We elucidate the design space of Representation Distribution Matching (RDM), our name for the paradigm that trains a one-step image generator by matching generated and reference feature distributions under frozen pretrained encoders. We identify two design axes, how the distributions are compared and the representations they are compared in, and controlled studies along them yield three findings. First, the classical MMD, which could not train convincing generators a decade ago, becomes a strong and scalable objective once estimated right. Second, the generated batch is then the operative variable, with an optimum above 2048, far beyond customary batch sizes. Third, any single representation can be gamed, driven below the real score while images stay visibly fake, so we match against a balanced battery of encoders and evaluate with SW_r14, a Sliced-Wasserstein distance over 14 encoders that is independent of the training loss and resists gaming. Combining the preferred choices yields improved RDM (iRDM): it sets the one-step state of the art on ImageNet at SW_r14 1.30, corroborated by PickScore, a human-preference proxy our objective never optimizes, which prefers it over the prior best one-step generator on 71.2% of matched samples. The same recipe post-trains the four-step FLUX.2 [klein] into a one-step generator, surpassing the four-step version on GenEval, 0.826 to 0.794, and on PickScore, 22.76 to 22.58, in 90 H200 GPU-hours. Project page: https://alan-lanfeng.github.io/rdm/.

AI.tldr: RDM identifies design axes for one-step image generation by matching generated and reference feature distributions with frozen encoders; proper MMD estimation, large batch sizes, and multi-encoder SW distance prevent gaming, yielding state-of-the-art iRDM and improvements to FLUX.2.
AI.motivation: Understand the design space of distribution-matching generators, address instability and gaming, and push one-step generation toward ImageNet-scale performance.
AI.method: Two design axes: how distributions are compared (MMD) and which representations are used (encoders). Use carefully estimated MMD, batch-size optimization (>2048), and a balanced battery of 14 encoders with SW_r14 distance; evaluate with SW distance and human proxies; apply to post-train FLUX.2 into a one-step generator.
AI.result: iRDM achieves ImageNet state-of-the-art on SW_r14 = 1.30 and PickScore favors it over prior one-step generator (71.2%). The approach also improves FLUX.2 to a one-step generator, outperforming the four-step version on GenEval (0.826 vs 0.794) and PickScore (22.76 vs 22.58) in 90 H200 GPU-hours.
AI.conclusion: Properly estimated MMD and multi-encoder SW-distance enable robust one-step generation; large batch sizes boost performance; the proposed iRDM provides a strong baseline and a practical recipe for high-quality single-step generators, validated by quantitative metrics and human-preference proxies.

title: Transformer Geometry Observatory TGO-II: Representational Similarity Observatory
summary: While Vision Transformers have achieved remarkable success across computer vision and language applications, the geometric evolution of their internal representations throughout training remains insufficiently understood. Existing analyses primarily focus on attention mechanisms and downstream performance, leaving the evolution of representation geometry largely unexplored. In this work, we present Transformer Geometry Observatory-II (TGO-II), a representation geometry analysis framework designed to investigate how Transformer representations evolve during supervised training. TGO-II analyzes Vision Transformer (ViT-Small/16) representations using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), Two-Nearest Neighbor Intrinsic Dimensionality (TwoNN-ID), and token covariance analysis. Our experiments reveal three key observations. First, both CKA and SVCCA progressively decrease throughout training, indicating increasing representational specialization across Transformer layers. Second, intrinsic dimensionality consistently increases before stabilizing, suggesting progressive expansion of the representation manifold into a larger set of locally accessible degrees of freedom. Third, token covariance and coupling analyses demonstrate that strong token interaction structure persists throughout training, challenging the hypothesis that increasing representational complexity arises primarily from progressive token independence. These findings suggest that representation complexity and layer specialization emerge simultaneously during training. Manifold expansion appears to occur without token decoupling. Together, these observations motivate a new hypothesis in which Vision Transformers increase representational complexity through progressively richer transformations while preserving strong token interaction structure during learning.

AI.tldr: TGO-II analyzes Vision Transformer geometry during supervised training, revealing decreasing CKA/SVCCA (increasing layer specialization), rising intrinsic dimensionality (manifold expansion), and persistent token interaction structure, implying simultaneous complexity growth without token decoupling.
AI.motivation: To understand how the representation geometry of Vision Transformers evolves during training beyond attention mechanisms and downstream performance.
AI.method: Apply the Transformer Geometry Observatory-II framework to ViT-Small/16 representations using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), Two-Nearest Neighbor Intrinsic Dimensionality (TwoNN-ID), and token covariance analysis across training.
AI.result: CKA and SVCCA decrease progressively, indicating increasing representational specialization across layers. Intrinsic dimensionality grows first and then stabilizes, suggesting expansion of the representation manifold. Token covariance and interaction structures remain strong throughout training, challenging the view that complexity arises from token independence. Overall, representation complexity and layer specialization emerge concurrently with manifold expansion but without token decoupling.
AI.conclusion: Vision Transformers may increase representational complexity through richer, more specialized transformations while preserving strong token interactions; this supports a hypothesis where learning drives simultaneous complexity growth and specialization without breaking token coupling.

title: Show Me Examples: Inferring Visual Concepts from Image Sets
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can follow complex textual instructions, yet they struggle to reason from purely visual context. In particular, current models fail to infer shared concepts from sets of example images and apply them to new inputs. We introduce Visual Concept Inference from Sets (VICIS), a task that evaluates this capability. Given a small context set of images sharing a concept and a query image, the model must generate new images that preserve the context-defined concept while remaining consistent with the query. We show that state-of-the-art VLMs perform poorly on this task, often ignoring the visual context or defaulting to biased generations. To address this gap, we propose a training framework and architecture that learn to infer visual concepts from image sets and extract concept-specific embeddings from queries. Experiments on synthetic data and large-scale ImageNet/WordNet data show that our model generates more accurate and diverse outputs and generalizes to unseen concepts and modalities such as sketches.

AI.tldr: Introduces VICIS, a benchmark for inferring shared concepts from image sets and generating query-consistent images; state-of-the-art VLMs underperform; presents a training framework and architecture that learns set-based visual concept inference and concept-specific embeddings; experiments show improved accuracy, diversity, and generalization to unseen concepts and sketch-like modalities.
AI.motivation: Current VLMs struggle to reason from purely visual context and to infer concepts that are common across a set of example images. There is a gap between perceptual similarity in sets and applying inferred concepts to new queries.
AI.method: Define the VICIS task and develop a training framework and architecture that aggregate information from image sets to infer visual concepts, and extract concept-specific embeddings from query images. Train on synthetic data and large-scale ImageNet/WordNet data; evaluate the ability to generate outputs that reflect the context-defined concepts while remaining aligned with the query.
AI.result: The proposed model generates more accurate and diverse outputs and generalizes to unseen concepts and modalities (e.g., sketches) better than baselines.
AI.conclusion: Inferring visual concepts from image sets is feasible and beneficial for VLMs. The VICIS framework provides a viable path to improve concept reasoning from sets, with potential extensions to additional modalities and broader concept categories.

title: Object-centric LeJEPA
summary: Image encoders trained with LeJEPA can deliver strong features for downstream tasks, but, like other image-level self-supervised methods, typically require large training datasets. Aligning representations at the level of objects rather than whole scenes promises greater data efficiency, but doing this in a completely self-supervised way, effectively jointly partitioning a scene and representing its objects, is unstable: the two are locked in a cyclic dependency, partitioning requires meaningful representations, while meaningful representations require consistent partitioning. We sidestep this instability by taking object masks as given during training, using cheap, off-the-shelf SAM proposals. We extend LeJEPA - whose distributional anti-collapse objective ports naturally from whole images to variable-sized sets of objects - to align object-centric representations rather than whole images. An additional instance-separating loss, which treats other objects in the same scene as negatives, further boosts downstream performance. Across two model scales and 10-100% of COCO, object-level LeJEPA outperforms image-level LeJEPA on tracking (DAVIS), classification (ImageNet-1k), segmentation (ADE20k), and re-identification (NAVI).

AI.tldr: Object-level LeJEPA uses fixed SAM masks to align object-centric representations with a distributional anti-collapse objective and an instance-negatives loss, improving data efficiency and outperforming image-level LeJEPA across DAVIS, ImageNet-1k, ADE20k, and NAVI when trained on 10-100% COCO.
AI.motivation: Image-level self-supervised methods typically need large datasets; object-centric alignment promises better data efficiency but is unstable due to a cyclic dependency between segmentation/partitioning and representation quality. Providing masks sidesteps this instability.
AI.method: Extend LeJEPA's distributional anti-collapse objective to variable-sized sets of objects. Train using provided object masks from SAM proposals. Add an instance-separating loss that treats other objects in the same scene as negatives. Evaluate across two model scales on 10-100% of COCO, comparing to the image-level baseline.
AI.result: Object-centric LeJEPA outperforms image-level LeJEPA across tasks: tracking (DAVIS), classification (ImageNet-1k), segmentation (ADE20k), and re-identification (NAVI). Gains observed across two model scales and partial COCO data (10-100%).
AI.conclusion: Using fixed object masks to guide object-centric self-supervised learning with a distributional anti-collapse objective and instance negatives yields stronger, more data-efficient representations than image-level self-supervision, with broad cross-task gains.

title: Wavelet-Guided Semantic Signal Compensation for Inversion-Free Image Editing
summary: Text-guided image editing aims to modify visual content according to a target prompt while preserving the background. Recent inversion-free image editing frameworks such as FlowEdit have demonstrated strong editing capability without requiring inversion. Empirically, FlowEdit can achieve substantial semantic changes under appropriate hyperparameter settings. However, we observe that under certain global attribute shifts, the editing trajectory may not effectively move away from the source distribution in the early timesteps. Our analysis suggests that in the high-noise regime, the dominant manifold-seeking flow toward the data manifold can reduce the influence of the text-conditioned direction, leading to limited global modification while background structures remain only moderately preserved. Inspired by this observation, we propose an inversion-free, frequency-aware semantic compensation strategy that strengthens the effective signal in the early stage of generation, while maintaining structural consistency in the background. The proposed method improves global editing capacity without sacrificing background fidelity.

AI.tldr: A frequency-aware inversion-free editing method that enhances early-stage semantic signals to boost global edits while preserving background fidelity.
AI.motivation: Inversion-free editors like FlowEdit can struggle with global attribute shifts; in high-noise regimes, the dominant data-manifold flow dominates early steps, diminishing text-conditioned directions and limiting global changes.
AI.method: Propose an inversion-free, frequency-aware semantic compensation strategy that strengthens the effective signal in early generation steps, by adjusting signal across frequency components to bias toward the target prompt without disrupting background structure.
AI.result: Improved global editing capacity with preserved background fidelity compared to baseline inversion-free methods under challenging prompts.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-aware semantic compensation effectively mitigates early-stage manifold attraction, enabling stronger, more global edits in inversion-free diffusion-based image editing.

title: Learning to Evolve Scenes: Reasoning about Human Activities with Scene Graphs
summary: Understanding human behavior while interacting with the surrounding world is crucial for many applications of embodied AI. First-person videos are particularly informative for this problem, as they well capture how activities reshape the scene over time. However, existing approaches often rely on implicit visual or language-aligned representations, disregarding structured reasoning over the scene dynamic. We argue that explicit, compositional and editable representations of human-environment interactions can play a crucial role for rich grounded activity understanding. To this end, we introduce SG-Ego, a large scale annotation set extending Ego4D with spatio-temporal scene graphs, where relations triplets are consolidated over time into explicit time-evolving descriptions of the scene state. To reason over this representation, we propose GLEN, a graph-based model that operates over scene graph sequences to both align them with textual actions and model their temporal evolution. In addition, we formulate the activity-driven graph-edit forecasting (A-GEF) problem, a novel task that casts scene dynamics as a sequence of structured transformations conditioned on ongoing actions, enabling explicit reasoning about how scenes change over time. We validate our approach across multiple downstream tasks, spanning retrieval benchmarks as EgoMCQ and EgoCVR, as well as long-horizon reasoning benchmarks as EXPLORE-Bench and the newly introduced A-GEF. GLEN achieves strong results compared to raw video baselines and it excels in reasoning settings, typically addressed only with MLLMs, while enabling controllable and structured predictions of scene dynamics driven by human activities. We believe our results establish spatio-temporal scene graphs, together with models that reason over them, as strong compositional and interpretable representations for video understanding and potentially beyond.

AI.tldr: Proposes SG-Ego with spatio-temporal scene graphs for first-person video understanding, a graph-based model GLEN for aligning scene graphs with text and modeling temporal evolution, and a novel A-GEF forecasting task; demonstrates strong performance on retrieval and long-horizon reasoning benchmarks, favoring explicit, compositional representations.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of implicit, view-specific representations by adopting explicit, editable, compositional scene graphs to reason about human–environment interactions and their dynamics in egocentric videos.
AI.method: 1) Construct SG-Ego, a large-scale annotation set extending Ego4D with time-evolving scene graphs. 2) Propose GLEN, a graph-based model that operates on graph sequences to align with textual actions and capture temporal evolution. 3) Define Activity-driven Graph-Edit Forecasting (A-GEF), forecasting structured scene-dynamics as transformations conditioned on ongoing actions. 4) Evaluate on tasks including EgoMCQ, EgoCVR, EXPLORE-Bench, and A-GEF.
AI.result: GLEN achieves strong performance versus raw video baselines, particularly in reasoning settings typically tackled by large language models, and enables controllable, structured predictions of scene dynamics driven by activities.
AI.conclusion: Spatio-temporal scene graphs, combined with graph-based reasoning models, offer a strong, interpretable, and editable representation for video understanding and potentially beyond; they support both accurate grounding and explicit forecasting of human–scene interactions.

title: MARVEL: Margin-Aware Robust von Mises-Fischer Expert Learning for Long-Tailed Out-of-Distribution Detection
summary: For clinical deployment, it is essential that automated diagnostic systems remain reliable when confronted with previously unseen cases, yet deep models routinely misclassify out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs with high confidence, underscoring the need for more robust OOD detection methods. Although substantial effort has been devoted to improving model robustness, most of the existing literature assumes balanced datasets, evaluates OOD detection on coarse or non-clinical OOD sources, or lacks comprehensive assessment across diverse OOD scenarios. To address the gaps, we propose a novel methodology trained on diverse and imbalanced medical datasets and evaluated across a clinically reflective OOD spectrum. Our framework comprises three key components: (1) a Nonlinear von Mises-Fisher (NvMF) classifier capable of learning non-linear decision boundaries, with theoretical proof of its asymptotic connection to cosine classifiers; (2) a multi-expert framework in which margin-aware NvMF classifiers specialise in different regions of label distribution to better handle imbalance; and (3) an outlier expert trained explicitly to distinguish inlier from outlier data, thereby strengthening OOD detection. Evaluation on RFMiD, ISIC2019, and NCTCRC datasets demonstrates consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, achieving mean FPR95 reductions of 8.45%, 13.02%, and 36.90% respectively. These gains are further supported by comprehensive ablations that validated the contributions of each component. This enables reliable identification of unfamiliar cases for deferral to clinicians, supporting safer AI-assisted diagnosis in real-world workflows. Our code is available at https://github.com/redboxup/MARVEL.

AI.tldr: Proposes MARVEL: a three-component OOD-detection framework for medical AI combining nonlinear NvMF, a multi-expert imbalance-aware setup, and an outlier expert, yielding notable FPR95 reductions across three medical datasets.
AI.motivation: Clinical deployment requires reliable OOD detection; existing work often assumes balanced data, uses coarse or non-clinical OOD sources, and lacks diverse evaluation across OOD scenarios.
AI.method: 1) Nonlinear von Mises-Fisher (NvMF) classifier learning non-linear decision boundaries with an asymptotic link to cosine classifiers; 2) a multi-expert framework with margin-aware NvMF classifiers specializing in different regions of the label distribution to handle imbalance; 3) an outlier expert trained to distinguish inliers from outliers to strengthen OOD detection.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on RFMiD, ISIC2019, and NCTCRC shows consistent improvements with mean FPR95 reductions of 8.45%, 13.02%, and 36.90% respectively; comprehensive ablations validate each component's contribution; code is available at the provided URL.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables reliable identification of unfamiliar cases for deferral to clinicians, supporting safer AI-assisted diagnosis in real-world workflows; demonstrates robustness of OOD detection under diverse clinical conditions.

title: OrbitQuant: Data-Agnostic Quantization for Image and Video Diffusion Transformers
summary: Diffusion transformers (DiTs) achieve state-of-the-art image and video generation, but their multi-step sampling and growing parameter count make inference expensive. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is the natural remedy, yet DiT activations shift across timesteps, prompts, and guidance branches, forcing prior methods to re-fit calibration data for every new checkpoint or modality. We present OrbitQuant, a data-agnostic weight-activation quantizer that bypasses range estimation by quantizing in a normalized, rotated basis. In this basis, a randomized permuted block-Hadamard (RPBH) rotation concentrates each coordinate around one fixed, known marginal regardless of the input, so a single Lloyd-Max codebook serves all timesteps, prompts, and layers of a given input dimension. We extend the same quantizer to weight rows offline, absorbing the rotation into the weights so that it cancels inside each linear layer and only a forward rotation on the activations remains at runtime. The same recipe transfers from image to video with no per-modality tuning. Across FLUX.1, Z-Image-Turbo, Wan 2.1, and CogVideoX, it sets the state of the art for PTQ at several low-bit settings. It also pushes PTQ of image diffusion transformers to W2A4 with usable generation quality.

AI.tldr: OrbitQuant is a data-agnostic PTQ method for diffusion transformers that uses a randomized permuted block-Hadamard rotation to normalize activations, enabling a single codebook for all timesteps, prompts, and layers and canceling rotations offline in weights. It achieves state-of-the-art PTQ performance across multiple diffusion models and modalities, including image and video, at very low bit-widths (up to W2A4).
AI.motivation: Diffusion transformers achieve high-quality generation but incur expensive inference due to multi-step sampling and growing parameter count. Existing PTQ methods require per-checkpoint or per-modality calibration because activations shift across timesteps, prompts, and guidance branches.
AI.method: Apply RP-Hadamard rotation to activations to concentrate each coordinate around a fixed marginal, enabling a single Lloyd-Max codebook to quantize activations across timesteps/prompts/layers. Absorb the same rotation into weights offline so it cancels within each linear layer; at runtime only a forward rotation on activations remains. The approach is data-agnostic and transferable from image to video without per-modality tuning.
AI.result: OrbitQuant achieves state-of-the-art PTQ performance for several low-bit settings across multiple diffusion-model benchmarks (FLUX.1, Z-Image-Turbo, Wan 2.1, CogVideoX), and pushes PTQ of image diffusion transformers to W2A4 with usable generation quality.
AI.conclusion: A data-agnostic PTQ framework for diffusion transformers is feasible and effective, enabling cross-modality PTQ without calibration data re-fitting. OrbitQuant reduces calibration overhead and maintains generation quality at very low bit-widths, with potential applicability to other transformer-based diffusion models.

title: Interpretation-Oriented Cloud Removal via Observation-Anchored Residual Flow with Geo-Contextual Alignment
summary: Cloud removal (CR) is essential for optical remote sensing, serving as a prerequisite for reliable downstream interpretation, such as semantic segmentation and change detection. However, existing CR approaches often prioritize visual realism while overlooking their impact on subsequent analytical tasks, leading to semantic drift and degraded downstream performance. To address this issue, we propose Geo-Anchored Cloud Removal (GACR), a unified framework that jointly ensures faithful reconstruction and robust interpretability. At its core, GACR incorporates Observation-Anchored Residual Flow (OAR-Flow), which reformulates CR as a physically grounded residual inversion process. By anchoring the generative trajectory to the cloudy observation rather than pure noise, OAR-Flow enables fast, stable, and faithful reconstruction. To further preserve semantic structures critical for downstream interpretation, GACR integrates Geo-Contextual Prior Alignment (GCPA) to constrain the reconstruction within a semantic manifold induced by a Vision Foundation Model (VFM). Consequently, GACR strictly maintains the spatial-semantic integrity of complex landscapes. Extensive experiments across six CR datasets and twelve downstream tasks demonstrate that GACR produces superior reconstruction quality while consistently improving downstream task accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/wzy6055/GACR.

AI.tldr: GACR is a unified cloud removal framework that preserves semantic structure for downstream tasks by combining observation-anchored residual flow (OAR-Flow) with geo-contextual prior alignment (GCPA); it achieves better reconstruction and downstream accuracy.
AI.motivation: Current cloud removal methods optimize visual realism but often degrade downstream analyses due to semantic drift; there is a need for a CR method that preserves semantic integrity while enabling faithful reconstruction.
AI.method: Propose OAR-Flow to invert the clouding process via residual flow anchored to the observed cloudy image; integrate Geo-Contextual Prior Alignment (GCPA) to constrain reconstruction within a semantic manifold induced by a Vision Foundation Model; train end-to-end to balance reconstruction fidelity and semantic consistency.
AI.result: Demonstrated on six cloud removal datasets and twelve downstream tasks; GACR achieves superior reconstruction quality and consistently improves downstream task accuracy.
AI.conclusion: GACR maintains spatial-semantic integrity and enhances robustness of downstream analyses; code for reproduction is provided.

title: EAGLE-360: Embodied Active Global-to-Local Exploration in 360$^\circ$
summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in standard visual understanding, adapting them for active visual search in 360$^\circ$ panoramic environments exposes fundamental limitations. Specifically, standard MLLMs struggle to effectively model inherent panoramic properties, such as severe polar distortion and continuous cylindrical topologies, which significantly degrades target detection accuracy. Consequently, existing panoramic search methods attempt to compensate by relying heavily on fragmented local viewpoints. Burdened by rigid initialization and a lack of global panoramic priors, these approaches suffer from myopic, inefficient exploration and struggle with robust error recovery when targets are out of view. To overcome these challenges, we propose EAGLE-360, a novel Embodied Active Global-to-Local Exploration framework. Rather than performing exhaustive local searches, EAGLE-360 leverages global priors to establish an initial holistic perspective, iteratively reasoning and progressively narrowing the search space. Architecturally, we adapt RoPE Rolling, a coordinate-shifting positional encoding mechanism, to seamlessly model the continuous topologies of panoramas. To facilitate this paradigm, we construct the large-scale EAGLE-360 dataset, comprising 14,000+ 4K panoramas and 70,000+ rounds of high-quality VQA dialogues. By employing a training pipeline that integrates Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), we effectively elicit complex spatial reasoning and tool-calling capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EAGLE-360 establishes a new state-of-the-art for 360$^\circ$ visual search, achieving nearly an 8-fold increase in accuracy over the base model while significantly enhancing exploration efficiency.

AI.tldr: EAGLE-360 is an Embodied Active Global-to-Local Exploration framework for 360° visual search. It uses global priors and RoPE Rolling to model continuous panoramic topology, builds a large panoramic-VQA dataset, and combines SFT with GRPO to achieve state-of-the-art search performance with far more efficient exploration.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs struggle with panoramic distortions and continuous cylindrical topologies in 360° environments, leading to myopic local-view searches and poor error recovery. There is a need for global panoramic priors and representations that can guide efficient, robust active search.
AI.method: Propose EAGLE-360: an embodied, global-to-local search framework that starts from a holistic global perspective using priors, iteratively reasons and narrows the search space. Architectural novelty includes RoPE Rolling for coordinate-shifting positional encoding to model continuous panorama topology. Construct a large EAGLE-360 dataset (14k+ 4K panoramas, 70k+ high-quality VQA dialogues). Train via a pipeline combining Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to elicit spatial reasoning and tool-calling capabilities.
